entries.heading: NPU, VPU & LPU: What They Are and How They Differ
entries.text: "NPU", "VPU", and "LPU" name overlapping classes of AI accelerator. GPU and NPU are the established terms; VPU and LPU are largely vendor labels. The one axis that explains most of the differences is how much generality each design trades away for performance-per-watt or deterministic latency. NPU

entries.heading: Neural Processing Unit
entries.text: Dedicated neural-inference accelerator, usually an IP block inside a mobile or PC SoC. MAC / systolic arrays plus small on-chip SRAM, integer-native (INT8/INT4). Optimizes inferences-per-watt at unit batch. Examples: Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon, Intel/AMD PC NPUs. VPU

entries.heading: Vision Processing Unit
entries.text: Low-power (sub-1.5 W) CNN/vision accelerator for edge and embedded devices: SIMD/VLIW DSP cores, fixed-function image signal processing, and direct camera interfaces. Intel Movidius Myriad X, Hailo-8, Mobileye EyeQ. Increasingly folded into the term "NPU". LPU

entries.heading: Language Processing Unit
entries.text: Groq's deterministic, compiler-scheduled Tensor Streaming Processor. SRAM-only (~230 MB at ~80 TB/s), no HBM, no caches or reactive schedulers. Wins single-stream, jitter-free LLM decoding, but a real model must be sharded across many chips. GPU

entries.heading: Graphics Processing Unit
entries.text: Fully programmable, massively-parallel SIMT engine backed by off-chip HBM (CUDA / ROCm). Dominates training and high-throughput batched inference at hundreds of watts. The flexible, high-power end of the spectrum. Examples: NVIDIA H100 / B200. TPU

entries.heading: Tensor Processing Unit
entries.text: Google's systolic-array ASIC (128×128 weight-stationary MXU, bfloat16 × FP32 accumulate). Cloud TPU pods do training and serving; the Coral Edge TPU is the INT8, ~2 W sibling — same compute principle, opposite end of the deployment spectrum. Caveat

entries.heading: Naming & the TOPS trap
entries.text: VPU and NPU overlap: Intel rebranded its Movidius "VPU" block to "NPU" in Meteor Lake with no technology change. When comparing accelerators, always check precision — INT8 TOPS is not comparable to INT4 or FP16 TOPS, and peak TOPS rarely reflects real, memory-bound throughput. OpenAI-compatible GroqCloud API These accelerators trade generality for efficiency along a clear axis: GPUs are fully programmable HBM-backed engines that dominate training and batched inference at high power, while NPUs and VPUs sacrifice programmability for extreme performance-per-watt on quantized inference at the edge (VPU being the vision/CNN-specialized subclass increasingly folded into "NPU"). Groq's LPU sits at the opposite extreme from the GPU: a deterministic, compiler-scheduled, SRAM-only design that wins single-stream LLM latency but must shard models across many chips because each holds only ~230 MB. The core trade-offs are memory model (off-chip HBM vs on-chip SRAM/scratchpad), throughput vs latency bias, and programmability vs fixed-function efficiency, with "VPU" and "LPU" being largely vendor-specific labels versus the more established GPU/NPU terms. entries.heading: How AI Accelerators Are Deployed
entries.text: The same trained model can target a phone, a laptop NPU, an edge camera, or a datacenter GPU. What changes is the memory model, the power budget, and the runtime/execution-provider layer that dispatches operators to the device with CPU fallback. Mobile SoC

entries.heading: ~1–5 W, unified LPDDR
entries.text: An integrated NPU (Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon, MediaTek APU, Google Tensor) shares unified memory with the CPU/GPU and runs INT8/INT4 for camera pipelines, speech, and small on-device LLMs. Edge / embedded

entries.heading: Single-digit W, SRAM + sensors
entries.text: VPUs and small NPUs (Movidius, Coral Edge TPU, Jetson, Mobileye EyeQ) use SRAM scratchpads and direct sensor interfaces for vision, robotics, and ADAS, keeping inference off the cloud. AI PC

entries.heading: 40+ TOPS in laptop thermals
entries.text: Copilot+ PCs mandate a 40+ TOPS integrated NPU (for example Intel Core Ultra 200V / Series 2, AMD Ryzen AI 300, and Snapdragon X / X2 platforms) to offload on-device AI from the CPU/iGPU for battery efficiency. Datacenter

entries.text: Discrete GPUs, TPUs, and LPUs with multi-GB HBM and rack-scale interconnect (NVLink, ICI, RealScale) handle large-scale training and high-throughput batched serving. In ONNX Runtime, each backend (CUDA, TensorRT, OpenVINO, QNN, CoreML, NNAPI, DirectML) is a pluggable execution provider: the graph is partitioned, each subgraph is assigned to the best available EP, and unsupported operators fall back to the CPU. entries.heading: LLVM & MLIR for AI Compilers
entries.text: Modern AI compilers do the tensor-level work (fusion, tiling, quantization, dataflow mapping) in a high-level, domain-specific IR, then lower to LLVM for mature scalar/vector code generation. MLIR is the multi-level IR that makes this progressive lowering practical — and it is an LLVM sub-project.

entries.heading: LLVM IR and the three-stage pipeline
entries.text: LLVM IR is a strongly-typed, three-address, SSA-form virtual instruction set. Its single-definition property makes use-def chains trivial, so passes like constant propagation, GVN, and dead-code elimination are simple. The pipeline is front-end (Clang, rustc) → middle-end ( opt ) → back-end ( llc : instruction selection, register allocation, codegen), all centered on IR.

entries.heading: Why ML stacks reuse LLVM as a terminal back-end
entries.text: Graph- and tensor-level concerns are best solved in a higher-level IR where the semantics are still visible. Once resolved, stacks lower to LLVM IR to inherit its mature scalar/vector optimization, register allocation, and code emission (including NVPTX and AMDGPU for GPUs). XLA, Triton, IREE, and TorchInductor all follow this "lower, then hand off to LLVM" pattern.

entries.heading: MLIR dialects and progressive lowering
entries.text: MLIR has no fixed opcode set: dialects ( tosa , linalg , affine , scf , vector , memref , gpu , llvm ) coexist in one module and are lowered gradually. Domain semantics — tensors, convolutions, tiling structure — survive as long as they are useful, then are lowered away. Tiling and fusion run on immutable linalg tensors, where they are provably safe; bufferization runs later.

entries.heading: Where NPU vendors intercept
entries.text: Because MLIR is multi-level, a vendor can intercept at the abstraction that matches their hardware (commonly linalg or a custom dialect), inject micro-kernels and dataflow mappings, and reuse upstream tiling, fusion, and bufferization instead of rebuilding a compiler. The llvm dialect is the near-1:1 convergence point back to LLVM IR. TableGen then makes standing up a new NPU or DSP back-end largely declarative.

entries.heading: Technical Deep Dive: A Grid-of-Cores NPU
entries.text: TT-Metalium exposes more hardware detail than a typical framework runtime, which makes it valuable for study: the programmer sees where compiler decisions land — core placement, tile layout, SRAM buffering, NoC transfers, and kernel synchronization.

entries.heading: 1. Tensix is a grid-first accelerator model
entries.text: Tenstorrent describes the accelerator as a grid of specialized compute nodes called Tensix cores. Each core includes local L1 SRAM, two NoC interfaces, data movement control, a matrix engine/FPU, a vector engine/SFPU, pack/unpack hardware, and small RISC-V controllers that issue commands to those engines. This is different from CUDA-style SIMT thinking. Instead of hiding latency behind many threads, the Metalium mental model is software-pipelined dataflow: explicitly move tiles, overlap movement with compute, and keep useful intermediate data close to the core.

entries.heading: 2. The basic operation is reader -> compute -> writer
entries.text: A typical TT-Metalium program creates three kernel roles. The reader data-movement kernel moves tiles from DRAM or another core into L1 circular buffers. The compute kernel waits on those buffers, runs tile operations through FPU/SFPU engines, and pushes output tiles to another circular buffer. The writer data-movement kernel drains output tiles and writes them back to DRAM or sends them onward. The compiler lesson is direct: an NPU backend is not only selecting arithmetic instructions. It must schedule producer-consumer movement, buffer capacity, tile order, and synchronization so compute does not stall on memory.

entries.heading: 3. Circular buffers are the local synchronization contract
entries.text: Circular buffers are small FIFO queues in core-local SRAM. They are the connection point between data movement kernels and compute kernels. Calls such as cb_reserve_back , get_write_ptr , cb_push_back , cb_wait_front , and cb_pop_front express producer-consumer ownership. In performance terms, the circular buffer depth controls how much movement and compute can overlap. Too little buffering starves compute. Too much buffering wastes scarce L1 SRAM that could hold other intermediate data.

entries.heading: 4. Tiles and page size are core compiler concerns
entries.text: Tenstorrent hardware is optimized around tiled tensors. A common tile shape is 32x32 elements. A tensor may be converted from row-major host layout into a tiled layout so the matrix/vector engines can consume data efficiently. Padding can be required when dimensions are not tile aligned. This makes page_size , tensor layout, tilization, untilization, and sharding more than storage details. They become backend decisions that affect NoC traffic, L1 residency, and whether the compute engine receives data in the shape it wants.

entries.heading: 5. NoC and memory placement replace hidden caches
entries.text: TT-Metalium documentation emphasizes explicit data placement. The model is not "trust the cache." DRAM, local L1 SRAM, remote core SRAM, interleaved buffers, and sharded tensors are visible design choices. The NoC moves data between those locations. For an NPU compiler engineer, this maps to locality decisions: keep reused blocks close to the consuming core, use multicast when many cores need the same data, shard tensors when the access pattern matches the core grid, and avoid unnecessary trips to DRAM.

entries.heading: 6. Work distribution is explicit SPMD
entries.text: TT-Metalium supports SPMD, but the developer or compiler decides which cores receive work and which runtime arguments each core sees. Utilities such as split_work_to_cores help divide tiles across available cores, but the program still needs correct per-core arguments. This is exactly where compiler scheduling meets runtime setup: a graph partition becomes core ranges, tile ranges, reader/writer offsets, per-core work counts, and no-op behavior for unused cores. entries.heading: TT-Metalium Terms to Know
entries.text: This glossary turns Tenstorrent documentation terms into NPU compiler study notes.

entries.heading: Tensix processor
entries.text: The full accelerator chip or device organization built from a grid of nodes, including Tensix compute cores plus memory, PCIe, Ethernet, and management nodes.

entries.heading: Tensix core
entries.text: The compute tile/node. It contains local L1 SRAM, NoC interfaces, RISC-V controllers, matrix/vector engines, and pack/unpack hardware.

entries.heading: L1 SRAM
entries.text: Core-local scratchpad memory used for circular buffers, temporary tiles, and kernel code. It is explicit storage, not a transparent cache.

entries.heading: NoC
entries.text: Network-on-Chip. The on-chip interconnect used to move data among DRAM, Tensix cores, and other device resources.

entries.heading: Tile
entries.text: A hardware-friendly tensor block, commonly 32x32 elements, used by matrix and vector engines for efficient local computation.

entries.heading: Tilize / untilize
entries.text: Conversion between row-major host-style layout and Tenstorrent tiled layout. This can happen on device to reduce host-side overhead.

entries.heading: Circular buffer (CB)
entries.text: A small FIFO queue in L1 SRAM. Reader, compute, and writer kernels use CBs to exchange tiles safely and asynchronously.

entries.heading: Reader kernel
entries.text: A data movement kernel that usually reads tiles from DRAM or another core into input circular buffers.

entries.heading: Compute kernel
entries.text: The kernel that issues FPU/SFPU work, consumes input circular buffers, writes destination registers, and packs result tiles.

entries.heading: Writer kernel
entries.text: A data movement kernel that waits for output circular buffers and writes result tiles to DRAM or another destination.

entries.heading: FPU / matrix engine
entries.text: The matrix/tensor computation engine used for tile operations such as matmul and elementwise arithmetic.

entries.heading: SFPU / vector engine
entries.text: The vector unit for scalar/vector style functions such as exp, log, sin, comparisons, and custom SFPI operations.

entries.heading: Pack / unpack
entries.text: Hardware stages that move tiles between circular buffers, engine registers, and output buffers in the format the engines expect.

entries.heading: Runtime arguments
entries.text: Per-kernel and per-core parameters such as buffer addresses, tile counts, work offsets, and core-specific ranges.

entries.heading: SPMD
entries.text: Single Program, Multiple Data. Multiple cores run the same kernel program with different runtime arguments and tile ranges.

entries.heading: Multicast
entries.text: A data movement pattern that sends the same data to multiple cores, useful for reuse in multi-core matmul and attention-like workloads.

entries.heading: Interleaved memory
entries.text: A default memory placement style that spreads pages across memory controllers for balanced access.

entries.heading: Sharded tensor
entries.text: A tensor distributed across multiple Tensix cores or memory regions to improve locality and reduce long-distance data movement.

entries.heading: Fast dispatch
entries.text: An asynchronous command queue mode where the device processes queued work, reducing host CPU involvement compared with slow dispatch.

entries.heading: Accelerators: VPU, LPU, NPU & GPU (10)
entries.text: 1. What is a Neural Processing Unit (NPU), and how does its design goal differ from that of a CPU and a GPU? Basic An NPU is a domain-specific accelerator optimized for the dense linear algebra (matrix-multiply and convolution) at the heart of neural-network inference. Unlike a CPU, which is latency-optimized and general-purpose, and a GPU, which is a throughput-optimized SIMT engine built for both training and inference, an NPU trades generality for extreme energy efficiency (TOPS per watt) on quantized, low-precision math. Most consumer NPUs are IP blocks integrated into a mobile or PC SoC (Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon, Arm Ethos, Intel/AMD PC NPUs), sharing system DRAM and thermal budget with the CPU and GPU. The design point is inferences-per-watt at small batch sizes, not peak FLOPS or large-batch throughput. 2. What does the TOPS metric measure, and why is a headline TOPS number an unreliable way to compare two accelerators? Basic TOPS is Tera-Operations-Per-Second, and headline figures are almost always quoted for peak INT8 throughput, scaling roughly with (number of MACs x clock x 2), since a multiply-accumulate counts as two ops. It is unreliable first because it is precision-dependent: INT8 TOPS is not comparable to INT4 or FP16 TOPS, so numbers are only meaningful at equal precision. Second, peak TOPS is a theoretical ceiling that rarely reflects effective throughput (ops actually executed divided by latency), because real workloads are usually memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. This gap is especially large for LLM decode, where the autoregressive, one-token-at-a-time pattern is dominated by weight-fetch bandwidth, not MAC utilization. 3. What is a Vision Processing Unit (VPU), and why has the term become largely interchangeable with 'NPU'? Basic A VPU is a class of AI accelerator purpose-built to run computer-vision and CNN inference at very low power (typically sub-1.5 W) for edge and embedded devices, exemplified by Intel's Movidius Myriad 2 and Myriad X. Architecturally it combines arrays of programmable SIMD/VLIW vector DSP cores (Movidius 'SHAVE' cores) with fixed-function ISP and vision hardware, large on-chip scratchpad, and direct camera interfaces, all tuned for inferences-per-watt rather than absolute throughput. The terms converged because Intel historically branded Movidius silicon a 'VPU,' but when it integrated a Movidius-derived inference block into Meteor Lake / Core Ultra CPUs it rebranded that block an 'NPU' with no fundamental technology change. So 'VPU' and 'NPU' are overlapping, largely marketing-driven names for the same broad low-power inference category, with 'VPU' foregrounding vision/CNN heritage and 'NPU' being the now-dominant general term. 4. What is a systolic array, and why is it the canonical datapath for tensor accelerators like the Google TPU? Intermediate A systolic array is a 2D grid of processing elements (multiply-accumulate units) through which operands and partial sums flow rhythmically between neighbors, so each data element is reused across many PEs as it propagates. This maximizes data reuse and minimizes traffic to the register file and SRAM, which is critical because memory movement, not the multiply itself, dominates energy in dense matrix multiply. Google's TPU Matrix Multiply Unit is the canonical example: a 128x128 (16,384 MAC) systolic array in current generations, with the Edge TPU using a smaller array on the same principle. The array is fed by a chosen stationarity (the TPU is weight-stationary, preloading and holding weights in the PEs while activations stream through) that the compiler matches to the operand-reuse pattern of the workload. 5. Contrast the memory model of an integrated SoC NPU with that of a discrete datacenter accelerator such as a Cloud TPU or datacenter GPU. Why does this distinction matter for a compiler engineer? Intermediate An integrated SoC NPU shares the system's LPDDR/DRAM with the CPU and GPU under a unified-memory model: there is no explicit host-to-device copy, but bandwidth is limited and contended, so the NPU leans heavily on small managed on-chip SRAM scratchpads to keep weights and tiles resident. A discrete accelerator has its own dedicated high-bandwidth memory (HBM or GDDR, tens of GB at TB/s), requires explicit host-device transfers over PCIe or NVLink, and draws hundreds of watts for orders of magnitude more compute. For a compiler this shapes tiling and memory planning: on an integrated NPU you tile aggressively to fit tiny SRAM and schedule around shared-bus contention, whereas on a discrete part you plan HBM staging, double-buffered DMA, and host-device transfer overlap. It also drives roofline reasoning, since the two tiers have very different memory-bandwidth ceilings. 6. Why do many NPUs require quantization to run a model at all, and how do PTQ and QAT differ in achieving it? Intermediate Many NPU MAC arrays are integer-native, so quantization is part of the compiler rather than an optional pass; Qualcomm's Hexagon backend in QNN, for example, accepts only quantized graphs (int8/int16, uint8/uint16) expressed as Quantize-Dequantize (QDQ) graphs, and FP32 must be converted before it can execute. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) converts a trained FP model to INT8/INT4 directly, using a small calibration dataset to pick activation ranges via min-max, entropy/KL, or percentile methods; it is fast and needs no retraining but degrades at very low bit-widths. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) inserts fake-quant nodes and fine-tunes so weights adapt to rounding, recovering accuracy at INT4/FP4 where PTQ falls off. Granularity also matters: per-tensor is cheapest, per-channel is standard for convolutions, and per-block schemes like NVFP4/MXFP are emerging for LLMs. 7. The Microsoft Copilot+ PC program sets a 40+ TOPS NPU bar. Which vendor NPUs currently clear it, and how does software on Windows actually dispatch a model to the NPU? Intermediate Qualcomm's Snapdr

entries.heading: Deployment & Systems (10)
entries.text: 11. Walk me through the canonical export-and-deploy pipeline that takes a trained PyTorch/TensorFlow model to a target accelerator. What are the distinct stages? Basic The common pipeline has five stages. (1) Train in a framework (PyTorch/TensorFlow/JAX); (2) export the model to an interchange graph IR such as ONNX, StableHLO, TorchScript, or Core ML; (3) compile and optimize for the specific target, which includes post-training INT8/INT4 quantization with calibration plus operator fusion and layout canonicalization; (4) load the compiled artifact into a runtime or execution-provider abstraction that partitions the graph and dispatches ops to the device; and (5) execute on hardware. The export-to-interchange step is what decouples the framework from the backend, and the runtime/EP layer is the portability abstraction that lets one exported model target many devices with CPU fallback for unsupported ops. 12. Contrast latency-optimized versus throughput-optimized inference deployment. Where does batching fit, and what is the fundamental tradeoff? Basic Latency-optimized serving minimizes time-to-result for a single request (small or unit batch), which is what interactive/on-device workloads and autoregressive LLM decode need; throughput-optimized serving maximizes aggregate requests processed per second, which is how datacenter GPUs and TPUs are typically run. Batching is the primary lever for throughput: grouping requests amortizes weight loads and keeps the MAC/systolic array well-fed, raising arithmetic intensity and hardware utilization. The tradeoff is that larger batches increase per-request tail latency, because a request may wait to fill a batch and then shares compute with others. Edge NPUs deliberately optimize inferences-per-watt at unit batch, while Groq's LPU is an extreme latency point that flattens per-token latency with deterministic dataflow rather than chasing batch throughput. 13. A model runs fine on CPU but must ship on a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. Why is quantization not optional here, and what graph form does the QNN backend expect? Intermediate Qualcomm's Hexagon Tensor Processor (HTP) is integer-native, so the QNN (AI Engine Direct) backend targeting the HTP accepts quantized graphs (int8/uint8, int16/uint16); a plain FP32 graph cannot execute on the HTP. This makes the quantizer effectively part of the compiler rather than an optional pass. Models are commonly expressed as QDQ (Quantize-Dequantize) graphs, where explicit quantize/dequantize nodes carry the scales and zero-points the compiler folds into integer kernels. In practice you run PTQ with a calibration set (or QAT if accuracy degrades at low bit-width), producing per-channel weight scales, then compile and serialize to a QNN context binary. This is typically surfaced through the ONNX Runtime QNN execution provider. 14. Explain the ONNX Runtime execution-provider model. How does one ONNX model target CUDA, TensorRT, OpenVINO, QNN, or CoreML, and what happens when an EP lacks an operator? Intermediate ONNX Runtime treats each backend as a pluggable execution provider (EP): CUDA, TensorRT, OpenVINO, QNN, NNAPI, CoreML, DirectML, CANN, and others. At session load, the runtime partitions the model graph and assigns each supported subgraph to the highest-priority EP that can run it, so the same ONNX file retargets to many devices without re-authoring. When an EP does not implement an operator, that op or subgraph falls back to the CPU EP, which preserves correctness but can hurt performance if fallbacks are frequent or force host-device round trips. Some EPs also build and cache an optimized artifact on first run — TensorRT caches an "engine" and QNN caches a "context binary" — so subsequent loads skip recompilation. On Windows, Windows ML sits above ONNX Runtime and auto-selects the vendor EP (QNN for Qualcomm, OpenVINO for Intel, TensorRT-RTX for NVIDIA) with graceful GPU/CPU fallback. 15. Compare deployment across the four tiers: mobile SoC, edge/embedded, AI PC, and datacenter/cloud. What distinguishes them in memory model, power, and accelerator type? Intermediate Mobile SoC deployment uses an integrated NPU (Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon, MediaTek APU, Google Tensor) at roughly 1-5 W that shares unified LPDDR with the CPU/GPU and runs INT8/INT4 for camera pipelines, speech, and small on-device LLMs. Edge/embedded uses VPUs and small NPUs (Movidius, Coral Edge TPU, Jetson, Mobileye EyeQ) with SRAM scratchpads and direct sensor interfaces at single-digit watts for vision, robotics, and ADAS. AI PCs use integrated 40+ TOPS NPUs (for example Intel Core Ultra 200V / Series 2, AMD Ryzen AI 300, and Snapdragon X / X2 platforms) within laptop thermals for Copilot+ features, offloading from the CPU/iGPU for battery efficiency. Datacenter/cloud uses discrete GPUs, TPUs, and LPUs with dedicated multi-GB HBM, hundreds of watts to ~1 kW per package, and rack-scale interconnect (NVLink for GPUs, ICI for TPUs, RealScale for Groq); they alone do large-scale training plus high-throughput batched serving. The sharpest divide is memory: shared LPDDR or on-chip SRAM at the edge versus dedicated HBM requiring explicit host-device transfers in the datacenter. 16. What is the Copilot+ PC NPU requirement, and how do applications actually reach the NPU on Windows versus on Apple and Android platforms? Intermediate Microsoft requires a 40+ TOPS integrated NPU (alongside 16 GB RAM and 256 GB storage) for Copilot+ PC certification, enabling on-device features like Recall, live captions/translation, Windows Studio Effects, and image generation; Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite (~45 TOPS) shipped first, followed by Intel Lunar Lake / Core Ultra 200V (~48 TOPS) and AMD Ryzen AI 300 (~50 TOPS). On Windows, apps increasingly reach the NPU through Windows ML — the strategic successor to DirectML for on-device inference, layered over ONNX Runtime — which auto-loads the vendor execution provider (QNN for Qualcomm, OpenVINO for Intel, Vitis AI

entries.heading: LLVM (10)
entries.text: 21. What is LLVM IR, and which three of its properties make dataflow optimizations straightforward? Basic LLVM IR is a strongly-typed, three-address, SSA-form virtual instruction set that decouples language front-ends from hardware back-ends. Its SSA property means every value has exactly one static definition, so use-def chains are trivial and passes like constant propagation, global value numbering, and dead-code elimination become simple. It is three-address (operations name their operands and result explicitly) and strongly typed, with memory modeled explicitly through load/store on typed pointers rather than implicit register aliasing. It also exists in three isomorphic forms — in-memory C++ objects, human-readable .ll text, and compact .bc bitcode — which lets tools inspect, serialize, and re-ingest the same IR losslessly. 22. Describe the canonical three-stage LLVM pipeline and name the tool that embodies each stage. Basic The pipeline is front-end, middle-end, and back-end, all centered on LLVM IR. The front-end (e.g., Clang for C/C++/Objective-C, or rustc/swiftc/flang) lowers source to LLVM IR; for Clang this is source to AST to IR. The middle-end, driven by opt, runs target-independent analyses and transforms directly on IR. The back-end, driven by llc, lowers IR to target-specific machine code through instruction selection, scheduling, register allocation, and prologue/epilogue insertion before emitting assembly or object code via the MC layer. This clean separation is why one optimizer-and-codegen investment is amortized across dozens of front-end languages and hardware targets. 23. Why do ML and NPU compiler stacks overwhelmingly reuse LLVM as a terminal back-end rather than as a whole-program solution? Intermediate Graph- and tensor-level concerns — operator fusion, tiling, layout and quantization, and dynamic shapes — are best handled in a higher-level, domain-specific IR where the semantics are still visible. Once those are resolved, stacks lower to LLVM IR specifically to inherit LLVM's mature scalar and vector optimization, register allocation, instruction scheduling, and battle-tested code emission for CPUs and GPUs. This avoids re-implementing low-level compiler engineering per accelerator and lets teams focus their effort on the parts unique to their hardware. XLA, Triton, IREE, Mojo/MAX, TorchInductor, and vendor NPU stacks all follow this 'lower-then-hand-off-to-LLVM' pattern. 24. Name several representative target-independent middle-end passes and explain what mem2reg/SROA accomplishes and why it matters. Intermediate Representative target-independent passes include mem2reg/SROA, function inlining, instcombine (peephole simplification), GVN (redundancy elimination), the loop passes LICM and unrolling, loop and SLP vectorization, and various interprocedural passes. mem2reg (and its more general sibling SROA, scalar replacement of aggregates) promotes stack allocas into SSA virtual registers, replacing memory traffic with pure SSA values reconciled by phi nodes at control-flow merges. This matters because most front-ends, including Clang, initially emit locals as alloca/load/store; putting them into SSA form is what unlocks the rest of the SSA-based optimizers. The new PassManager organizes all of these by scope into Module, CGSCC, Function, and Loop pass managers. 25. Contrast SelectionDAG and GlobalISel as instruction-selection frameworks in an LLVM back-end. Advanced SelectionDAG is the legacy framework: it builds a dataflow DAG per basic block, legalizes types and operations, runs DAG-combines, and then greedily tree-pattern-matches nodes to target instructions — so selection is fundamentally block-local. GlobalISel is the newer replacement that operates on Generic Machine IR (gMIR) across whole functions through a pipeline of IRTranslator, Legalizer, RegBankSelect, and InstructionSelect. Working at whole-function scope enables faster and more global selection and avoids rebuilding a DAG per block. Importantly, both frameworks can share TableGen-described selection patterns, so a target's pattern investment is not wasted when migrating. 26. What does register allocation do in LLVM, which allocators ship in-tree, and which is the production default? Advanced Register allocation maps an unbounded number of virtual registers onto the finite set of physical registers, inserting spill code to memory when register pressure exceeds what is available. LLVM ships four allocators selectable via -regalloc=: Fast (used at -O0, prioritizing compile speed), Basic, Greedy (the default at -O1 and above), and PBQP (Partitioned Boolean Quadratic Programming). Greedy is the production workhorse and performs global live-range splitting to reduce spills. After allocation, prologue/epilogue insertion finalizes the stack frame and resolves references to abstract stack slots. 27. What is TableGen, and why is it central to standing up a new NPU or DSP back-end cheaply? Intermediate TableGen is LLVM's declarative DSL in which target .td files describe registers, register classes, instruction encodings and operands, calling conventions, scheduling models, and instruction-selection patterns. TableGen back-ends consume these files and auto-generate large swaths of C++ — instruction info, register info, matcher tables, and GlobalISel selectors — so a new target is defined largely by data rather than hand-written code. For an accelerator vendor this dramatically lowers bring-up cost: custom RISC-V, DSP, or NPU instructions are added declaratively and can be upstreamed into LLVM before silicon tapes out. It is the mechanism that makes retargeting economical instead of a from-scratch C++ effort. 28. How does MLIR relate to LLVM, and what is the role of the llvm dialect in an ML compilation flow? Intermediate MLIR is an LLVM sub-project providing a multi-level, dialect-extensible IR for progressive (partial) lowering of abstractions that plain LLVM IR cannot represent well, such as tensors, stru

entries.heading: MLIR (10)
entries.text: 31. What is a dialect in MLIR, and why are dialects central to the framework's design? Give a few examples of dialects and their abstraction levels. Basic A dialect is a namespaced collection of operations, types, and attributes that together define a coherent unit of IR at some abstraction level; it is MLIR's primary extensibility mechanism, since MLIR has no fixed, built-in opcode set. The key property is that multiple dialects can coexist within the same module, so a program can hold high-level and low-level ops side by side and be lowered gradually between them. Examples span the abstraction spectrum: tosa and stablehlo represent high-level ML operators, linalg captures structured linear algebra, affine and scf express loop nests and structured control flow, vector models SIMD, memref represents buffers, and the llvm dialect mirrors LLVM IR nearly 1:1 as a terminal dialect. This open, layered design is exactly what lets hardware vendors add their own dialects without forking the whole infrastructure. 32. Describe MLIR's structural nesting model. What are Operations, Regions, Blocks, and Values, and how do they relate? Basic MLIR IR is a nested structure where Operations are the nodes and Values are the SSA edges connecting them. The containment hierarchy is recursive: an Operation can contain zero or more Regions, a Region contains a list of Blocks, and each Block contains a list of Operations, which can themselves contain Regions. Every Value is either an operation result or a block argument, has exactly one definition and a Type, and thus satisfies static single assignment. Blocks end in a terminator and take block arguments in place of PHI nodes, so control-flow merges pass values as successor-block arguments. This uniform, self-similar structure is what lets one framework represent everything from a whole tensor-graph op with nested regions down to a single llvm.add. 33. What does "progressive (partial) lowering" mean in MLIR, and why is it especially valuable for NPU/AI-compiler backends? Intermediate Progressive lowering means a compiler translates a program through a sequence of dialects step by step (e.g. tosa to linalg to scf/affine plus vector to memref to llvm) rather than in one monolithic frontend-to-backend jump, and partial lowering means only some ops are converted at each stage so mixed-abstraction IR is legal in between. This matters because domain semantics like convolutions, tiling structure, and tensor value semantics are preserved as long as they are useful for analysis and optimization, then discarded only when lowered away. For NPU backends specifically, it lets a vendor intercept at whatever abstraction best matches their hardware, commonly linalg or a custom vendor dialect, and inject custom micro-kernels or dataflow mappings there. Crucially, they reuse upstream tiling, fusion, and bufferization instead of rebuilding a full compiler stack, which is the core economic argument for multi-level IR. 34. Why are tiling and fusion in MLIR typically performed on tensor-valued ops (like linalg) rather than after bufferization? What role does the linalg dialect play? Intermediate Tiling and fusion are performed while values are still immutable, value-semantic tensors because that immutability makes the transforms provably safe and freely composable: there is no aliasing or mutable-buffer hazard to reason about, so producers and consumers can be split and merged without worrying about clobbering shared memory. The linalg dialect is the workhorse here because its named and generic structured ops carry explicit indexing maps and iterator types, which expose the loop and reuse structure needed to tile and fuse mechanically. Once tiled, loops are materialized via scf or affine and inner data movement via the vector dialect. Doing this before bufferization is deliberate; bufferization runs late, after the tiling and fusion decisions are locked in, so the resulting buffers reflect an already-optimized loop nest. 35. Explain MLIR's dialect-conversion framework. What are the roles of ConversionTarget, ConversionPatterns, and TypeConverter, and how does partial vs full conversion differ? Intermediate The dialect-conversion framework drives lowering from one set of dialects to another. A ConversionTarget declares legality: each operation is marked Legal, Illegal, or Dynamically Legal (legal only if a predicate holds, e.g. on operand types). ConversionPatterns are rewrite rules that transform illegal ops into legal ones, and the framework can transitively compose an A-to-C lowering from separate A-to-B and B-to-C patterns. A TypeConverter maps types across the boundary, supporting 1-to-1 and 1-to-N conversions, and the framework inserts unrealized_conversion_cast ops to bridge temporary type mismatches that later patterns reconcile. Full conversion requires every op to end up legal or it fails, whereas partial conversion tolerates remaining illegal ops, which is what enables the incremental, mixed-abstraction lowering MLIR is built around. 36. How are transformations expressed and scheduled in MLIR? Contrast rewrite patterns with the PassManager, and mention declarative rewrite mechanisms. Intermediate Transformations are expressed as pattern-based rewrites: a RewritePattern matches an op subgraph and replaces it, and these are commonly applied by the greedy pattern rewriter, which repeatedly applies patterns until it reaches a fixpoint. Patterns can be written in C++ or declaratively via DRR (table-driven declarative rewrite rules in TableGen) or PDL (the pattern-description-language dialect), which reduces boilerplate for structural matches. Passes bundle related transformations and are scheduled by the PassManager, which nests pass pipelines over the op hierarchy, for example running a pass per func.func nested inside a module pipeline. So patterns are the fine-grained rewriting mechanism, while the PassManager handles orchestration, ordering, and nesting; tools like mlir-opt

entries.heading: NPU Compilers & Optimization (10)
entries.text: 41. What is operator fusion in an NPU compiler, and why is it typically the single most impactful latency optimization? Basic Operator fusion merges a chain of adjacent operators (for example conv + bias + ReLU, or the softmax chain inside attention) into a single kernel so intermediate activations stay in on-chip registers/SRAM instead of being written out to and re-read from DRAM/HBM. The dominant cost in edge and inference workloads is off-chip memory traffic, not arithmetic, so eliminating those round-trips directly cuts both latency and energy. Fusion also raises a kernel's arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved), pushing it away from the memory-bound region of the roofline. It runs early as a mostly target-independent graph-level pass alongside constant folding, CSE, and dead-code elimination. Because it removes materialization of intermediate tensors, it is usually the highest-leverage single transform a stack applies. 42. Explain the difference between post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT), and when you would reach for each. Basic PTQ takes an already-trained FP model and converts it to INT8/INT4/FP8 directly, using a small calibration set to pick activation ranges via min-max, entropy/KL, or percentile clipping; it needs no retraining and is fast, making it the default first attempt. QAT instead inserts fake-quant (simulated rounding) nodes into the graph and fine-tunes, so the weights learn to compensate for quantization error, which recovers accuracy at aggressive bit-widths like INT4/FP4 where PTQ degrades noticeably. You reach for PTQ when you need a quick deployment and INT8 accuracy loss is acceptable, and for QAT when the target precision is low or the model is accuracy-sensitive. The tradeoff is cost: QAT requires a fine-tuning pipeline, representative data, and GPU time, whereas PTQ needs only a calibration pass. 43. What does roofline analysis tell you, and how does an NPU compiler use it to guide optimization decisions? Basic A roofline plot graphs attainable throughput (FLOP/s) against arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte of memory traffic), bounded by two ceilings: a horizontal peak-compute line and a diagonal peak-memory-bandwidth line. Where a kernel lands classifies it as compute-bound (under the flat ceiling) or memory-bound (under the sloped ceiling). Compilers use this to justify fusion and tiling: both raise arithmetic intensity by reusing data on-chip, moving a memory-bound kernel rightward until it escapes the bandwidth-limited region. Hardware designers 'steepen the roofline' by adding HBM or larger on-chip SRAM. The model is coarse because it ignores on-chip locality across fused ops, so finer tools like Timeloop or Stream model tiling more precisely. 44. Why is tiling/blocking necessary on NPUs, and what makes tile-shape selection a hard problem? Intermediate NPUs have small, explicitly-managed on-chip SRAM/scratchpads rather than large caches, so large weight and activation tensors cannot fit resident; tiling splits them into blocks sized to fit on-chip, letting operands be staged once and reused heavily across the MAC array to maximize arithmetic intensity instead of being restreamed from DRAM/HBM. The difficulty is that the optimal tile shape depends jointly on SRAM capacity and banking, the array's dataflow/stationarity, DMA bandwidth, and the operator's reuse pattern, and these interact non-linearly. It is effectively a large search space over tile sizes, loop order, vectorization, and PE binding. That is why stacks like TVM (Ansor/MetaSchedule) auto-tune tiling by benchmarking many candidate schedules on the real device. A poor tile choice either overflows SRAM or leaves the array starved and underutilized. 45. Describe dataflow mapping and the common stationarity choices (weight-, output-, input-, row-stationary). How does a compiler pick one? Intermediate Dataflow mapping assigns the loop nest of a tensor op onto the physical MAC/systolic array, choosing which operand stays resident in the processing elements to maximize on-chip reuse. Weight-stationary preloads and holds weights in the PEs and streams activations, best when weights are reused across many activations (Google's TPU MXU is weight-stationary); output-stationary keeps partial sums accumulating locally in each PE while both operands stream, minimizing psum writeback; input-stationary holds activations; row-stationary (Eyeriss) balances reuse of weights, activations, and partial sums simultaneously. The compiler picks the mapping whose stationary operand matches the layer's dominant reuse pattern — e.g., weight-stationary for weight-heavy convolutions, output-stationary when accumulation traffic dominates. The goal is to minimize the most expensive data movement given the layer's operand-reuse profile and the array's structure. 46. What is bufferization in an MLIR-based NPU flow, and how does double-buffering (ping-pong) hide memory latency? Intermediate Bufferization converts value-semantic tensor SSA values into explicit mutable memref buffers, computing liveness and doing buffer allocation and reuse to minimize peak on-chip SRAM footprint. MLIR's One-Shot Bufferize analyzes tensor use-def chains whole-function, prefers in-place reuse anchored by destination-passing-style 'outs' operands, and inserts copies only on read-after-write conflicts. It typically runs late, after tiling and fusion, so those transforms operate on immutable tensors where they are provably safe. Double-buffering (ping-pong) allocates two buffers per pipeline stage so the DMA of the next tile writes into one buffer while the compute engine consumes the other, overlapping data movement with computation. This software-pipelining hides DMA latency and keeps the MAC array fed rather than stalling on loads. 47. entries.text: NPU and AI-compiler work sits between computer architecture, compiler engineering, deep learning, quantization, and runtime systems. These are the foundations and the core topics worth going deep on.

entries.heading: Foundations
entries.text: Computer architecture: memory hierarchy, SRAM/DRAM/HBM, SIMD, DMA, and data movement. Linear algebra and deep learning: GEMM, convolution, attention, and numerical precision. Algorithms and graphs: search, scheduling, and dynamic programming for compiler passes. Systems programming: C++, pointers/memory, concurrency, and Linux debugging. Parallel programming: kernels, tiling, synchronization, and profiling (CUDA/OpenMP concepts).

entries.text: Compiler design: IR, SSA, lowering, legalization, scheduling, allocation, and codegen. MLIR/LLVM: dialects, progressive lowering, rewrite patterns, bufferization, and TableGen. Efficient AI: quantization (PTQ/QAT), pruning/sparsity, operator fusion, and graph partitioning. Accelerator dataflow: systolic arrays, stationarity, tiling, and roofline analysis. Runtime and deployment: execution providers, memory planning, profiling, and driver interfaces. entries.text: Review neural-network execution, modern model architectures, transformers, profiling, quantization, and deployment parity.

entries.heading: Phase 1: Neural-network basics
entries.text: Review tensors, modules, parameters, forward pass, loss, gradients, and optimizer update flow. Be able to explain a training step from input batch to parameter update.

entries.heading: Phase 2: Training behavior
entries.text: Practice questions on initialization, learning rates, regularization, validation, overfitting, gradient clipping, mixed precision, and train/eval mode.

entries.heading: Phase 3: CNN and vision
entries.text: Study convolution shape math, padding, stride, pooling, normalization, residual blocks, augmentation, object detection, segmentation, and feature maps.

entries.heading: Phase 4: Transformer systems
entries.text: Cover tokenization, embeddings, attention, masking, positional encoding, KV cache, prefill/decode, batching, and long-context memory costs.

entries.heading: Phase 5: Deployment and debugging
entries.text: Connect training knowledge to ONNX export, quantization, operator fusion, runtime parity checks, profiling, and numerical debugging.

entries.heading: Training loop
entries.text: A standard loop runs forward inference, computes loss, calls backward to populate gradients, steps the optimizer, and clears gradients before the next batch.

entries.heading: Autograd
entries.text: Modern frameworks record tensor operations into a computation graph and apply the chain rule automatically for differentiable operations.

entries.heading: Generalization
entries.text: Validation performance estimates whether the model learned patterns that transfer beyond training examples. Data leakage breaks this estimate.

entries.heading: Convolution
entries.text: Convolution uses local receptive fields and shared weights, making it efficient for image-like signals and spatial feature extraction.

entries.heading: Attention
entries.text: Self-attention builds token-to-token interactions using query, key, and value projections, then mixes values according to normalized similarity scores.

entries.heading: Numerical precision
entries.text: FP32 is useful for reference accuracy, while BF16/FP16/INT8 can reduce memory and improve throughput when supported and validated.

entries.heading: Deployment parity
entries.text: Always compare framework, exported graph, and runtime outputs on representative inputs before trusting performance numbers.

entries.heading: Performance bottleneck
entries.text: Deep learning inference can be compute-bound, memory-bandwidth-bound, launch-overhead-bound, or shape/operator-support-bound.

entries.heading: Foundations
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is a trainable parameter?
entries.text: A value learned by optimization, such as a weight or bias. A value chosen only by the operating system. A random metric printed after training. A file format for images. Trainable parameters are updated by the optimizer using gradients from the loss.

entries.heading: What is a hyperparameter?
entries.text: A learned weight inside a layer. A setting chosen outside training, such as learning rate or batch size. The final prediction vector. The gradient of the loss. Hyperparameters control the training or model design but are not directly learned from one backward pass.

entries.heading: Why are nonlinear activations needed?
entries.text: They make every model smaller. Without them, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map. They remove the need for data. They guarantee zero loss. Compositions of linear transformations are still linear, so nonlinearities expand representational power.

entries.heading: What does a loss function measure?
entries.text: The number of CPU cores. How far predictions are from the desired target according to a training objective. Only model file size. Only GPU temperature. The loss is the scalar objective differentiated during training.

entries.heading: What does backpropagation compute?
entries.text: Dataset download speed. Gradients of the loss with respect to parameters. The number of classes in the dataset. HTML page layout. Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the computation graph.

entries.heading: What is the purpose of an optimizer?
entries.text: To update parameters using gradients and an update rule. To label raw data automatically. To convert Python to HTML. To remove all nonlinearities. SGD, Adam, and similar optimizers turn gradients into parameter updates.

entries.heading: Why split train, validation, and test data?
entries.text: To make training slower only. To separate parameter fitting, model selection, and final generalization estimate. To avoid using labels. To force all classes into one file. Each split has a different purpose; using test data for tuning leaks information.

entries.heading: What is overfitting?
entries.text: The model performs well on training data but poorly on unseen data. The model never learns training data. The loss is exactly zero on all future data. The model uses too few parameters by definition. Overfitting means training performance no longer predicts generalization.

entries.heading: What does batch size affect?
entries.text: Only the spelling of layer names. Gradient noise, memory use, throughput, and sometimes generalization. The number of labels in the world. Whether the model has parameters. Batch size changes both systems behavior and optimization behavior.

entries.heading: What is an epoch?
entries.text: One full pass over the training dataset. One hidden unit. One GPU register. One activation function only. Epochs count dataset passes, while iterations or steps count mini-batch updates.

entries.heading: Training, Optimization, and Regularization
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What happens if the learning rate is too high?
entries.text: Training may diverge or oscillate. The model becomes perfectly calibrated. The batch size becomes zero. The validation set disappears. Large updates can overshoot useful minima and destabilize training.

entries.heading: What happens if the learning rate is too low?
entries.text: Training may be very slow or stall. Gradients become labels. All models become linear. The optimizer skips the loss. Tiny updates may not make meaningful progress within the training budget.

entries.heading: Why use momentum?
entries.text: To smooth update directions and reduce zig-zag behavior. To delete gradients. To avoid all matrix multiplies. To replace the dataset. Momentum accumulates a velocity-like state from past gradients.

entries.heading: What is Adam known for?
entries.text: Adaptive moment estimates for parameter updates. Only integer arithmetic. Converting labels to images. Disabling backpropagation. Adam tracks running estimates of gradient mean and variance-like magnitude.

entries.heading: What does weight decay encourage?
entries.text: Smaller parameter magnitudes. Larger image dimensions. More file descriptors. No validation data. Weight decay penalizes large weights and can improve generalization.

entries.heading: What does dropout do during training?
entries.text: Randomly disables some activations to regularize the model. Deletes training labels permanently. Forces every tensor to INT4. Turns the model into a filesystem. Dropout discourages fragile co-adaptation and is disabled or made deterministic during evaluation.

entries.heading: Why use gradient clipping?
entries.text: To limit very large gradients and prevent unstable updates. To improve CSS styles. To remove loss functions. To make labels random. Clipping is common when gradients can explode, such as sequence models or difficult RL settings.

entries.heading: What does model.eval() change in PyTorch-style workflows?
entries.text: Inference behavior for layers such as dropout and batch normalization. The number of classes. The operating system scheduler. The optimizer source code. Evaluation mode is required for meaningful validation and deployment checks.

entries.heading: Why call optimizer.zero_grad() or clear gradients?
entries.text: Gradients accumulate by default in many frameworks. It deletes the model. It changes images to text. It disables all parameters. If gradients are not cleared, updates may include stale accumulation.

entries.heading: What is mixed precision training?
entries.text: Using lower precision for many operations while preserving stability where needed. Mixing labels from train and test sets. Using only strings as tensors. Training without gradients. Mixed precision can improve throughput and memory use but must manage numerical stability.

entries.heading: CNN and Vision
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: Why are convolutions parameter-efficient for images?
entries.text: Weights are shared across spatial positions. Every pixel gets a separate full network. They require no data. They only run on CPUs. Shared filters reduce parameters and exploit spatial locality.

entries.heading: What does stride control in convolution?
entries.text: The step size of the filter over the input. The number of classes. The loss formula only. The optimizer state. Higher stride usually reduces output spatial resolution.

entries.heading: What does padding control?
entries.text: How borders are handled and output size is affected. Only model checkpoint names. Whether labels exist. The number of GPUs. Padding can preserve spatial size or control border behavior.

entries.heading: Why is a 1x1 convolution useful?
entries.text: It mixes channels at each spatial location. It only changes image file format. It removes all nonlinearities. It cannot be learned. 1x1 convolutions are channel projections and are common in bottleneck blocks.

entries.heading: What does pooling often provide?
entries.text: Spatial downsampling or local aggregation. Random labels. Database indexing. A replacement for all training. Pooling can reduce resolution and improve local invariance.

entries.heading: What is batch normalization's practical role?
entries.text: Stabilize and often speed training by normalizing intermediate activations. Make all tensors images. Remove the need for optimization. Force CPU execution. Batch normalization uses training batch statistics and inference running statistics.

entries.heading: Why do residual connections help deep networks?
entries.text: They give gradients shorter paths through the model. They prevent all overfitting. They remove all parameters. They make convolution illegal. Residual paths make optimization of very deep networks easier.

entries.heading: What is data augmentation?
entries.text: Applying label-preserving transformations to increase training diversity. Deleting difficult examples. Using test data as training labels. Turning off validation. Common augmentations include crops, flips, color jitter, noise, and geometric transforms.

entries.heading: What does non-maximum suppression do in object detection?
entries.text: Removes overlapping duplicate boxes after scoring. Trains the backbone. Computes batch norm statistics. Creates image pixels. NMS is a post-processing step for many detectors.

entries.heading: How does semantic segmentation differ from classification?
entries.text: Segmentation predicts labels per pixel or region, not one label for the whole image. Segmentation has no inputs. Classification always uses lidar. Segmentation cannot use CNNs. Segmentation preserves spatial output structure.

entries.heading: Transformers and LLMs
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is self-attention?
entries.text: A mechanism where tokens attend to other tokens in the same sequence. A file compression algorithm. A CPU scheduler. A camera calibration method. Self-attention computes token interactions using learned projections.

entries.heading: What are Q, K, and V?
entries.text: Query, key, and value projections used to score and mix token information. Three image file extensions. Three optimizer names only. Three Linux signals. QK similarity determines attention weights applied to V.

entries.heading: Why scale attention logits by sqrt(d)?
entries.text: To avoid overly large dot products that saturate softmax. To change text into images. To skip embeddings. To remove all masking. Scaling helps keep gradients healthy as feature dimension grows.

entries.heading: What is an attention mask?
entries.text: A rule that blocks attention to padding, future tokens, or invalid positions. A GPU fan setting. A filesystem permission. A loss function replacement. Masks encode sequence validity and causal constraints.

entries.heading: What does a tokenizer do?
entries.text: Maps text to token IDs and back. Computes gradients directly. Allocates CUDA memory only. Runs the operating system scheduler. Tokenization shapes sequence length, vocabulary coverage, and special-token handling.

entries.heading: What is a positional encoding or embedding for?
entries.text: Providing order information to a model whose attention is otherwise permutation-like. Deleting repeated tokens. Replacing all activations. Skipping the loss. Transformers need positional information to reason about order.

entries.heading: What is the KV cache?
entries.text: Stored key/value tensors from prior tokens reused during autoregressive decoding. A database of labels. A CPU-only optimizer. A way to remove attention. KV cache reduces repeated computation but increases memory use.

entries.heading: How do prefill and decode differ?
entries.text: Prefill processes the prompt in parallel; decode generates one or a few new tokens using cache. Prefill is training and decode is labeling. Decode never uses attention. Prefill only runs on CPUs. LLM serving often has separate throughput bottlenecks for prefill and decode.

entries.heading: Why is batching tricky for LLM inference?
entries.text: Requests have variable sequence lengths and decode progress. All requests have exactly equal cost. Batching disables KV cache. Batching removes tokenization. Schedulers must balance latency, padding waste, cache memory, and throughput.

entries.heading: What is temperature in text generation?
entries.text: A sampling control that changes distribution sharpness. GPU temperature only. A model weight type. A tokenizer vocabulary rule. Higher temperature makes sampling more random; lower temperature makes it more deterministic.

entries.heading: Deployment and Debugging
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is quantization?
entries.text: Representing weights or activations with lower precision. Increasing every tensor to FP64. Deleting the validation set. Replacing neural networks with SQL. Quantization can reduce memory and improve inference speed when accuracy survives.

entries.heading: What is operator fusion?
entries.text: Combining adjacent operations to reduce memory traffic and launch overhead. Combining datasets without labels. Changing all shapes to dynamic. Turning attention into HTML. Fusion is a major runtime and compiler optimization.

entries.heading: Why export to ONNX?
entries.text: To exchange a model graph with runtimes and compilers. To improve labels automatically. To remove all unsupported operations. To make training mandatory. ONNX export still requires operator support and numerical parity checks.

entries.heading: What should you compare after export?
entries.text: Framework output, exported graph output, and target runtime output. Only file names. Only CSS colors. Only class labels from one example. Parity checks catch conversion, dtype, preprocessing, and runtime differences.

entries.heading: What is latency?
entries.text: Time for one request or operation to complete. Number of model parameters only. The size of the dataset. The learning rate. Latency is user-visible response time.

entries.heading: What is throughput?
entries.text: Work completed per unit time, such as images/sec or tokens/sec. Time for one sample only. A type of activation. A loss metric only. Batching often improves throughput even when it changes latency.

entries.heading: What is a memory-bandwidth bottleneck?
entries.text: Performance is limited by moving data rather than arithmetic. The model has no weights. The CPU has no scheduler. The dataset has no labels. Many inference workloads are limited by reads/writes of activations and weights.

entries.heading: What is a good first debug step when training fails?
entries.text: Overfit a tiny batch. Immediately deploy to production. Delete the loss. Only change the theme. A tiny-batch overfit test catches many wiring, label, and optimizer bugs.

entries.heading: What does data leakage do?
entries.text: Makes validation or test metrics unrealistically good. Reduces all memory use. Improves true generalization by definition. Makes gradients unnecessary. Leakage lets the model use information that will not be available in real deployment.

entries.heading: Why profile before optimizing?
entries.text: To identify the real bottleneck before changing code. To avoid measuring anything. To make every model larger. To replace validation. Profiling prevents wasting effort on non-bottlenecks.
