entries.heading: C programming practice
entries.text: Practice the C language, memory, pointers, concurrency, and systems-level reasoning needed at runtime and driver boundaries.

entries.heading: Phase 1: Language and memory model
entries.text: Review objects, lvalues, storage duration, linkage, sequence points, integer promotion, strict aliasing, const/volatile/restrict, and where undefined behavior comes from.

entries.heading: Phase 2: Dynamic memory
entries.text: Practice malloc/calloc/realloc/free semantics, alignment, ownership, leaks, dangling pointers, double free, and use-after-free, plus safe allocation patterns.

entries.heading: Phase 3: Systems and low-level
entries.text: Study file descriptors, syscalls and errno, fork/exec, mmap, signals and async-signal safety, endianness, bit manipulation, and memory-mapped I/O.

entries.heading: Phase 4: Performance
entries.text: Cover cache locality, access patterns, branch prediction, inlining, false sharing, restrict-enabled optimization, vectorization, and measuring before tuning.

entries.heading: Phase 5: Libraries and tooling
entries.text: Master string/memory functions and their footguns, formatted I/O safety, pthreads primitives, build/link basics, and sanitizers and profilers.

entries.heading: Undefined behavior
entries.text: UB is any construct for which the standard imposes no requirements. Signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, and data races are UB; the compiler may assume they never happen.

entries.heading: Object lifetime
entries.text: Automatic objects live for their block, static objects for the whole program, and allocated objects until freed. A pointer outliving its object becomes dangling.

entries.heading: Strict aliasing
entries.text: An object generally may not be accessed through a pointer of an incompatible type. A char pointer is the exception and may alias any object, which is why byte-wise copies are always legal.

entries.heading: Ownership
entries.text: Every allocation needs exactly one clear owner responsible for freeing it exactly once. Fuzzy ownership causes leaks, double frees, and use-after-free.

entries.heading: Cache behavior
entries.text: Memory is moved in cache lines. Sequential, stride-one access reuses whole lines; scattered access wastes bandwidth and stalls on misses.

entries.heading: errno discipline
entries.text: Many library and system calls report failure with a sentinel return value and set errno. Check the return first, then read errno, because errno is only meaningful after a documented failure.

entries.heading: Async-signal safety
entries.text: A signal handler may interrupt code mid-operation, so it may call only async-signal-safe functions. malloc, printf, and most of the standard library are not safe there.

entries.heading: Measure first
entries.text: Optimization should be driven by a profiler. Cache misses, branch mispredicts, and memory bandwidth often matter more than raw instruction count.

entries.heading: Language and Memory Model
entries.text: 31 questions

entries.heading: What is undefined behavior in C?
entries.text: A construct for which the standard imposes no requirements at all. Any behavior that differs between compilers but is documented. A runtime error that always aborts the program. A warning the compiler is required to emit. Under UB the implementation may do anything, and optimizers may assume it never occurs, so effects can be non-local and surprising.

entries.heading: What happens on signed integer overflow?
entries.text: It is undefined behavior. It always wraps around modulo 2^N. It saturates at the maximum value. It is a required compile-time error. Signed overflow is UB, unlike unsigned arithmetic, which is defined to wrap modulo 2^N.

entries.heading: What does the strict aliasing rule allow the compiler to assume?
entries.text: That two pointers of incompatible types do not refer to the same object. That all pointers may freely alias each other. That char pointers can never alias anything. That aliasing is only relevant at -O0. Accessing an object through an incompatible type is UB, so the compiler assumes no such aliasing; a char pointer is the explicit exception.

entries.heading: What does the restrict qualifier on a pointer promise?
entries.text: For its lifetime, the object it points to is accessed only through that pointer (or values derived from it). The pointed-to object is read-only. The pointer never changes value. The memory is guaranteed to be cache-aligned. restrict is a no-aliasing promise from the programmer; violating it is UB, but it lets the compiler avoid conservative reloads.

entries.heading: What is the value of sizeof(char) in C?
entries.text: Always 1. Always 8. Implementation-defined, often 1. Equal to sizeof(int). sizeof is measured in units of char, so sizeof(char) is 1 by definition, even though a byte may have more than 8 bits (CHAR_BIT).

entries.heading: What does a sequence point guarantee?
entries.text: That all side effects before it are complete before those after it begin. That the program pauses for the scheduler. That floating point is flushed to memory. That the optimizer is disabled at that line. Modifying an object more than once between sequence points, or reading it other than to compute the new value, is UB (e.g. i = i++).

entries.heading: What do the usual arithmetic conversions do to a char or short in an expression?
entries.text: Promote it to int (or unsigned int) before the operation. Keep it as char and produce a char result. Always make the result unsigned. Only convert floating-point operands. Integer promotions apply first, so narrow operands become int, which affects overflow and result type.

entries.heading: In the declaration `const int *p`, what is const?
entries.text: The pointed-to int is read-only through p; p itself can be reassigned. The pointer p is read-only; the int can change. Both the pointer and the int are read-only. It is a syntax error. `const int *p` is a pointer to const int; `int *const p` is a const pointer to mutable int. Read right-to-left.

entries.heading: What does the static keyword mean on a function or variable at file scope?
entries.text: It gives the identifier internal linkage, limiting it to that translation unit. It allocates the object on the stack. It makes the variable thread-local. It forces the function to be inlined. At file scope static means internal linkage; inside a function it means static storage duration instead.

entries.heading: Why does volatile matter for a hardware register or an ISR-updated flag?
entries.text: It forces each access to actually read or write memory instead of being optimized away or cached in a register. It makes the access atomic across threads. It inserts a full memory barrier. It guarantees the value never changes. volatile only prevents the compiler from eliding or reordering the access; it provides neither atomicity nor inter-thread ordering.

entries.heading: What is the type of a string literal such as "abc", and can you modify it?
entries.text: An array of char (here char[4]); attempting to modify it is undefined behavior. A pointer to heap memory you must free. A const int array you may modify freely. A single char equal to 'a'. String literals have static storage and may be placed in read-only memory, so writing through them is UB even though the type is not const.

entries.heading: What happens to an array when passed as a function argument?
entries.text: It decays to a pointer to its first element; size information is lost. The whole array is copied by value. It becomes a reference that carries its length. It is converted to a linked list. Because of array-to-pointer decay you must pass the length separately; sizeof inside the callee gives the pointer size.

entries.heading: What is the difference between a declaration and a definition?
entries.text: A declaration introduces a name and type; a definition also reserves storage or provides the body. They are identical in C. A definition only appears in headers. A declaration always allocates memory. A variable may be declared many times (extern) but defined once; the linker complains about missing or duplicate definitions.

entries.heading: What is size_t?
entries.text: An implementation-defined unsigned integer type used for sizes and indices, and the result type of sizeof. A signed 32-bit integer. A pointer type. Always exactly 8 bytes. Being unsigned, size_t wraps rather than going negative, which is a common source of comparison surprises.

entries.heading: What is a valid null pointer constant?
entries.text: An integer constant expression with value 0, or such a value cast to void*. Any negative integer. The address 0xFFFFFFFF. An uninitialized pointer. NULL expands to a null pointer constant; dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behavior.

entries.heading: What is the value of an uninitialized automatic (local) variable?
entries.text: Indeterminate; reading it can be undefined behavior. Guaranteed to be 0. The last value that memory held, always readable safely. A compile-time error. Only static and thread-local objects are zero-initialized; automatics must be initialized before use.

entries.heading: What does the extern keyword express?
entries.text: A declaration of an identifier with external linkage that is defined in another translation unit. That the variable is stored in a register. That the function is inlined. That the object is thread-local. extern lets multiple files share one global definition without each defining its own copy.

entries.heading: What is the order of evaluation of function arguments in C?
entries.text: Unspecified; you cannot rely on left-to-right or right-to-left. Always strictly left to right. Always right to left. Alphabetical by parameter name. Because order is unspecified, arguments with interacting side effects (e.g. f(i++, i++)) are a bug.

entries.heading: In C, how is the subscript expression a[i] defined?
entries.text: As *(a + i), which is why i[a] is also valid. As a special array-only operator unrelated to pointers. As a bounds-checked access that traps on overflow. As a[i] only for heap arrays. Subscripting is pointer arithmetic plus a dereference; C performs no bounds checking, so overflow is UB.

entries.heading: What is a flexible array member?
entries.text: A final struct member declared as an incomplete array (arr[]) sized when the struct is allocated. An array whose size changes automatically at runtime. A pointer member disguised as an array. A VLA declared at file scope. It allows a header struct plus a variable-length trailing buffer in a single allocation.

entries.heading: Why does a struct sometimes occupy more bytes than the sum of its members?
entries.text: The compiler inserts padding so each member meets its alignment requirement. Because C stores type names inside each struct. Because members are always 8 bytes. Because structs are heap-allocated. Reordering members from largest to smallest alignment can reduce padding and shrink the struct.

entries.heading: What is the difference between the character constant 'A' and the string "A"?
entries.text: 'A' is an int-valued character constant; "A" is a two-element char array {'A','\0'}. They are identical. 'A' is a string and "A" is a number. Both are single bytes. A character constant has type int in C, while a string literal is a null-terminated array.

entries.heading: What does the comma operator (as in `a, b`) do?
entries.text: Evaluates a for its side effects, discards it, and yields b; there is a sequence point between them. Creates a pair of both values. Is the same as logical AND. Is only valid inside function calls. Note that commas separating function arguments are punctuation, not the comma operator.

entries.heading: What is a compound literal like (int[]){1, 2, 3}?
entries.text: An unnamed object with automatic (or static at file scope) storage that you can take the address of. A macro expansion. A read-only constant that cannot be addressed. A syntax error before C23. Compound literals let you create anonymous array/struct objects inline, useful for passing temporaries by pointer.

entries.heading: What does C23 require about the representation of signed integers?
entries.text: Two's complement representation. Sign-and-magnitude representation. That signed and unsigned share the same overflow rules. That int is exactly 16 bits. Earlier standards allowed one's complement and sign-magnitude; C23 standardized two's complement.

entries.heading: What does converting an out-of-range value to a signed integer type do?
entries.text: It is implementation-defined (the result or a raised signal). It is always undefined behavior. It always wraps modulo 2^N like unsigned. It saturates to the type maximum. Unsigned conversion is defined to wrap, but signed out-of-range conversion is implementation-defined, not portable.

entries.heading: What is the practical difference between ++i and i++?
entries.text: Both increment i, but ++i evaluates to the new value and i++ to the old value. ++i is faster and i++ is slower for all types. They differ only for pointers. i++ does not modify i. For built-in scalar types the codegen is usually identical; the difference is the value the expression yields.

entries.heading: What is the effect of a data race on a shared object between threads?
entries.text: It is undefined behavior unless the accesses are synchronized or atomic. It is always safe if the variable is volatile. It merely produces a stale but valid value. It is defined to pick one thread's value. Use mutexes or _Atomic types; volatile does not make concurrent access well-defined.

entries.heading: What is the storage duration of a variable declared static inside a function?
entries.text: Static: it persists for the whole program and keeps its value across calls. Automatic: it is recreated each call. Allocated: it must be freed. Thread-local by default. It is initialized once and retains state between invocations, which also makes it non-reentrant.

entries.heading: Why is the expression i = i++ + 1 problematic?
entries.text: It modifies i twice without an intervening sequence point, which is undefined behavior. It is a compile-time error in all compilers. It always sets i to 1. It is fine and portable. Multiple unsequenced modifications of the same object are UB; write clear, single-update statements instead.

entries.heading: What does taking the address of a function-local array and returning it produce?
entries.text: A dangling pointer, because the array's lifetime ends when the function returns. A valid heap pointer the caller must free. A copy of the array. A compile error in standard C. To return array data, allocate it (malloc) or have the caller pass in a buffer.

entries.heading: Dynamic Memory Management
entries.text: 30 questions

entries.heading: What does malloc return, and what is in the returned memory?
entries.text: A pointer to uninitialized memory of the requested size, or NULL on failure. A pointer to zero-initialized memory, never NULL. A pointer that is always page-aligned. The number of bytes allocated. malloc does not initialize memory and can fail, so the return value must be checked before use.

entries.heading: How does calloc differ from malloc?
entries.text: It zero-initializes the memory and guards against nmemb*size overflow. It is identical but faster. It never returns NULL. It allocates on the stack. calloc(nmemb, size) both clears the block and checks that the multiplication does not overflow, which a raw malloc(nmemb*size) does not.

entries.heading: What does free(NULL) do?
entries.text: Nothing; it is well-defined and safe. It is undefined behavior. It aborts the program. It frees the most recent allocation. Passing NULL to free is explicitly a no-op, which simplifies cleanup paths.

entries.heading: After a successful realloc that moves the block, what is true of the original pointer?
entries.text: It is freed by realloc and must not be used again; only the returned pointer is valid. It still points to valid memory. It must be freed manually afterward. It is unchanged and identical to the new pointer. On success realloc may move data and free the old block; using the old pointer is use-after-free. Assign to a temporary in case realloc returns NULL.

entries.heading: What is a dangling pointer?
entries.text: A pointer that refers to memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope. A pointer that was never initialized. A pointer equal to NULL. A pointer to read-only memory. Dereferencing a dangling pointer is use-after-free, a classic source of crashes and security bugs.

entries.heading: What is the consequence of calling free twice on the same pointer?
entries.text: Undefined behavior (double free), often exploitable heap corruption. It is safe and simply ignored. It reallocates the block. It returns an error code. Double free corrupts allocator metadata; a common defense is setting the pointer to NULL after freeing, since free(NULL) is safe.

entries.heading: What alignment does memory from malloc have?
entries.text: Suitable for any object type, i.e. at least alignof(max_align_t). Exactly 1 byte. Always 4096 bytes (a page). Whatever the caller last requested. The standard guarantees fundamental alignment; for larger alignment use aligned_alloc or posix_memalign.

entries.heading: Which statement about the stack and the heap is correct?
entries.text: Stack objects have automatic lifetime tied to scope; heap objects live until explicitly freed. The heap is always faster to allocate from than the stack. Returning a pointer to a local stack array is safe. The heap has automatic lifetime and the stack is manual. Returning the address of an automatic variable produces a dangling pointer once the function returns.

entries.heading: What is the safest way to detect multiplication overflow when sizing an allocation?
entries.text: Check that count does not exceed SIZE_MAX / element_size before multiplying, or use calloc. Multiply and check if the result is negative. Trust that malloc will reject overly large sizes. Cast the operands to int first. size_t is unsigned so it wraps silently; an unchecked count*size can produce a tiny allocation and a heap overflow.

entries.heading: What is a memory leak?
entries.text: Allocated memory that is no longer reachable and is never freed. Memory that is freed too early. A pointer that is set to NULL. Stack memory reused between calls. Leaks grow process memory over time; tools like Valgrind or LeakSanitizer report the unreleased blocks and their allocation sites.

entries.heading: In standard C, should you cast the result of malloc?
entries.text: No; void* converts implicitly, and casting can hide a missing <stdlib.h> include. Yes; the cast is required by the standard. Yes; otherwise the memory is uninitialized. It makes malloc faster. In C89 an implicit int declaration from a missing include, combined with a cast, could mask a real bug; C++ differs.

entries.heading: What is realloc(NULL, size) equivalent to?
entries.text: malloc(size). free of nothing. A no-op returning NULL. Undefined behavior. This lets a grow-as-you-go loop start from a NULL pointer without special-casing the first call.

entries.heading: What is the behavior of reading memory after it has been freed?
entries.text: Use-after-free: undefined behavior. It safely returns the last stored value. It returns zero. It reallocates the block. The allocator may reuse or unmap the memory, so any access after free is invalid.

entries.heading: What is heap fragmentation?
entries.text: Free memory scattered into non-contiguous blocks, so a large request can fail despite enough total free space. A corruption of allocator metadata. A guaranteed crash after many frees. A feature that speeds up malloc. Long-running programs may use pools or arenas to reduce fragmentation from mixed-size allocations.

entries.heading: Why must you free memory only with the matching allocator?
entries.text: Mixing allocators (e.g. freeing a malloc block with a custom free, or vice versa) is undefined behavior. Because free is slower than delete. Because free zeroes memory. It is always fine to mix them. Only pointers returned by the malloc family may be passed to free; other pointers are UB.

entries.heading: What does aligned_alloc(alignment, size) require in C11?
entries.text: alignment must be a supported power of two and size a multiple of alignment. alignment must be a multiple of size. size must be a power of two. Nothing; any values work. It is used when a type or hardware needs stronger-than-fundamental alignment, such as SIMD or DMA buffers.

entries.heading: What is a heap buffer overflow?
entries.text: Writing past the end of an allocated block, corrupting adjacent heap data or metadata. Allocating more than physical RAM. Calling malloc in a loop. Freeing NULL. It is a top security vulnerability class; AddressSanitizer detects it by placing redzones around allocations.

entries.heading: Why is returning a pointer to a function-local static buffer risky?
entries.text: It is shared and overwritten on the next call, making the function non-reentrant and thread-unsafe. The buffer is freed when the function returns. The compiler forbids it. It leaks memory each call. Callers that hold the pointer across another call, or across threads, see corrupted data; prefer caller-provided buffers.

entries.heading: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy of a struct containing a pointer?
entries.text: A shallow copy duplicates the pointer value; a deep copy duplicates the pointed-to data too. They are identical. A deep copy only copies the pointer. A shallow copy allocates new memory. Two shallow copies sharing one buffer risk a double free or use-after-free when one is destroyed.

entries.heading: What does strdup do, and who owns the result?
entries.text: It allocates a new copy of a string; the caller must free it. It copies into a static buffer with no ownership. It returns a read-only literal. It frees the original string. strdup (POSIX, and C23) is a convenient malloc+strcpy, so forgetting to free it leaks.

entries.heading: What typically causes a stack overflow in C?
entries.text: Very deep or infinite recursion, or huge automatic arrays exceeding the stack limit. Calling free too often. Allocating with malloc. Using const variables. Stack overflow is UB and often crashes; large or unbounded data should go on the heap.

entries.heading: What is a clean pattern for freeing resources on error paths in C?
entries.text: A single cleanup label reached by goto, freeing acquired resources in reverse order. Duplicating free calls before every early return. Never freeing until program exit. Calling exit() on the first error. The goto-cleanup idiom avoids leaks and double frees when a function acquires several resources.

entries.heading: What may malloc(0) return?
entries.text: Either NULL or a unique non-null pointer that must not be dereferenced but can be freed. Always a valid 1-byte buffer. Always NULL, guaranteed. Undefined behavior. Because it is implementation-defined, do not dereference the result and always pair it with free.

entries.heading: What does ownership transfer mean for a function that returns allocated memory?
entries.text: The caller becomes responsible for freeing the returned pointer. The function will free it automatically later. The memory is on the stack. The pointer is read-only. Documenting who frees what (the ownership contract) is essential to avoid leaks and double frees.

entries.heading: What does memset(p, 0, n) do?
entries.text: Sets the first n bytes at p to zero. Allocates n zeroed bytes. Frees n bytes. Compares n bytes to zero. memset is byte-wise; note that all-bits-zero is not portably a null pointer or floating-point zero for every type, though it is for integers.

entries.heading: Why can setting a freed pointer to NULL be a useful habit?
entries.text: A later accidental free or dereference then hits NULL (safe free / detectable crash) instead of reusing a dangling pointer. It frees the memory a second time safely. It reallocates the block. It prevents fragmentation. free(NULL) is a no-op and dereferencing NULL faults predictably, unlike silent use-after-free.

entries.heading: What is an arena or pool allocator good for?
entries.text: Fast allocation of many objects with a bulk free, reducing per-object overhead and fragmentation. Guaranteeing every allocation is page-aligned. Replacing the need to ever free. Making single large allocations. Arenas trade fine-grained frees for speed and simplicity, common in parsers and request-scoped work.

entries.heading: What is the risk of an integer used as a size being signed and negative?
entries.text: Converting it to size_t yields a huge value, causing an enormous or failing allocation. malloc rejects it with a clear error. It allocates zero bytes safely. The compiler prevents it. Validate sizes as non-negative and within bounds before passing them to allocation functions.

entries.heading: What does double-freeing typically corrupt?
entries.text: The allocator's internal free-list metadata, which can be leveraged for exploits. Only the freed block's contents. The stack canary. Nothing; it is harmless. Modern allocators add some detection, but the behavior is still UB and must be avoided by clear ownership.

entries.heading: How do you allocate a 2D grid of R rows and C cols contiguously?
entries.text: malloc(R * C * sizeof(elem)) and index as grid[r*C + c]. Only an array of R separate malloc calls works. Use calloc(R, C) which returns a 2D pointer. 2D allocation is impossible in C. A single contiguous block improves locality and needs just one free, unlike an array-of-pointers layout.

entries.heading: Systems and Low-Level Programming
entries.text: 29 questions

entries.heading: What is a file descriptor?
entries.text: A small non-negative integer that indexes a process's open file table. A pointer to a FILE structure. A disk block number. The size of a file in bytes. Descriptors 0, 1, 2 are stdin, stdout, stderr; higher-level FILE* streams wrap descriptors with buffering.

entries.heading: What does a read() of a regular file returning 0 mean?
entries.text: End of file was reached. An error occurred; check errno. Zero bytes were requested. The file descriptor is invalid. A return of 0 is EOF; -1 signals an error with errno set, and a positive value is the byte count, which may be short.

entries.heading: What does fork() return?
entries.text: 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, and -1 on failure. The parent's PID in both processes. Always 0 on success. A file descriptor for the child. The differing return value is how the two processes, which share code, tell themselves apart after fork.

entries.heading: How should errno be used after a library or system call?
entries.text: Only after the call reports failure via its return value, since errno is not cleared on success. As the primary success/failure indicator on every call. It is reset to 0 automatically before each call. It is only valid inside signal handlers. Check the documented failure return first; a stale errno from an earlier call can otherwise be misread.

entries.heading: What is mmap commonly used for?
entries.text: Mapping a file or anonymous memory into the process address space. Allocating a new file descriptor. Sending data over a socket. Forcing a context switch. mmap enables file-backed I/O, shared memory, and large lazily-populated allocations without explicit read/write copies.

entries.heading: Which functions are safe to call from within a signal handler?
entries.text: Only async-signal-safe functions such as write() and _exit(). Any standard library function. printf and malloc, since they are reentrant. None; handlers may only set global variables. A handler can interrupt a non-reentrant call mid-update; the accepted pattern is to set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or write to a self-pipe.

entries.heading: What does the expression `x & (1u << n)` test?
entries.text: Whether bit n of x is set. Whether x is divisible by n. Whether x equals 2^n. The number of set bits in x. Masking with a single shifted bit isolates one flag; use |= to set, &= ~mask to clear, and ^= to toggle.

entries.heading: What is endianness?
entries.text: The byte order in which a multi-byte value is stored in memory. The alignment requirement of a type. Whether integers are signed or unsigned. The size of a pointer. Little-endian stores the least significant byte first; it matters for binary file formats, network protocols, and type punning.

entries.heading: Why must a memory-mapped device register usually be declared volatile?
entries.text: So the compiler performs every read and write instead of caching the value or eliding accesses. So the access becomes atomic. So the register is placed in the .bss section. So the address is page-aligned. Hardware can change the value between reads, and reads/writes can have side effects, both of which volatile preserves.

entries.heading: What is the practical difference between a process and a thread?
entries.text: Threads in one process share the address space; processes have separate address spaces. Threads cannot run concurrently. Processes share memory by default. Threads each have a private copy of all global variables. Shared memory makes thread communication cheap but requires synchronization; separate address spaces isolate processes.

entries.heading: What are the standard file descriptors 0, 1, and 2?
entries.text: Standard input, standard output, and standard error. The first three files a process opens. Reserved kernel handles a process cannot use. Network sockets. Redirection (e.g. 2>&1) manipulates these descriptors; dup2 is the underlying mechanism.

entries.heading: What does write() return, and why must the caller often loop?
entries.text: The number of bytes actually written, which may be fewer than requested (a short write). Always the full requested count or -1. 0 on success. The file descriptor number. Especially for pipes and sockets, robust code writes in a loop until all bytes are sent or an error occurs.

entries.heading: What does the exec family of functions do?
entries.text: Replaces the current process image with a new program, keeping the same PID. Creates a new child process. Waits for a child to finish. Opens a new file descriptor. The common pattern is fork then exec in the child, so exec does not return on success.

entries.heading: What is the purpose of wait()/waitpid()?
entries.text: To reap a terminated child and retrieve its exit status, preventing zombies. To pause the CPU. To close all file descriptors. To create a new thread. Without a wait, a finished child stays a zombie holding a process-table slot.

entries.heading: What does dup2(oldfd, newfd) do?
entries.text: Makes newfd refer to the same open file as oldfd, closing newfd first if needed. Duplicates a process. Creates a pipe. Copies a file's contents. dup2 is how shells implement redirection, e.g. pointing fd 1 at a file before exec.

entries.heading: What is a pipe used for?
entries.text: A unidirectional in-kernel channel connecting a write end to a read end, often between related processes. Mapping a file into memory. A synchronization mutex. A disk partition. Shell pipelines connect one process's stdout to the next process's stdin via a pipe.

entries.heading: What distinguishes a system call from an ordinary library function?
entries.text: A system call crosses into the kernel; a library function runs in user space (though it may wrap a syscall). System calls are written in C and library functions in assembly. There is no difference. Library functions require root privileges. For example fwrite is a buffered libc function that may eventually invoke the write system call.

entries.heading: Why is left-shifting a negative signed integer undefined behavior?
entries.text: The standard leaves shifts involving the sign bit of signed values undefined. Because shifting is always UB. Because negative numbers cannot be shifted at all. It is actually well-defined and wraps. Shifting by a count >= the type width is also UB; use unsigned types for portable bit manipulation.

entries.heading: In C, is reading a different union member than the one last written allowed?
entries.text: Yes; it reinterprets the stored bytes (type punning), a legal idiom in C unlike C++. No; it is always undefined behavior. Only if both members are pointers. Only inside a signal handler. The read value follows the object representation; watch out for trap representations and padding.

entries.heading: What does offsetof(type, member) give you?
entries.text: The byte offset of a member from the start of its struct. The size of the member. The address of a member. The alignment of the struct. It is used for serialization and container_of-style tricks in low-level and kernel-style code.

entries.heading: Why use the fixed-width types in <stdint.h> such as uint32_t?
entries.text: To get a guaranteed exact width and signedness across platforms. Because they are always faster. Because int is illegal in modern C. To force heap allocation. Protocols and hardware layouts need exact sizes; int/long widths vary between platforms.

entries.heading: What is a bitfield in a struct?
entries.text: A member declared with a specific bit width; its packing and layout are largely implementation-defined. A pointer to a bit array. A guaranteed portable on-wire format. A 1-byte boolean only. Because ordering and padding of bitfields are not portable, prefer explicit masks and shifts for wire formats.

entries.heading: What does getpid() return?
entries.text: The process ID of the calling process. The parent's process ID. A file descriptor. The thread ID always. getppid() returns the parent's PID; PIDs identify processes to signals and waitpid.

entries.heading: What are select, poll, and epoll used for?
entries.text: Waiting for I/O readiness on multiple file descriptors at once. Allocating memory. Creating processes. Sorting arrays. epoll scales better than select/poll for very large descriptor sets on Linux.

entries.heading: What does a variable declared with _Atomic (or in <stdatomic.h>) provide?
entries.text: Indivisible operations and a defined memory ordering for concurrent access. Faster non-atomic access. Automatic mutex locking of the whole program. Read-only storage. Atomics are the correct tool for lock-free sharing between threads, unlike volatile which lacks atomicity.

entries.heading: What is a memory barrier / fence for?
entries.text: To constrain the ordering of memory operations as seen by other threads or hardware. To free memory. To zero a buffer. To flush a file to disk. Modern CPUs and compilers reorder accesses; fences (or acquire/release atomics) enforce needed ordering.

entries.heading: Why can unaligned access to a multi-byte value be a problem?
entries.text: On some architectures it faults or is slow; portable code uses memcpy into a properly typed variable. It always works with no cost. It changes endianness. It is a compile-time error everywhere. memcpy-based access avoids strict-aliasing and alignment issues when parsing byte buffers.

entries.heading: What does the close() return value being checked protect against?
entries.text: Detecting deferred write errors that surface only when the descriptor is closed. Preventing the file from reopening. Making close faster. Nothing; close never fails. For data integrity, especially over networks or with buffered writeback, fsync and a checked close matter.

entries.heading: What does the & (bitwise AND) with a mask like 0xFF accomplish?
entries.text: Extracts the low 8 bits of a value. Adds 255 to the value. Checks equality with 255. Negates the value. Masking and shifting are the basic tools for packing and unpacking fields in registers and protocols.

entries.heading: Performance Optimization
entries.text: 30 questions

entries.heading: Why is stride-one, sequential array access usually faster than scattered access?
entries.text: It uses full cache lines and enables hardware prefetching, reducing cache misses. It uses fewer CPU instructions per element. It avoids integer overflow. It disables branch prediction. Memory moves in cache lines; contiguous access amortizes each miss over many useful bytes and the prefetcher can stay ahead.

entries.heading: For a 2D array in C, which loop order is cache-friendly?
entries.text: Iterate the last index (columns) in the inner loop, matching row-major storage. Iterate the first index in the inner loop. Order does not affect performance. Always iterate columns then rows. C stores arrays row-major, so varying the rightmost index fastest walks memory contiguously.

entries.heading: What is false sharing?
entries.text: Two threads writing different variables that happen to share one cache line, causing coherence traffic. Two threads reading the same constant. Sharing a file descriptor across processes. A data race on a single variable. Even without a logical conflict the line ping-pongs between cores; padding or aligning per-thread data to a cache line avoids it.

entries.heading: What does function inlining primarily eliminate?
entries.text: Call overhead, and it exposes the body to further optimization across the boundary. All memory allocations. Cache misses. The need for a stack. Inlining removes the call/return and argument setup and lets the optimizer specialize the code, at the cost of code size.

entries.heading: How can restrict improve generated code?
entries.text: By promising no aliasing so the compiler can keep values in registers instead of reloading after every store. By forcing SIMD instructions. By zeroing memory faster. By making pointers 64-bit. Without an aliasing guarantee the compiler must assume a write through one pointer may change data read through another.

entries.heading: What is the difference between a memory-bandwidth-bound and a compute-bound loop?
entries.text: Bandwidth-bound is limited by moving data; compute-bound is limited by arithmetic throughput. They are the same thing. Compute-bound loops never touch memory. Bandwidth-bound loops have no arithmetic. The right fix differs: improve locality or reduce traffic for bandwidth-bound code; increase parallelism or reduce work for compute-bound code.

entries.heading: What is the recommended first step before optimizing C code?
entries.text: Profile to find the actual hotspot and bottleneck class. Rewrite the hottest guess in assembly. Enable every compiler flag available. Replace all loops with recursion. Profiling prevents wasted effort on code that is not the bottleneck and reveals whether misses, mispredicts, or arithmetic dominate.

entries.heading: How does an unpredictable branch inside a hot loop hurt performance?
entries.text: Frequent mispredictions flush the pipeline, so branchless or sorted-data approaches can be faster. It increases memory alignment. It disables the cache. It always causes a page fault. A mispredict wastes many cycles; techniques include making the branch predictable, using conditional moves, or masking.

entries.heading: What does compiling with -O2 versus -O0 change about the semantics of correct C?
entries.text: Nothing for well-defined programs; it only changes performance, but it may expose latent UB. It changes the language rules the code must follow. It makes signed overflow defined. It disables the standard library. Optimizers rely on the absence of UB, so a program that only appeared to work at -O0 can break at -O2 by exposing existing bugs.

entries.heading: What is the benefit of packing a hot data structure into fewer cache lines?
entries.text: Fewer lines touched per operation means fewer misses and better bandwidth use. It guarantees vectorization. It removes the need for locks. It makes malloc faster. Reducing the working-set footprint and avoiding straddling loads keeps more of the structure hot in cache.

entries.heading: What is the difference between temporal and spatial locality?
entries.text: Temporal reuses the same data soon; spatial uses nearby addresses soon. Temporal is about threads; spatial is about processes. They are the same. Temporal refers to disk and spatial to RAM. Caches and prefetchers exploit both; good algorithms are designed to maximize reuse and contiguity.

entries.heading: Roughly how expensive is a main-memory (DRAM) access compared to an L1 cache hit?
entries.text: Often about two orders of magnitude slower (tens of thousands of cycles vs a few). About the same. Slightly slower, within 2x. Faster, because DRAM is larger. This gap is why cache misses dominate many workloads and why locality optimizations pay off; DRAM latency is on the order of ~100 ns.

entries.heading: What does loop unrolling aim to achieve?
entries.text: Reduce loop-control overhead and expose more instruction-level parallelism. Guarantee the loop runs fewer times. Eliminate all memory access. Force single-threaded execution. Compilers often unroll automatically; excessive manual unrolling can bloat code and hurt the instruction cache.

entries.heading: What is SIMD / vectorization?
entries.text: Executing one instruction on multiple data elements at once (e.g. SSE/AVX/NEON). Running multiple processes. A memory allocation strategy. A branch-prediction technique. Contiguous, aligned, branch-free inner loops vectorize best; the compiler auto-vectorizes when it can prove safety.

entries.heading: How does integer division compare to multiplication in cost?
entries.text: Division and modulo are typically much slower than multiplication. Division is faster than multiplication. They cost exactly the same. Multiplication is not supported in hardware. Compilers replace division by a constant with multiply-and-shift; avoid division in tight loops when possible.

entries.heading: For unsigned integers, how can the compiler optimize division by a power of two?
entries.text: Replace it with a right shift. Replace it with addition. It cannot optimize it. Replace it with a function call. For signed values the compiler must add correction for rounding toward zero, so the transformation is less trivial.

entries.heading: What does __builtin_expect (likely/unlikely hints) influence?
entries.text: Branch layout and prediction hints so the common path is favored. The alignment of data. The number of threads. Memory allocation size. It helps only when the programmer truly knows the bias; misuse can hurt. Profile-guided optimization is often better.

entries.heading: Why can struct-of-arrays (SoA) outperform array-of-structs (AoS)?
entries.text: Processing one field across many elements gives contiguous, vectorizable access with no wasted cache-line bytes. SoA uses less code. AoS cannot be allocated on the heap. SoA avoids all cache misses. Data-oriented design lays out data by access pattern, which matters most in tight numeric loops.

entries.heading: What does link-time optimization (LTO) enable?
entries.text: Cross-translation-unit optimization such as inlining functions defined in other files. Faster linking only, with no code changes. Running the linker on the GPU. Stripping debug symbols. LTO defers optimization to link time when the whole program is visible, at the cost of longer builds.

entries.heading: Why should you hoist allocations out of a hot loop?
entries.text: malloc/free per iteration adds latency and can fragment the heap; reuse a buffer instead. malloc is faster inside loops. Allocation cannot happen outside loops. It changes the result. Reusing a preallocated buffer or arena removes per-iteration allocator overhead.

entries.heading: What does amortized O(1) mean for an operation like appending to a doubling dynamic array?
entries.text: Most appends are cheap and the occasional resize is spread out so the average per-append cost is constant. Every single append is exactly one instruction. The worst case is O(1). It never reallocates. Geometric growth (e.g. doubling) is what makes the amortized cost constant; growing by a fixed amount would be O(n) amortized.

entries.heading: What is software prefetching (e.g. __builtin_prefetch)?
entries.text: Hinting the CPU to load data into cache before it is used, to hide memory latency. Loading the whole file into RAM at startup. Precomputing all results. Disabling the hardware prefetcher. It helps irregular access the hardware prefetcher cannot predict, but wrong hints waste bandwidth.

entries.heading: What distinguishes instruction latency from throughput?
entries.text: Latency is time to finish one operation; throughput is how many can complete per cycle when pipelined. They are identical. Latency applies only to memory. Throughput is always higher-numbered. Independent operations can overlap to hit throughput limits even when each has high latency; dependency chains are latency-bound.

entries.heading: Why is volatile a poor tool for ordinary multithreaded performance code?
entries.text: It disables useful optimizations and provides neither atomicity nor cross-thread ordering; use atomics instead. It is the fastest way to share data. It automatically inserts locks. It guarantees sequential consistency. volatile is for memory-mapped I/O and signal flags, not general thread synchronization.

entries.heading: What is a data dependency chain's effect on performance?
entries.text: Serial dependencies prevent overlap, so the loop is limited by cumulative latency rather than throughput. It has no effect. It always improves vectorization. It reduces cache misses. Breaking a long reduction into several independent partial sums exposes parallelism to the CPU.

entries.heading: What is the risk of premature optimization?
entries.text: Added complexity and bugs for gains that are unmeasured or irrelevant to the real bottleneck. The code always gets slower. It violates the C standard. It prevents compilation. Optimize hot paths identified by measurement; keep cold code simple and correct.

entries.heading: How can memory bandwidth become a scaling limit with many threads?
entries.text: Threads sharing the memory subsystem can saturate bandwidth, so adding cores stops helping. More threads always scale linearly. Bandwidth is per-core and never shared. Threads never touch memory. For bandwidth-bound kernels, reducing bytes moved (blocking, compression, better layout) helps more than more threads.

entries.heading: What does cache blocking (tiling) do for a matrix operation?
entries.text: Restructures the loops so each tile fits in cache and is reused before eviction. Splits work across disks. Removes the need for multiplication. Forces single-threaded execution. Tiling raises arithmetic intensity (work per byte loaded), turning a bandwidth-bound loop into a compute-bound one.

entries.heading: Why can `const` and good const-correctness sometimes help the optimizer or at least the compiler?
entries.text: It documents intent and can enable read-only placement and better diagnostics, though it is not a strong aliasing guarantee like restrict. const guarantees a value is cached in a register regardless of aliasing. const forces inlining. const makes code slower. restrict, not const, is the aliasing tool; const mainly aids correctness and API clarity.

entries.heading: What is a hot/cold code split?
entries.text: Separating rarely executed paths (error handling) from hot paths to keep the instruction cache dense. Splitting data by temperature sensors. Running half the code on the GPU. A malloc strategy. Compilers move unlikely branches out of line; keeping hot loops compact improves I-cache and branch behavior.

entries.heading: C Libraries and Tooling
entries.text: 30 questions

entries.heading: Why is strcpy considered dangerous?
entries.text: It performs no bounds checking and overflows the destination if the source is too long. It is slower than a manual loop. It does not null-terminate. It only works on read-only strings. Prefer snprintf or carefully used bounded copies, and remember strncpy may not null-terminate on truncation.

entries.heading: What is the difference between memcpy and memmove?
entries.text: memmove handles overlapping source and destination correctly; memcpy does not. memcpy handles overlap; memmove does not. They are identical. memmove only works on strings. Calling memcpy with overlapping regions is UB; use memmove when the ranges may overlap.

entries.heading: Why is printf(user_input) a serious bug?
entries.text: The user controls the format string, allowing memory disclosure or corruption via specifiers like %n. It is merely slower than puts. It cannot print newlines. It always truncates the output. Always use a fixed format string: printf("%s", user_input). Uncontrolled format strings are an exploitable vulnerability class.

entries.heading: What does sizeof evaluate to, and what is its type?
entries.text: A compile-time constant of type size_t (for non-VLA operands). A runtime int computed by the CPU. A signed long that can be negative. A pointer to the object. Because size_t is unsigned, mixing sizeof results with signed values in comparisons can cause surprising conversions.

entries.heading: When would you use a mutex versus a plain shared variable in pthreads?
entries.text: A mutex protects a critical section so only one thread accesses shared mutable state at a time. Never; volatile is sufficient for thread safety. Only for read-only data. Mutexes are only for inter-process use. Unsynchronized concurrent access to shared mutable data is a data race and therefore UB; volatile does not fix it.

entries.heading: What class of bugs does Valgrind's memcheck detect?
entries.text: Invalid reads/writes, use of uninitialized memory, and leaks. Compile-time type errors. Logic errors in correct memory use. Network protocol mistakes. It instruments memory operations at runtime; AddressSanitizer catches a similar class faster at the cost of recompilation.

entries.heading: What does AddressSanitizer (ASan) primarily catch?
entries.text: Heap/stack/global buffer overflows and use-after-free at runtime. Race conditions only. Format string bugs at compile time. Slow functions for profiling. ASan adds redzones and shadow memory; ThreadSanitizer targets data races and UBSan targets undefined behavior.

entries.heading: Why do C header files typically use include guards or #pragma once?
entries.text: To prevent the same declarations from being included more than once in a translation unit. To make compilation slower but safer. To force functions to be inlined. To hide functions from the linker. Multiple inclusion would cause redefinition errors; a guard macro or #pragma once makes the header idempotent.

entries.heading: What is a common reason to put `static inline` functions in a header?
entries.text: To provide a definition usable in every including file without multiple-definition linker errors. To force the function onto the heap. To give it external linkage. To prevent inlining. static gives internal linkage per translation unit, so each unit gets its own copy and the linker sees no duplicate symbol.

entries.heading: What does the linker do that the compiler does not?
entries.text: Resolve symbol references across object files and libraries into a single executable. Check C syntax. Perform type checking of expressions. Expand preprocessor macros. Undefined-reference errors come from the linker when a declared symbol has no definition in any linked object or library.

entries.heading: What does strlen return?
entries.text: The number of characters before the terminating null byte. The allocated size of the buffer. The length including the null byte. The number of bytes malloc reserved. strlen walks to the first '\0', so an unterminated buffer causes an out-of-bounds read.

entries.heading: How do you detect truncation with snprintf?
entries.text: It returns the number of characters that would have been written; a value >= buffer size means truncation. It returns -1 on truncation only. It sets errno to ETRUNC. You cannot detect truncation. snprintf always null-terminates (given size > 0), and its return lets you size a second buffer exactly.

entries.heading: Why is gets() removed from standard C?
entries.text: It cannot be used safely because it has no bound and always risks buffer overflow; use fgets. It is too slow. It only reads numbers. It was replaced by printf. gets was removed in C11; fgets takes a size and is the safe replacement for line input.

entries.heading: Why prefer strtol over atoi for parsing integers?
entries.text: strtol reports errors and the parse endpoint; atoi has no error reporting and is UB on overflow. atoi is more precise. strtol is deprecated. They are identical. strtol sets errno on range errors and gives an end pointer, enabling robust input validation.

entries.heading: What is the comparator signature required by qsort?
entries.text: int cmp(const void *a, const void *b) returning negative, zero, or positive. int cmp(int a, int b). bool less(void *a, void *b). void cmp(void *a, void *b). The comparator must impose a consistent total order; an inconsistent comparator gives undefined results.

entries.heading: What does bsearch require of its input?
entries.text: The array must already be sorted by the same comparator ordering. The array must be a linked list. The array must be unsorted. Nothing about ordering. bsearch is O(log n) binary search and returns NULL if the key is not found.

entries.heading: What does memcmp return?
entries.text: A negative, zero, or positive value based on the first differing byte. 1 if equal, 0 otherwise. The number of differing bytes. A pointer to the difference. memcmp compares raw bytes, so it is not suitable for comparing structs with padding or floating-point values.

entries.heading: What do perror and strerror provide?
entries.text: A human-readable message for the current errno value. The numeric errno only. A stack trace. The exit code of the program. perror prints to stderr with a prefix; strerror returns the message string for a given errno.

entries.heading: What happens to assert() when NDEBUG is defined?
entries.text: The assertions are removed (compiled out), so their expressions must have no needed side effects. They become fatal errors. They start logging to a file. Nothing changes. Never put required side effects inside assert, since a release build with NDEBUG will drop them.

entries.heading: What is the key difference between <stdio.h> FILE* streams and raw file descriptors?
entries.text: FILE* streams add user-space buffering on top of the underlying descriptor. FILE* is unbuffered and fds are buffered. They are the same object. FILE* cannot access files. Mixing buffered stream I/O and raw descriptor I/O on the same file without flushing can interleave data unexpectedly.

entries.heading: What is the effect of fflush(stdin)?
entries.text: Undefined behavior in standard C; flushing is defined only for output/update streams. It safely discards pending input. It is the correct way to clear the input buffer. It flushes stdout. To discard input, read and drop characters until newline or EOF; fflush is for output streams.

entries.heading: What is a classic pitfall of a function-like macro such as #define SQ(x) x*x?
entries.text: Missing parentheses cause precedence bugs, and arguments with side effects are evaluated more than once. Macros cannot take arguments. It is slower than a function. It allocates memory. Write #define SQ(x) ((x)*(x)), but even then double evaluation makes SQ(i++) wrong; prefer inline functions.

entries.heading: What does ThreadSanitizer (TSan) detect?
entries.text: Data races between threads at runtime. Memory leaks only. Buffer overflows only. Slow functions. TSan complements ASan (memory errors) and UBSan (undefined behavior) in the sanitizer family.

entries.heading: What does UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) catch?
entries.text: Runtime UB such as signed overflow, invalid shifts, and misaligned or null pointer use. Compile-time syntax errors. Memory leaks. Data races. UBSan is cheap to enable and catches many latent bugs that optimizers would otherwise exploit.

entries.heading: What is the role of the C preprocessor?
entries.text: Textual transformation before compilation: #include, macro expansion, and conditional compilation. It links object files. It type-checks expressions. It optimizes machine code. The preprocessor is unaware of C types and scope, which is why macros are error-prone compared to real language features.

entries.heading: What does the const qualifier communicate in an API like `void f(const char *s)`?
entries.text: That f will not modify the string through s, improving safety and documentation. That s is stored in a register. That s must be a string literal. That f runs faster. const-correctness lets callers pass read-only data and lets the compiler catch accidental writes.

entries.heading: Why should you check the return value of scanf or fread?
entries.text: They return how many items/bytes were successfully read, which may be fewer than requested on error or EOF. They always read exactly what you asked. Their return value is meaningless. They set the buffer to NULL on failure. Ignoring short reads leads to using uninitialized data; validate the count before trusting the buffer.

entries.heading: What is typically the purpose of a build tool like make or CMake?
entries.text: To describe how sources are compiled and linked and to rebuild only what changed. To run the program. To detect memory leaks. To format source code. Correct dependency tracking avoids stale objects; CMake also generates platform-specific build files.

entries.heading: What does linking against a static library (.a) versus a shared library (.so) change?
entries.text: A static library's code is copied into the executable; a shared library is loaded at run time and can be shared between programs. There is no difference. Static libraries load at run time. Shared libraries cannot export symbols. Shared libraries save memory and allow updates without relinking, but add a runtime dependency and load-time resolution.

entries.heading: Why should error handling avoid ignoring the return value of malloc, open, or write?
entries.text: These calls can fail, and silently continuing leads to null dereferences, data loss, or security bugs. Their returns are always success. Checking them slows the program too much. The compiler checks them automatically. Robust C code treats every fallible call's return as data to validate, not decoration.

entries.heading: Git practice
entries.text: Practice repository history, collaboration, debugging, release, and recovery workflows.

entries.heading: Phase 1: Repository management
entries.text: Review init, clone, the working tree/index/HEAD model, remotes, .gitignore, tags, bare repos, submodules, and object cleanup.

entries.heading: Phase 2: Branching strategies
entries.text: Study branches as pointers, HEAD, fast-forward vs three-way merges, rebase, detached HEAD, and models like trunk-based and Git Flow.

entries.heading: Phase 3: Collaboration
entries.text: Practice fetch/pull/push, forks and upstream, pull requests and review, conflict resolution, protected branches, and staying in sync.

entries.heading: Phase 4: Core operations
entries.text: Master commit and amend, reset soft/mixed/hard, revert, cherry-pick, stash, reflog, bisect, and reading log and diff.

entries.heading: Phase 5: Best practices
entries.text: Cover atomic commits and messages, never rewriting shared history, secrets hygiene, small PRs, signing, hooks, and safe force pushes.

entries.heading: Three trees
entries.text: Git tracks the working directory, the staging area (index), and HEAD (the last commit). Most commands move changes between these three.

entries.heading: Commits are snapshots
entries.text: Each commit records a full tree plus parent links and is identified by a content hash. Branches and tags are just named pointers to commits.

entries.heading: Branch is a pointer
entries.text: A branch is a lightweight movable reference to a commit; creating and switching branches is cheap because no files are copied.

entries.heading: Merge vs rebase
entries.text: Merge joins histories with a merge commit and preserves what really happened; rebase replays commits onto a new base for a linear history but rewrites commit IDs.

entries.heading: Local vs remote
entries.text: fetch updates remote-tracking refs without touching your work; pull also integrates; push publishes your commits. You always commit locally first.

entries.heading: Rewriting history
entries.text: amend, rebase, and reset --hard rewrite commits. This is fine on local/unpushed work but breaks collaborators when done to shared branches.

entries.heading: Reflog safety net
entries.text: The reflog records where HEAD and branches have pointed, so 'lost' commits after a bad reset or rebase are usually recoverable.

entries.heading: Undo tools
entries.text: revert makes a new commit that undoes another and is safe for public history; reset moves branch pointers and is best for local history.

entries.heading: Repository Management
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What does `git init` do?
entries.text: Creates a new empty repository by adding a .git directory in the current folder. Downloads a repository from a server. Creates the first commit automatically. Connects to a remote named origin. It initializes the object database and refs; nothing is committed until you stage and commit.

entries.heading: What does `git clone <url>` do?
entries.text: Copies a remote repository including its history and sets up a remote named origin. Copies only the latest files with no history. Creates a bare mirror only. Initializes an empty repo. clone also checks out the default branch and creates remote-tracking branches for origin.

entries.heading: What is the staging area (index)?
entries.text: A place where you assemble exactly the changes that will go into the next commit. A backup of the remote. The list of ignored files. A branch that holds work in progress. git add moves changes into the index; git commit records the index as a new commit.

entries.heading: What does a .gitignore file control?
entries.text: Which untracked files Git should not show or stage. Which committed files to delete. Which branches are protected. Which remotes are trusted. .gitignore only affects untracked files; a file already tracked keeps being tracked until you git rm --cached it.

entries.heading: What is a remote in Git?
entries.text: A named reference (like origin) to another copy of the repository, usually on a server. A branch on your local machine. A snapshot of the working tree. A type of commit. You interact with remotes via fetch, pull, and push; a repo can have several remotes such as origin and upstream.

entries.heading: What does `git remote add origin <url>` do?
entries.text: Registers a remote named origin pointing at the given URL. Pushes your code immediately. Creates a new branch called origin. Clones the repository. After adding the remote you still need to push (often with -u to set the upstream tracking branch).

entries.heading: What is a bare repository?
entries.text: A repository with no working tree, used as a shared/central remote to push to and pull from. A repository with no commits. A repository with no branches. A read-only clone. Server-side repos are bare because a checked-out working tree there would conflict with incoming pushes.

entries.heading: What is the difference between a lightweight and an annotated tag?
entries.text: An annotated tag is a full object with tagger, date, message, and can be signed; a lightweight tag is just a name pointing to a commit. They are identical. Lightweight tags can be signed but annotated cannot. Annotated tags cannot point to commits. Releases usually use annotated (or signed) tags so the tag carries metadata; tags are not pushed automatically.

entries.heading: What does `git gc` do?
entries.text: Cleans up and compresses the object database, removing unreachable objects and packing loose ones. Deletes all branches. Garbage-collects the working directory files. Removes remote-tracking branches. Git runs gc automatically at times; unreachable objects may still be recoverable from the reflog until it expires.

entries.heading: What is a Git submodule?
entries.text: A separate repository embedded in a parent repo at a pinned commit. A branch inside another branch. A compressed archive of history. A backup of the index. The parent records the submodule's URL and exact commit; you must update submodules explicitly to move that pointer.

entries.heading: Branching Strategies
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is a branch in Git?
entries.text: A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit. A full copy of the repository files. A snapshot of the staging area. A remote server. Because a branch is just a ref, creating one is instant and cheap; the commit graph does the real work.

entries.heading: What does HEAD refer to?
entries.text: A reference to the currently checked-out commit, usually via the current branch. The first commit in history. The remote's latest commit. The staging area. Normally HEAD points at a branch; when it points directly at a commit you are in 'detached HEAD' state.

entries.heading: What is a fast-forward merge?
entries.text: Moving the branch pointer forward to the target commit because there was no divergence, creating no merge commit. A merge that always creates a merge commit. A rebase in disguise. A merge that deletes the other branch. Fast-forward is possible when the current branch is a direct ancestor of the branch being merged in.

entries.heading: What is a three-way (true) merge?
entries.text: Combining two diverged branches using their common ancestor, producing a merge commit with two parents. Merging three branches at once. A merge that rewrites history. A merge that requires a rebase first. Git uses the merge base plus both tips to compute the result; conflicts arise where both sides changed the same lines.

entries.heading: What does `git rebase <base>` do?
entries.text: Reapplies your branch's commits on top of <base>, creating new commits and a linear history. Merges base into your branch with a merge commit. Deletes commits since base. Pushes your branch to base. Rebase rewrites commit IDs, so it should be used on local/unpublished commits to avoid disrupting collaborators.

entries.heading: What is a key difference between merge and rebase?
entries.text: Merge preserves the true, branching history with a merge commit; rebase produces a linear history by rewriting commits. Merge rewrites history and rebase does not. They produce identical commit graphs. Rebase can only be done on the main branch. Choose merge to keep an accurate record, or rebase to keep history tidy; never rebase shared branches.

entries.heading: What is a detached HEAD state?
entries.text: HEAD points directly at a commit rather than a branch, so new commits are not on any branch. A corrupted repository. A branch with no commits. A branch that was deleted remotely. Commits made while detached can be lost when you switch away unless you create a branch to keep them.

entries.heading: What characterizes trunk-based development?
entries.text: Everyone integrates small changes into one main branch frequently, using very short-lived branches or none. Many long-lived feature branches merged once a quarter. No use of a main branch. Every developer keeps a permanent personal branch. Frequent integration keeps merges small and pairs well with feature flags and continuous integration.

entries.heading: What is Git Flow?
entries.text: A branching model with long-lived main and develop branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches. A single-branch workflow. A Git command that auto-merges. A hosting service. Git Flow suits scheduled releases but can be heavy; many teams prefer simpler trunk-based or GitHub-flow models.

entries.heading: Why keep feature branches short-lived?
entries.text: The longer a branch diverges from main, the larger and riskier the eventual merge and conflicts become. Git deletes old branches automatically. Long branches use too much disk space. Short branches cannot have conflicts by definition. Frequent integration (or rebasing onto main) keeps a branch close to the mainline and easy to merge.

entries.heading: Collaboration Workflows
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
entries.text: fetch only downloads remote changes into remote-tracking branches; pull fetches and then merges (or rebases) into your branch. They are identical. fetch merges and pull only downloads. pull only works on the main branch. fetch is non-destructive to your work, letting you inspect changes before integrating them.

entries.heading: What does `git push` do?
entries.text: Uploads your local commits to a branch on a remote repository. Downloads commits from the remote. Creates a local branch. Stages your changes. You can only push commits; uncommitted working-tree changes are never pushed.

entries.heading: What is a fork in the pull-request workflow?
entries.text: A server-side copy of a repository under your own account that you push to and propose changes from. A local branch. A merge conflict. A detached HEAD. Forks let outside contributors work without write access to the original, then open pull requests back to it.

entries.heading: What does 'upstream' usually refer to?
entries.text: The original repository a fork was made from, or the remote branch a local branch tracks. The newest commit on main. A protected branch. The staging area. Contributors often add an 'upstream' remote to sync their fork with the original project.

entries.heading: What is the purpose of a pull request (or merge request)?
entries.text: To propose merging a branch's changes, enabling review, discussion, and automated checks before integration. To pull the latest code from main. To force-push to a shared branch. To delete a remote branch. Pull requests are a collaboration and review gate, not a Git command themselves.

entries.heading: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
entries.text: Edit the conflicted files to the desired result, remove the conflict markers, stage them, and commit. Delete the repository and re-clone. Run git push --force. Wait for Git to resolve it automatically. Conflicts occur where both sides changed the same region; Git needs a human to choose the correct combined content.

entries.heading: What do the markers <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> indicate in a file?
entries.text: A conflict region: your side, the divider, and the other side's version. A syntax error in the code. A signed commit. A submodule boundary. You must edit out all three markers and keep the intended content before the merge can be committed.

entries.heading: What is a protected branch?
entries.text: A branch with rules such as no force-push, no deletion, and required reviews or passing CI before merge. A branch only the owner can see. A branch stored in a bare repo. A branch that cannot be checked out. Protecting main prevents accidental history rewrites and enforces review/quality gates.

entries.heading: When is `git pull --rebase` useful?
entries.text: When syncing with a shared branch and you want to replay your local commits on top, avoiding an extra merge commit. When you want to force-push. When deleting a branch. When creating a tag. It keeps history linear, but like any rebase it rewrites your local commit IDs before you push them.

entries.heading: Why sync your feature branch with main frequently during collaboration?
entries.text: To surface and resolve conflicts in small increments instead of one large painful merge later. Because Git requires a daily merge. To reduce repository size. To avoid needing pull requests. Regular merges or rebases from main keep divergence small and integration smooth.

entries.heading: Core Git Operations
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What does `git commit --amend` do?
entries.text: Replaces the most recent commit with a new one, letting you fix its message or contents. Adds a second parent to the commit. Merges the last two commits on the remote. Creates a new branch. Because it rewrites the last commit, avoid amending a commit you have already pushed to a shared branch.

entries.heading: How do `git reset --soft`, `--mixed`, and `--hard` differ?
entries.text: soft moves HEAD only (keeps index and working tree), mixed also resets the index, hard resets index and working tree, discarding changes. They are all identical. hard is the safest of the three. soft deletes files from disk. --hard is destructive to uncommitted work; --soft is useful to uncommit while keeping everything staged.

entries.heading: What does `git revert <commit>` do?
entries.text: Creates a new commit that undoes the changes of the given commit, without rewriting history. Deletes the commit from history. Resets HEAD to the commit. Amends the commit. revert is the safe way to undo something already public, since it adds rather than rewrites history.

entries.heading: What does `git cherry-pick <commit>` do?
entries.text: Applies the changes from a specific commit onto the current branch as a new commit. Merges an entire branch. Removes a commit from history. Renames a branch. It is handy for pulling one fix into another branch, though it duplicates the change as a new commit ID.

entries.heading: What does `git stash` do?
entries.text: Saves your uncommitted changes and reverts the working tree to a clean state so you can switch context. Commits your changes to main. Deletes your uncommitted changes permanently. Pushes changes to a remote. git stash pop (or apply) restores the saved changes later; stashes are stored in a stack.

entries.heading: What is the git reflog useful for?
entries.text: Recovering commits after a bad reset, rebase, or branch deletion by showing where HEAD and refs pointed. Listing remote branches. Showing the staged diff. Configuring hooks. Even 'lost' commits usually remain reachable via the reflog until it expires and gc runs.

entries.heading: What does `git bisect` help you do?
entries.text: Binary-search the commit history to find the commit that introduced a bug. Split a commit into two. Merge two branches by half. Bisect a file into halves. You mark a known-good and known-bad commit, and bisect checks out midpoints until it isolates the culprit.

entries.heading: What is the difference between `git diff` and `git diff --staged`?
entries.text: git diff shows unstaged changes (working tree vs index); --staged shows staged changes (index vs HEAD). They show the same thing. git diff shows staged changes only. --staged compares two branches. Understanding the working tree/index/HEAD trio is key to knowing which diff you are looking at.

entries.heading: What does `git log --oneline --graph --all` display?
entries.text: A compact, visual commit history showing branch and merge topology across all refs. Only the current file's changes. The list of remotes. The staged files. The graph view is invaluable for understanding how branches diverged and merged.

entries.heading: How do you unstage a file while keeping its changes in the working tree?
entries.text: git restore --staged <file> (or git reset HEAD <file>). git checkout <file>. git rm <file>. git commit <file>. This moves the change out of the index back to unstaged; git restore <file> (without --staged) would instead discard the changes.

entries.heading: Best Practices
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: Why should you avoid rewriting history on a shared/published branch?
entries.text: Force-pushing rewritten commits breaks everyone else's history and causes painful re-syncs and lost work. It makes the repo larger. Git forbids it entirely. It has no downside. Rewrite freely on local, unpushed work; once others may have based work on it, prefer revert over rewrite.

entries.heading: What makes a good commit message?
entries.text: A concise imperative summary line, a blank line, then a body explaining what and why when needed. A single word like 'fix'. The full diff pasted as text. The author's name repeated. Clear messages make history, blame, and reviews far more useful than 'update' or 'stuff'.

entries.heading: What is an atomic commit?
entries.text: A commit containing one logical, self-contained change that builds and could be reverted on its own. A commit that touches every file. A commit with no message. A commit made by a bot. Small focused commits make review, revert, cherry-pick, and bisect much more effective.

entries.heading: Why should you never commit secrets like API keys or passwords?
entries.text: They persist in history even after deletion and must be treated as compromised and rotated. They make commits larger. Git blocks them automatically. They only matter in public repos. Removing them requires history rewriting (e.g. git filter-repo) plus rotating the credential; prevention via .gitignore and secret scanning is better.

entries.heading: How do you stop tracking a file that is already committed while keeping it on disk?
entries.text: git rm --cached <file>, then add it to .gitignore and commit. git rm <file>. Just add it to .gitignore. git reset --hard. Plain git rm deletes it locally too; --cached removes it only from the index/tracking.

entries.heading: What are Git hooks?
entries.text: Scripts that run automatically on events like pre-commit, commit-msg, or pre-push. Remote branches. Tags that trigger releases. A type of merge. Hooks enforce local checks (linting, tests, message format); server-side hooks or CI enforce them for everyone.

entries.heading: What problem does Git LFS solve?
entries.text: It stores large binary files outside normal history using lightweight pointers, keeping the repo small. It compresses commit messages. It speeds up branching. It signs commits. Committing large binaries directly bloats every clone; LFS keeps the working files but offloads their storage.

entries.heading: What does a signed commit or tag provide?
entries.text: A cryptographic (GPG or SSH) signature verifying who authored it, improving trust and integrity. Faster pushes. Automatic conflict resolution. A smaller repository. Signing helps prove provenance, which matters for releases and supply-chain security.

entries.heading: Why prefer small, focused pull requests?
entries.text: They are easier and faster to review thoroughly, so they catch more bugs and merge sooner. They use less bandwidth. Git requires them to be small. Large PRs cannot be merged. Huge PRs get shallow reviews; splitting work into reviewable units improves quality and velocity.

entries.heading: When is `git push --force-with-lease` safer than `git push --force`?
entries.text: It refuses to overwrite the remote if someone else pushed changes you have not seen, preventing you from clobbering their work. It is never safer. It skips authentication. It force-pushes to every branch at once. --force-with-lease checks the remote ref matches your expectation first, unlike a blind --force.
