entries.heading: Operating systems practice
entries.text: Study processes, threads, virtual memory, synchronization, scheduling, I/O, and kernel interfaces.

entries.heading: Phase 1: Process model
entries.text: Master process creation, fork, exec, wait, exit status, signals, process IDs, zombies, and file descriptor inheritance.

entries.heading: Phase 2: Scheduling and concurrency
entries.text: Review runnable, blocked, preemption, context switch cost, mutexes, condition variables, semaphores, atomics, and deadlock.

entries.heading: Phase 3: Virtual memory
entries.text: Study address spaces, page tables, TLBs, page faults, mmap, copy-on-write, demand paging, and memory protection.

entries.heading: Phase 4: Files and I/O
entries.text: Practice file descriptors, open file descriptions, page cache, blocking I/O, epoll, fsync, pipes, sockets, and zero-copy ideas.

entries.heading: Phase 5: Debug and real time
entries.text: Use strace, perf, gdb, logs, stack traces, scheduling metrics, and real-time latency analysis to diagnose real systems.

entries.heading: Process vs thread
entries.text: Processes have separate virtual address spaces. Threads share the process address space but have independent execution contexts and stacks.

entries.heading: fork and copy-on-write
entries.text: Linux avoids copying all pages at fork by sharing pages until a process writes, then copying the changed page.

entries.heading: Synchronization contract
entries.text: Locks protect invariants. Condition variables wait for state changes and should be used with a predicate loop.

entries.heading: Virtual memory
entries.text: Virtual memory hides physical placement, enforces protection, enables demand paging, and supports shared mappings.

entries.heading: Page cache
entries.text: Buffered file I/O usually goes through the page cache, which can improve performance but complicates durability and memory accounting.

entries.heading: File descriptor inheritance
entries.text: Descriptors can survive fork and exec unless close-on-exec is set, which matters for servers and subprocess management.

entries.heading: Real-time concern
entries.text: Real-time systems optimize worst-case latency and predictability, not just average throughput.

entries.heading: Debugging rule
entries.text: When stuck, classify the wait: CPU-bound, blocked on I/O, blocked on a lock/futex, sleeping on a timer, or stopped by a signal.

entries.heading: Processes, Threads, and Signals
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What does fork() create?
entries.text: A child process that initially resembles the parent. A new kernel filesystem. A GPU kernel. A new TCP packet only. fork duplicates the calling process and returns differently in parent and child.

entries.heading: What does execve() do?
entries.text: Replaces the current process image with a new program. Creates a second process without changing code. Only waits for a child. Only changes file permissions. exec does not create a new process by itself; it changes what the current process runs.

entries.heading: Why does a shell commonly fork before exec?
entries.text: So the shell can keep running while the child becomes the command. Because exec always creates two shells. To avoid using PATH. To disable signals. The child can exec the requested command while the parent shell waits or continues.

entries.heading: What is a zombie process?
entries.text: A terminated child whose status has not been reaped. A process using too much RAM. A process without a PID. A thread with no stack. The kernel keeps minimal status until the parent calls wait-like APIs.

entries.heading: What is an orphan process?
entries.text: A process whose parent exited. A process with no memory. A process that cannot open files by definition. A CPU interrupt. The OS reparents orphans, commonly to an init-like process.

entries.heading: What do threads in the same process share?
entries.text: Address space and many process resources. Separate address spaces by default. Nothing at all. Only their instruction pointer. Threads share memory, which makes communication easy and races possible.

entries.heading: What is the danger of fork() in a multithreaded program?
entries.text: Only the calling thread exists in the child, but locks may be inherited in locked states. The child has no address space. All files are always closed. Signals become impossible. After fork in a multithreaded process, async-signal-safe rules matter until exec.

entries.heading: What is a signal?
entries.text: An asynchronous notification delivered to a process or thread. A file descriptor offset. A page table entry. A compiler optimization flag. Signals can interrupt normal control flow and require careful handlers.

entries.heading: What is SIGCHLD used for?
entries.text: Notifying a parent that a child changed state. Allocating virtual memory. Locking a mutex. Flushing disk caches. Parents often use SIGCHLD plus wait to reap children.

entries.heading: What does close-on-exec prevent?
entries.text: Accidental descriptor inheritance across exec. Process creation. Page faults. Thread creation. FD_CLOEXEC helps avoid leaking descriptors into child programs.

entries.heading: Scheduling and Synchronization
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is a context switch?
entries.text: Saving one task state and restoring another. A type of file path. A neural network layer. A linker section. Context switches enable multitasking but have overhead.

entries.heading: What does preemption mean?
entries.text: The OS can interrupt a running task to run another. A process must finish before scheduling. Only one program can ever run. The disk cache is disabled. Preemption is central to responsive multitasking.

entries.heading: What is a runnable task?
entries.text: A task ready to execute if a CPU is available. A task waiting for disk I/O only. A terminated process. A file descriptor. Schedulers choose among runnable tasks.

entries.heading: What is a race condition?
entries.text: A correctness bug depending on timing between concurrent operations. A faster scheduler. A type of executable file. An intentional page fault. Races happen when shared state is accessed without correct synchronization.

entries.heading: What does a mutex protect?
entries.text: A critical section or shared invariant. Only process IDs. Only executable files. Only GPU memory. A mutex provides mutual exclusion around shared state.

entries.heading: Why use a condition variable with a mutex?
entries.text: To wait for a predicate while protecting shared state. To replace all memory allocation. To make fork impossible. To force CPU affinity. The mutex protects the predicate checked before and after waiting.

entries.heading: Why should condition waits use a while loop?
entries.text: Spurious wakeups or consumed conditions can occur. The compiler requires it for syntax. It always improves cache size. It prevents process creation. Always recheck the predicate after waking.

entries.heading: What is priority inversion?
entries.text: A high-priority task waits on a low-priority task while medium-priority tasks run. A high-priority task always runs forever. A file's permissions invert. A page table becomes invalid. Priority inheritance can reduce this problem.

entries.heading: What four conditions are associated with deadlock?
entries.text: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Fork, exec, wait, exit. Open, read, write, close. Text, data, bss, heap. Breaking one of these conditions can prevent deadlock.

entries.heading: When is a spinlock appropriate?
entries.text: For very short waits where sleeping is not allowed or too expensive. For blocking disk I/O. For long network requests. For user prompts. Spinlocks burn CPU while waiting and must be used carefully.

entries.heading: Virtual Memory
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is virtual memory?
entries.text: An address-space abstraction mapped to physical memory by the OS and MMU. A type of monitor cable. Only a compiler warning. A replacement for files. Virtual memory provides isolation, sharing, and demand paging.

entries.heading: What is a page table?
entries.text: A structure mapping virtual pages to physical frames and permissions. A filesystem directory. A scheduler queue only. An optimizer state. The MMU consults page-table data during address translation.

entries.heading: What does the TLB cache?
entries.text: Recent virtual-to-physical translations. Open file names. TCP connections only. Shell history. TLB hits avoid expensive page-table walks.

entries.heading: What is a page fault?
entries.text: An exception when a virtual access cannot be satisfied by current mappings. A failed shell command only. A disk sector size. A thread priority. The OS may allocate, load, fix permissions, or kill the process depending on the fault.

entries.heading: What is demand paging?
entries.text: Loading pages into memory only when needed. Loading all files at boot. Disabling virtual memory. Pinning every page. Demand paging improves memory efficiency and startup behavior.

entries.heading: What is copy-on-write?
entries.text: Shared pages are copied only when a writer modifies them. All pages are copied at fork immediately. Writes are never allowed. The disk becomes read-only. COW makes fork cheaper for common fork-then-exec workflows.

entries.heading: What does mmap do?
entries.text: Maps files or anonymous memory into a process address space. Creates a new process. Computes CPU priority. Only sends network packets. mmap supports file-backed memory, shared memory, and lazy loading.

entries.heading: Why can memory overcommit be risky?
entries.text: Allocation may appear to succeed but fail later when pages are actually touched. It prevents all paging. It makes files smaller. It removes page tables. Overcommit separates virtual reservation from physical backing.

entries.heading: What is swapping?
entries.text: Moving memory pages to/from storage under pressure. Changing process names. Rotating CPU cores. Compiling code. Swapping can keep systems alive but severely hurt latency.

entries.heading: Why use mlock in real-time code?
entries.text: To avoid page faults in locked memory during critical execution. To create a child process. To flush a socket. To sort page tables. Real-time code often avoids unpredictable page-fault latency.

entries.heading: Filesystems and I/O
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is a file descriptor?
entries.text: A per-process integer handle to an open file-like object. A disk block checksum. A thread ID only. A memory page size. Descriptors refer to open files, sockets, pipes, devices, and more.

entries.heading: What is an open file description?
entries.text: Kernel state shared by duplicated descriptors, including offset and status flags. A comment in source code. A file name string only. A page fault record. forked or duped descriptors can share the same open file description.

entries.heading: What does pipe() create?
entries.text: A unidirectional communication channel with read and write ends. A new address space. A disk partition. A mutex. Pipes are common for parent-child and shell pipeline communication.

entries.heading: What is blocking I/O?
entries.text: The caller waits until the operation can make progress or complete. I/O that never waits. I/O using only CPU registers. A type of lock file. Blocking calls can simplify code but may stall threads.

entries.heading: What is nonblocking I/O?
entries.text: Operations return immediately if they would block. Operations ignore errors. The kernel copies all files twice. The scheduler stops. Nonblocking I/O is often paired with event loops.

entries.heading: What is epoll used for?
entries.text: Waiting efficiently for readiness events on many descriptors. Replacing virtual memory. Compiling executables. Changing image resolution. epoll is important for scalable Linux network servers.

entries.heading: What does the page cache do?
entries.text: Caches file data in memory for buffered I/O. Stores only process IDs. Caches DNS names only. Disables writes. The page cache can improve read/write performance and merge I/O.

entries.heading: Why call fsync?
entries.text: To request durable persistence of file data and metadata needed for the file. To make fork faster. To clear gradients. To increase CPU clock. Without fsync-like durability points, data may still be in volatile caches.

entries.heading: What is zero-copy I/O trying to reduce?
entries.text: Unnecessary data copies between buffers or kernel/user space. The number of source files. The number of process IDs. The size of the scheduler. Avoiding copies can improve throughput and reduce CPU use.

entries.heading: Why can direct I/O be difficult?
entries.text: It often requires alignment and explicit buffering decisions. It always makes code shorter. It removes hardware constraints. It cannot fail. Bypassing the page cache shifts more responsibility to the application.

entries.heading: Debugging and Real-Time
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: When is strace useful?
entries.text: To observe system calls, errors, signals, and blocking behavior. To train a model. To edit a linker script. To generate images. strace is often the fastest way to see what a Linux process asks the kernel to do.

entries.heading: When is perf useful?
entries.text: To sample CPU hotspots and performance counters. To change file permissions only. To create a process. To send ROS messages. perf helps identify where CPU time and hardware events are spent.

entries.heading: How do you debug a deadlock?
entries.text: Inspect thread stacks and lock ownership/waiting relationships. Increase image resolution. Delete logs. Disable all tests. Deadlocks reveal themselves in wait chains and stuck lock acquisitions.

entries.heading: What does a futex wait often indicate?
entries.text: A thread is blocked on a user-space synchronization primitive backed by the kernel. A filesystem is formatted. A GPU kernel is compiling. A signal is impossible. pthread mutexes and condition variables often use futexes under contention.

entries.heading: What should you collect for a hung process?
entries.text: Thread stack traces, system-call state, CPU usage, logs, and lock/wait information. Only screenshots. Only final exit code. Only CSS files. A hang needs evidence about where execution is waiting.

entries.heading: What is tail latency?
entries.text: High-percentile latency such as p99 or p999. Average file size. The number of open descriptors. The first byte of a page. Tail latency matters for user-visible reliability and real-time systems.

entries.heading: What is a real-time system optimizing for?
entries.text: Predictable bounded timing behavior. Only maximum throughput. Only disk capacity. Only code size. Missing deadlines can be more important than average speed.

entries.heading: Why can paging hurt real-time behavior?
entries.text: Page faults can introduce unpredictable latency. Paging always improves deadlines. Paging disables scheduling. Paging removes all memory pressure. Real-time code often locks memory or pre-faults pages.

entries.heading: What is CPU isolation useful for?
entries.text: Reducing interference on selected CPUs for latency-sensitive work. Replacing memory protection. Deleting interrupts. Changing file ownership. Isolation can reduce scheduler noise but must be configured with interrupts and kernel threads in mind.

entries.heading: Why measure before tuning kernel parameters?
entries.text: Because tuning can shift bottlenecks or hurt other workloads. Because measurement is never useful. Because all defaults are wrong. Because logs are automatically perfect. Performance tuning should be driven by evidence and workload-specific goals.

entries.heading: Embedded systems practice
entries.text: Study firmware, interrupts, buses, DMA, memory-mapped I/O, real-time behavior, and board-level debugging.

entries.heading: Phase 1: C/C++ and memory
entries.text: Review volatile, const, static, alignment, stack, heap, memory-mapped registers, bit masks, undefined behavior, and ownership.

entries.heading: Phase 2: Interrupts and peripherals
entries.text: Study ISR rules, interrupt priority, NVIC concepts, timers, DMA, GPIO, UART, SPI, I2C, CAN, and cache coherency.

entries.heading: Phase 3: RTOS patterns
entries.text: Practice tasks, queues, semaphores, mutexes, priority inversion, timeouts, tick rate, task notifications, and ISR-to-task handoff.

entries.heading: Phase 4: Boot and linker
entries.text: Understand reset vectors, startup code, .text/.data/.bss, linker scripts, map files, bootloaders, firmware images, and update safety.

entries.heading: Phase 5: Debug and reliability
entries.text: Prepare for hard-fault analysis, watchdogs, brownout, logging, tracing, JTAG/SWD, timing jitter, and safe state-machine design.

entries.heading: volatile
entries.text: volatile prevents the compiler from assuming a value is unchanged, which is useful for MMIO registers and ISR-updated flags. It is not a mutex.

entries.heading: MMIO
entries.text: Memory-mapped I/O exposes hardware registers at addresses that firmware reads and writes like memory.

entries.heading: ISR discipline
entries.text: Interrupt handlers should do the minimum urgent work, acknowledge the hardware event, and defer heavier processing.

entries.heading: DMA ownership
entries.text: DMA reduces CPU copying but requires clear buffer ownership, alignment, cache maintenance, and completion/error handling.

entries.heading: RTOS task
entries.text: An RTOS task is an independently scheduled execution context with a stack, priority, and communication primitives.

entries.heading: Linker script
entries.text: A linker script maps input sections into target memory regions such as flash, SRAM, bootloader, or tightly coupled memory.

entries.heading: Startup code
entries.text: Startup code initializes runtime memory, sets the stack pointer, clears BSS, copies data to RAM, and calls main or the RTOS entry.

entries.heading: Watchdog
entries.text: A watchdog recovers from hangs by resetting or interrupting the system if firmware fails to service it in time.

entries.heading: C/C++ and Memory
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What does volatile tell the compiler?
entries.text: The value may change outside normal program flow. The variable is atomic. The value is always constant. The variable is stored only on disk. volatile is common for MMIO and ISR-shared flags, but it does not provide mutual exclusion.

entries.heading: Why is volatile not enough for thread safety?
entries.text: It does not make compound operations atomic or ordered across cores. It disables all interrupts. It creates a mutex automatically. It prevents all compiler output. Use atomics, locks, critical sections, or RTOS primitives for synchronization.

entries.heading: What is memory-mapped I/O?
entries.text: Peripheral registers accessed through specific memory addresses. A filesystem mount option only. A neural-network format. A UART baud rate. Firmware controls hardware by reading and writing register addresses.

entries.heading: Why can bit masks be safer than magic numbers?
entries.text: They name individual register fields and reduce accidental bit changes. They make code run without hardware. They replace linker scripts. They disable caches. Readable masks help preserve unrelated register bits.

entries.heading: What is alignment?
entries.text: Placing data at addresses suitable for its type or hardware access. Sorting functions alphabetically. Choosing task names. Changing PWM duty cycle. Misaligned access may fault or require extra bus cycles.

entries.heading: Why avoid unbounded dynamic allocation in firmware?
entries.text: Latency, fragmentation, failure, and ownership can be unpredictable. malloc always uses no memory. Static allocation is impossible. The compiler forbids heap use. Hard real-time systems often use static buffers or fixed pools.

entries.heading: What is stack overflow in embedded code?
entries.text: A task or ISR uses more stack than allocated. A network packet is too large. A flash sector is erased. A UART byte is dropped only. Small stacks make overflow a common firmware failure mode.

entries.heading: What is const useful for?
entries.text: Expressing read-only intent and enabling placement in read-only memory when possible. Making variables volatile. Disabling optimization. Starting the scheduler. const improves API clarity and can help memory placement.

entries.heading: What is undefined behavior?
entries.text: A program construct where the C/C++ standard imposes no required behavior. A recoverable UART timeout. A normal RTOS delay. A documented register reset value. Undefined behavior can break differently under optimization or compiler changes.

entries.heading: Why inspect generated assembly sometimes?
entries.text: To confirm timing, volatile accesses, barriers, or critical low-level code. To replace all tests. To remove comments. To change schematics. Embedded debugging often crosses the C/assembly/hardware boundary.

entries.heading: Interrupts, DMA, and Peripherals
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What should an ISR generally do?
entries.text: Handle urgent work, acknowledge the event, and defer heavy processing. Run a full neural-network training loop. Block forever on a queue. Format flash every time. Short ISRs reduce latency and avoid blocking other time-critical work.

entries.heading: Why keep ISRs short?
entries.text: Long ISRs increase interrupt latency and jitter. Short ISRs always use more memory. ISRs cannot access registers. Long ISRs improve every deadline. Interrupt latency matters for control, communication, and real-time systems.

entries.heading: What is interrupt priority?
entries.text: A rule deciding which interrupt can preempt another. A linker section name. A UART frame bit. A heap allocator type. Priority and grouping affect nesting and latency.

entries.heading: What is an interrupt vector table?
entries.text: A table of exception and interrupt handler addresses. A table of labels only. A queue of task messages. A boot logo. On Cortex-M, reset and interrupt dispatch start through the vector table.

entries.heading: What is DMA used for?
entries.text: Moving data between peripherals and memory without CPU copying each item. Generating source code. Replacing all interrupts. Changing clock frequency only. DMA can reduce CPU load but adds ownership and cache concerns.

entries.heading: What is cache coherency in DMA?
entries.text: Ensuring CPU cache contents and DMA-visible memory agree. Sorting cache files. Converting SRAM to flash. Increasing UART speed. Clean/invalidate operations or uncached buffers may be required.

entries.heading: What is debouncing?
entries.text: Filtering switch bounce so one press is not read as many transitions. Reducing stack size. Changing CPU priority. Erasing flash blocks. Mechanical contacts can oscillate during transitions.

entries.heading: What is UART?
entries.text: Asynchronous serial communication with configured baud rate and framing. A two-wire addressed bus only. A flash memory format. A clock tree. UART is common for logs, bootloaders, and simple device links.

entries.heading: How does SPI differ from I2C?
entries.text: SPI is clocked with chip-select lines and is often faster; I2C is two-wire addressed shared bus. SPI has no clock. I2C cannot share a bus. They are the same protocol. They have different wiring, arbitration, speed, and device-selection models.

entries.heading: Why use hardware timers?
entries.text: To generate precise periodic events, capture timings, PWM, or timeouts. To allocate heap memory. To compile code. To parse HTML. Timers are fundamental for scheduling and peripheral control.

entries.heading: RTOS and Concurrency
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is an RTOS task?
entries.text: A schedulable thread of execution with its own stack and priority. A flash erase block. A hardware register only. A linker expression. Tasks are the main unit of RTOS scheduling.

entries.heading: What is a FreeRTOS queue used for?
entries.text: Passing fixed-size items between tasks or from ISR-safe APIs to tasks. Changing CPU voltage. Mapping flash sections. Compiling the program. Queues combine synchronization and data transfer.

entries.heading: When should a mutex be used?
entries.text: To protect a shared resource with ownership semantics. To signal a one-time interrupt only. To write linker scripts. To configure UART parity. Mutexes are for mutual exclusion and may support priority inheritance.

entries.heading: When is a binary semaphore useful?
entries.text: For event signaling between ISR/task or task/task. For owning a shared object with priority inheritance by definition. For placing code in flash. For clearing BSS. Binary semaphores are commonly used for signaling, not ownership.

entries.heading: What is priority inversion?
entries.text: A high-priority task waits for a low-priority task holding a resource. The scheduler runs no tasks. The UART changes endian order. The heap grows downward. Priority inheritance can temporarily boost the lock holder.

entries.heading: Why avoid blocking in an ISR?
entries.text: ISRs should not wait for scheduler-managed resources like normal tasks. Blocking always improves latency. ISRs cannot read registers. It changes flash layout. Use ISR-safe APIs that wake tasks instead.

entries.heading: What is a tick rate?
entries.text: The periodic RTOS timer frequency used for time slicing and delays. The SPI bit order. The number of linker sections. A CAN identifier. Tick rate affects timing granularity, overhead, and power.

entries.heading: What is tickless idle?
entries.text: Suppressing periodic ticks during idle periods to save power. Running the tick interrupt faster. Disabling all timers forever. Removing the scheduler. Tickless modes use a timer wakeup for the next needed event.

entries.heading: Why use task notifications?
entries.text: They can be a lightweight direct signal to a task. They replace all queues with files. They configure flash wait states. They define interrupt vectors. In FreeRTOS, notifications can be faster and smaller than queues/semaphores for simple signals.

entries.heading: What should be considered when choosing task priorities?
entries.text: Deadline, blocking behavior, resource sharing, and priority inversion risk. Alphabetical task names only. Source file order only. LED color only. Priority design is a system-level timing decision.

entries.heading: Boot Flow and Linker Scripts
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What does startup code usually initialize?
entries.text: Stack pointer, .data copy, .bss zeroing, and runtime entry. Only UART baud rate. Only CSS files. Only network sockets. Startup bridges reset hardware state to a C/C++ runtime environment.

entries.heading: What is .text?
entries.text: Code and often read-only constants. Zero-initialized data. Heap metadata only. A queue item. .text is typically placed in executable flash or memory.

entries.heading: What is .data?
entries.text: Initialized writable data copied from flash to RAM at startup. Uninitialized zero data only. Interrupt vector only. A debug log file. Initial values live in nonvolatile memory but execute as writable RAM variables.

entries.heading: What is .bss?
entries.text: Zero-initialized writable data cleared at startup. Executable code. A bootloader image signature only. An SPI command. .bss does not need stored initial values beyond zeroing.

entries.heading: What does a linker script control?
entries.text: How sections are placed into memory regions. How interrupts are prioritized at runtime only. How UART bytes are framed. How labels are collected. Linker scripts map object-file sections to flash, RAM, boot regions, and special memory.

entries.heading: Why inspect a map file?
entries.text: To see symbol placement and memory usage. To decode UART frames. To change task priority at runtime. To measure voltage. Map files explain firmware size and section placement.

entries.heading: What is a bootloader?
entries.text: Small code that validates, loads, or jumps to an application image. A mutex type. An ADC sample. A C preprocessor macro only. Bootloaders enable startup control, recovery, and firmware updates.

entries.heading: What makes firmware update design hard?
entries.text: Power loss, corrupted images, rollback, versioning, and authenticity. Updates never fail. Flash is infinite. Boot code cannot check signatures. Robust update systems plan for interruption and invalid images.

entries.heading: Why reserve memory regions?
entries.text: For bootloader, vectors, calibration data, stacks, DMA buffers, or shared memory. To make code random. To force heap overflow. To disable debug. Embedded layouts often contain fixed hardware and product constraints.

entries.heading: What is a reset handler?
entries.text: The entry function executed after reset before main. A UART receive callback only. A task notification. A linker warning. The reset handler initializes low-level runtime state.

entries.heading: Interfaces, Timing, Debug, and Safety
entries.text: 10 questions

entries.heading: What is a watchdog timer?
entries.text: A timer that detects hangs if firmware fails to service it. A PWM output only. A compiler flag. A file descriptor. Watchdogs help recover from unrecoverable software stalls.

entries.heading: What is brownout detection?
entries.text: Detecting unsafe low supply voltage and resetting or protecting the system. A UART parity mode. A memory allocator. A queue overflow. Low voltage can cause undefined hardware behavior.

entries.heading: What is jitter?
entries.text: Variation in timing from one cycle or event to another. A flash page size. A register field width. A pointer type. Control loops and communication timing can be sensitive to jitter.

entries.heading: Why use a state machine?
entries.text: To make event-driven behavior explicit and testable. To hide all states in delays. To remove transitions. To replace hardware. State machines are useful for protocols, UI, boot flow, and control logic.

entries.heading: What is JTAG or SWD used for?
entries.text: Low-level debug, flash programming, stepping, and memory/register inspection. Audio playback. Only web deployment. Changing I2C addresses automatically. Debug probes are essential for bring-up and fault analysis.

entries.heading: How do you debug a hard fault?
entries.text: Capture stacked PC/LR, fault registers, stack pointer, and map addresses to symbols. Ignore the fault and reboot silently. Increase CSS padding. Only change baud rate. Fault context identifies the failing instruction and reason.

entries.heading: Why is logging difficult in embedded systems?
entries.text: Bandwidth, timing impact, storage limits, and ISR/task safety matter. Logs are always free. UART has infinite speed. Logging cannot affect timing. Instrumentation can change the behavior being measured.

entries.heading: What is fixed-point arithmetic useful for?
entries.text: Deterministic numeric work on hardware without fast floating point. Making pointers safe. Replacing all timers. Disabling overflow. Fixed-point needs careful scaling, saturation, and rounding.

entries.heading: What should a safe failure mode do?
entries.text: Move outputs to a known safe state and preserve useful diagnostics. Continue blindly at full power. Erase every log first. Disable all resets. Safety design defines what happens when assumptions fail.

entries.heading: Why test with real timing and hardware?
entries.text: Simulation and unit tests may miss interrupt timing, electrical behavior, and peripheral edge cases. Hardware tests are never needed. Timing cannot affect firmware. Peripherals always behave ideally. Embedded bugs often appear at the boundary between software and physical hardware.
