entries.heading: Architecture starts with a scenario and ends with reproducible proof
entries.text: Do not begin by choosing an array size or inventing opcodes. Each step consumes a reviewed artifact from the previous step and adds measurable obligations for the next one. 01 · Characterize Model workload Families, operators, shapes, state, arrivals, precision, quality 02 · Budget Product targets p50/p99 latency, throughput, energy, memory, cost, thermal 03 · Model Bounds and sweeps Operations, bytes, reuse, Roofline, sensitivity, bottleneck 04 · Design Architecture and ISA Engines, dataflow, hierarchy, commands, numerical rules 05 · Realize Compiler and runtime DSL, lowering, artifact, firmware, driver, execution, telemetry 06 · Qualify Correlated product proof Golden, simulator, RTL, tape-out, silicon, SDK, sustaining Keep three claims separate. Functional verification asks whether results and faults match the specification. Performance validation asks whether a fixed implementation meets its targets. Model correlation asks how closely one abstraction predicts another. Passing one does not imply the other two. Architecture and ISA definition

entries.heading: Translate workload reuse and product constraints into explicit resources
entries.text: A useful architecture document connects every resource to a workload need and every software-visible behavior to a test. The ISA is the stable contract; pipelines, arbitration, and implementation scheduling remain microarchitectural unless software can observe them. Compute budget required ops/s ≥ work ÷ deadline Include tail utilization, unsupported work, sparsity rules, and precision-specific peak rates. Bandwidth budget required B/s ≥ transferred bytes ÷ deadline Count traffic at a named boundary: DRAM, NoC, SRAM bank, or register file. Capacity budget live bytes = tensors + tiles + queues + state Include alignment, double buffers, fragmentation, firmware, and concurrent contexts. Roofline bound rate ≤ min(peak, bandwidth × intensity) Operational intensity is work divided by bytes observed at the same memory boundary. Architecture plane Decisions to make Evidence to demand Common failure Compute Matrix dimensions, vector/scalar lanes, accumulator width, special functions, sparsity, supported precisions. Shape-utilization sweep, dependency schedule, numerical tests, area and timing estimates. Quoting peak TOPS while awkward shapes, reductions, or elementwise work leave engines idle. Memory Register files, banked SRAM, cache or scratchpad policy, DMA, compression, address translation, coherency. Per-level traffic, bank conflicts, burst efficiency, residency plan, worst-case live set. Counting ideal reuse that the actual tile capacity or layout cannot retain. Interconnect Topology, multicast, reduction, routing, virtual channels, arbitration, quality of service, backpressure. Contention tests, saturation curves, deadlock proof, fairness and tail-latency distributions. Sizing links from average traffic while synchronized bursts overload one cut of the network. Execution Static schedule or dynamic issue, queues, dependencies, preemption, context state, firmware ownership. Queue occupancy, overlap timeline, progress guarantees, timeout/reset and multi-context tests. Optimizing engine cycles while host launch, DMA, queue wait, or firmware dominates latency. Observability Stable IDs, counters, trace events, error records, snapshots, clock correlation, replay data. Counter self-tests, trace schema, overflow behavior, timestamp uncertainty, first-divergence workflow. Discovering after RTL freeze that no counter can distinguish compute stalls from memory stalls. Normative contract

entries.heading: ISA and command definition checklist
entries.text: Encoding, reserved values, decode precedence, capability discovery, and version negotiation. Operand shapes, ranges, strides, layouts, alignment, address spaces, and alias rules. Accumulation width, rounding, saturation, overflow, NaN behavior, determinism, and quantization. Dependencies, barriers, fences, completion visibility, coherency, and memory ordering. Privilege, isolation, IOMMU behavior, context state, cancellation, timeout, reset, and watchdog. Illegal commands, page faults, engine faults, partial writes, recovery, and error propagation. Debug state, counters, trace identity, assembler/disassembler, simulator, and conformance tests. Example: one command as a testable contract Illustrative YAML command: GEMM_V1 encoding: opcode: 0x18 descriptor_bytes: 64 operands: A: {dtype: int8, layout: row_major, align: 64} B: {dtype: int8, layout: blocked_k32, align: 64} C: {dtype: int32, layout: row_major, align: 64} semantics: value: C[m,n] = sum_k(A[m,k] * B[k,n]) accumulator: signed_int32 overflow: wrap_twos_complement ordering: reads_after: dependency_tokens completion: order: release scope: system covers: [C_writes, status_record] faults: bad_alignment: INVALID_DESCRIPTOR unmapped_iova: PAGE_FAULT unsupported_shape: UNSUPPORTED observability: counters: [active_cycles, macs, sram_stall_cycles] trace: [command_id, start_tick, end_tick, status] Convention warning: this page uses two arithmetic operations per multiply-accumulate when presenting GEMM/Conv operation counts. Hardware data sheets sometimes count one MAC as one operation and sometimes as two. State the convention before comparing throughput claims. Deep dive: ISA and device integration Deep dive: interface contracts Deep dive: measurement formulas Modern model architectures and low-precision inference

entries.heading: Treat each model as a workload signature and each datatype as a full-stack contract
entries.text: Model names change faster than silicon. Study the stable architectural signatures: dominant operators, tensor shapes, arithmetic intensity, persistent state, dynamic control, communication, and the end-to-end service goal. Then decide precision with measured task quality and real kernels—not bit width alone. Model family Workload signature to study Accelerator consequence Required experiment Dense decoder Transformer Causal attention, RoPE, GQA/MQA, gated FFN, normalization, KV cache, continuous batching; separate prompt prefill from token decode. Prefill exposes large GEMMs; low-batch decode is often bandwidth- or launch-bound as it repeatedly moves weights and KV state through small GEMM/GEMV work. Batching, cache layout, and inter-token tail latency matter. Sweep batch, prompt, generated length, KV precision, and memory bandwidth; report time-to-first-token and inter-token latency separately. Vision and multimodal Transformer Patchification, encoders, projectors, cross-attention, variable image/video token counts, ragged inputs, and modality preprocessing. Resolution and patch size sharply change sequence length. Layout conversion, uncached encoder work, cache/reuse policy, host preprocessing, and variable-shape batching can dominate. Measure complete request latency across resolutions and modalities, including preprocessing, transfers, and reused versus uncached encoders. Diffusion models / DiT A diffusion system may use a Conv or Transformer denoiser; DiT specifically uses latent patch tokens and Transformer blocks. Study conditioning, guidance, scheduler, repeated model evaluations, and fixed text/VAE stages. Denoiser work grows roughly with the number of model evaluations, while fixed encode/decode and scheduler work remains. High-resolution activations, capacity, repeated weight reuse, and conditioning matter more than one block benchmark. Profile one denoiser evaluation, fixed stages, and the full generation loop; sweep resolution, evaluations, guidance, batch, memory high-water mark, and output quality. Sparse mixture of experts Router, top-k selection, token permutation, capacity, expert imbalance, expert GEMMs, and all-to-all communication when experts are sharded across devices. Nominal active FLOPs omit gather/scatter, padding, irregular tiles, routing latency, communication, and stragglers. Placement and load-aware scheduling become architectural. Simulate skewed routing; report expert load, padding, tile utilization, bytes, communication time, and p99—not only average active parameters. State-space / hybrid sequence model Selective state update, scan, short causal Conv, recurrent state, fusion boundaries, plus any interleaved attention layers. Linear sequence complexity does not guarantee utilization. Dependencies, elementwise work, state traffic, fusion, and recurrent versus parallel execution determine speed. Compare full-sequence and one-token modes; attribute time to projection GEMMs, scan/state movement, elementwise work, synchronization, and fallback. Recommendation / sparse features Large embedding tables, random gathers, pooling, feature interaction, dense MLPs, sharding, and model-parallel traffic. Capacity, locality, memory latency, and interconnect can outweigh tensor TOPS. Sparse and dense phases need different resource paths and scheduling policies. Sweep table size and access distribution; measure hit rate, effective bandwidth, gather latency, sharding traffic, and transition cost into dense compute. Architecture rule: “state of the art” is not a list of model names. Maintain a versioned workload census and trace each family to operator coverage, shapes, state, precision, memory traffic, control flow, system objective, and a reproducible model artifact. BF16 / FP16 range versus precision BF16 has an FP32-like exponent range with fewer fraction bits; FP16 has a narrower range with more fraction bits. Specify conversion, subnormals, special values, accumulation, and fallback. FP8 / microscaling tensor scale versus block scale Conventional FP8 may use current or delayed per-tensor scaling; amax history belongs to delayed recipes. MX formats share compact scales across fixed blocks, constraining metadata, layout, and tiles. INT8 activation + weight q = clamp(round(x / s) + z) Define symmetric/asymmetric mode, per-tensor/channel scales, zero point, INT32 accumulation, bias, requantization, rounding, and saturation. INT4 weights and activations packed values + group scales Separate weight-only W4A16/BF16 from W4A8 and fully low-bit W4A4/FP4. Count packing, scale metadata, alignment, dequantization, mixed fallback, and native kernel coverage. Precision stage Engineering work Evidence and gate 1 · Baseline Freeze model revision, tokenizer/preprocessing, dataset, seeds, FP32/BF16 quality, shapes, latency, memory, and power boundary. Reproducible reference metrics and tensor probes; no precision claim without the same evaluation contract. 2 · Calibrate Select representative data; sweep clipping, symmetric/asymmetric and tensor/channel/group/block granularity; inspect outliers, saturation, SQNR, and layer error. Calibration is separate from evaluation; rare and adversarial cases are retained. Use quantization-aware training (QAT) when post-training quantization (PTQ) cannot meet the quality target. 3 · Transform Apply PTQ or QAT, equalization or outlier handling such as SmoothQuant, choose weight-only versus W8A8, and mark higher-precision islands. Task quality, not only tensor MSE, passes across the required data distribution with a documented fallback policy. 4 · Lower Insert or fold conversions; propagate scales; pack weights and metadata; select aligned fused kernels; plan layouts, accumulation, and epilogues. Compiler dumps show every conversion, fallback, and kernel choice; unsupported shapes fail clearly or follow the declared path. 5 · Verify Compare a bit-accurate reference, simulator, RTL, and silicon on ties, overflow, minimum values, special floats, partial

entries.heading: Write precision semantics before selecting peak TOPS
entries.text: Encoding, exponent/mantissa or integer range, scale and zero-point ownership, and metadata layout. Per-tensor/channel/group/block granularity, block shape, packing order, alignment, and tail rules. Rounding mode, saturation or wrap, accumulator width, bias precision, reduction order, and determinism. NaN, Inf, signed zero, subnormal, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow, and conversion behavior. Supported operator/shape/layout combinations, higher-precision islands, fallback, capability discovery, and revisioning. Quality + systems proof

entries.heading: Avoid the low-bit performance illusion
entries.text: Count scale, zero-point, packed-weight, padding, conversion, and temporary-buffer traffic. Confirm that the target shape uses a native kernel rather than unpacking into a wider fallback. Measure end-task perplexity, accuracy, generation or perceptual quality and worst cases—not layer MSE alone. Separate theoretical footprint from allocated memory and theoretical operations/s from full-request latency. Preserve one bit-accurate executable reference shared by compiler, simulator, RTL, firmware, and validation. Practice: Transformer foundations Practice: quantization Next: map the dominant operators Conv, GEMM, and Attention

entries.heading: Use the same operator loop: semantics → work → traffic → mapping → proof
entries.text: Operator names hide the cases that determine a product: depthwise and grouped Conv, skinny and batched GEMM, attention prefill versus decode, odd tails, dynamic shapes, masks, layouts, and low-precision edge behavior. 1 Convolution Reuse, halos, groups, layouts 2 GEMM Hierarchical blocking and tails 3 Attention IO-aware prefill and decode NCHW notation

entries.heading: Convolution is a family of reuse patterns, not one kernel
entries.text: For output N×K×P×Q, filter K×(C/G)×R×S, and G groups, the conventional count is 2×N×P×Q×K×(C/G)×R×S operations . First derive P and Q from padding, stride, and dilation; then inspect reuse and tail behavior. Classify Regular, 1×1, depthwise, grouped, dilated, or transposed; each changes reuse, reduction width, and array utilization. Map Choose direct, implicit GEMM, explicit im2col, or Winograd; tile N/P/Q/K/C and account for halo fetches. Optimize Retain activations/weights/partial sums, align channels, double-buffer, compress zeros, and fuse bias/activation/pooling. Prove Randomized shape parity, padding/dilation/groups, quantized rounding, edge tiles, traffic counters, and end-to-end layout cost. Key trap: explicit im2col simplifies GEMM reuse but can replicate activations and inflate bandwidth. Implicit GEMM forms needed tiles during load, trading address-generation complexity for lower external traffic. C[M,N] = A[M,K] × B[K,N]

entries.heading: GEMM performance follows the entire blocking hierarchy
entries.text: The conventional count is 2×M×N×K operations . An idealized compulsory-traffic intensity is 2MNK ÷ (sA×MK + sB×KN + sC×MN), where sA, sB, and sC are bytes per element; add another C read when β is nonzero. Real intensity must also include packing, partial-sum spills, refetches, and the memory level being analyzed. Classify Square, tall-skinny, short-wide, batched, transposed, split-K, and small-launch cases stress different resources. Map Block DRAM→SRAM→array/register levels; assign M/N spatially, reduce K, and select stationary operands. Optimize Pack and align vectors, pipeline DMA, double-buffer, fuse epilogues, balance split-K reduction, and specialize edge tiles. Prove Compare reference output, achieved operations/s, array occupancy, per-level bytes, bank conflicts, launch overhead, and tails. Key trap: a tile that maximizes MAC occupancy may exceed SRAM capacity, create bank conflicts, or force partial-sum spills. Optimize measured end-to-end time, not one utilization counter. softmax(QKᵀ / √d + mask)V

entries.heading: Prefill is compute-rich; autoregressive decode is often KV-traffic dominated
entries.text: Dense attention score work scales as O(Lq×Lk); it is quadratic when query and key lengths are the same. A naïve implementation also materializes the score matrix. IO-aware tiling with online softmax keeps score blocks on chip and is mathematically exact, although floating-point reduction reordering can still produce tolerance-level differences. Classify Prefill versus decode, causal versus non-causal, self versus cross attention, MHA/GQA/MQA, batch, sequence, and head dimension. Map Tile Q/K/V, pipeline QKᵀ→online softmax→PV, retain running max/sum, and plan KV-cache layout and paging. Optimize Fuse masking/scaling/softmax, overlap KV fetch, use grouped query where allowed, fuse dequantization, and avoid score materialization. Prove Stable softmax, fully masked rows, causal boundaries, variable lengths, cache update/reuse, long sequences, and low-precision error. Key trap: changing the head count, attention approximation, or KV representation can change model semantics or quality. Separate an exact implementation optimization from a model-level approximation. Case Likely limiter First counter or experiment High-value lever 3×3 regular Conv SRAM/NoC traffic or MAC occupancy, depending on retained reuse. Bytes and reuse per level; halo overhead; active MAC lanes. Spatial/channel tiling, row/output stationary mapping, double buffering. Depthwise Conv Bandwidth and launch overhead; little cross-channel reuse. Operations per transferred byte and vector-lane utilization. Fuse adjacent pointwise/activation work and specialize layout. Large square GEMM Compute when blocking retains operands effectively. Array active cycles, partial-sum spills, SRAM bank conflicts. Hierarchical blocking, pipelined copies, aligned vector access. Skinny GEMM Array underfill, reduction/launch overhead, or bandwidth. Per-dimension lane occupancy and fill/drain cycles. Batch fusion, alternate array mapping, vector fallback, persistent kernel. Attention prefill Matrix compute plus score-matrix IO for naïve algorithms. Score bytes, Q/K/V reuse, softmax/vector overlap, tensor utilization. IO-aware tiled attention with online softmax and fusion. Attention decode KV-cache capacity/bandwidth and small GEMM utilization. KV bytes per output token, cache hit/page behavior, and inter-token latency; track time-to-first-token separately with prefill. KV layout/paging, GQA/MQA when model permits, request batching. Frontend compilers, backend interfaces, accelerator runtimes, and domain-specific languages

entries.heading: Choose the smallest durable extension seam, then preserve semantics to the device
entries.text: The frontend owns a verified IR handoff contract for the backend: graph optimization, operator lowering, dataflow and memory scheduling, IR invariants, and provenance. The backend turns that contract into target code; the runtime owns concrete execution and resource lifetimes. Correlated evidence must flow back across all three. 01 · Import Validate semantics IR/opset version, types, possible shapes, effects, source IDs 02 · Optimize Transform the graph Fold, CSE/DCE, canonicalize, graph/operator fusion, propagate layout/precision 03 · Decide Select ownership Contract-based capability query, cost selection, partition, specialization, fallback 04 · Lower & schedule Commit the implementation Operator/type conversion, tiles, layouts, memory spaces, liveness, DMA overlap 05 · Handoff & generate IR contract → target artifact Backend physical/resource legality, kernels/instructions, code object, executable ABI 06 · Run Execute and correlate Validate/cache, allocate, queue, synchronize, profile, recover, feed back Optimize Preserve defined observable semantics while improving a cost, usually without the deliberate target commitment of lowering; prove equivalence and measure the change. Partition Choose which compiler or device owns each legal region; keep unsupported and legal-but-not-selected reasons distinct. Lower Move to an IR with fewer abstractions and more target commitments while preserving padding, broadcasting, numerics, effects, and errors. Schedule Choose when and where computation and movement occur: producer-consumer or loop fusion, tiles, layouts, memory spaces, lifetimes, overlap, barriers, and tails. Extension seam Use it when Implementation evidence Boundary to respect TVM BYOC / external codegen A supported Relax subgraph can be partitioned and handed to an external compiler or library while TVM retains graph execution. Registered patterns and legality predicates; before/after partitioned IR; separate selection/cost decision; RunCodegen output; runtime module; fallback and copy trace. First determine legal support from shape, dtype, layout, quantization, alignment, and revision. Then let a separate cost/partition policy decide whether supported work is selected; report “unsupported” versus “supported, not selected.” Native TVM target/runtime The accelerator needs target properties, native code generation, runtime modules, and a device API rather than a bounded library offload. Target definition; TIR schedules/tensorization; artifact metadata; module load; allocation/copy/stream behavior; compile-host versus run-device tests. Compile-time codegen consumes declared target properties; it must not assume it can query the eventual device. MLIR dialect and conversion A reusable domain or accelerator IR needs custom operations, types, attributes, interfaces, verification, transformations, and progressive lowering. ODS/TableGen definitions; parser/printer; valid and invalid tests; canonicalization; conversion legality; type conversion; complete pass-pipeline snapshots. Publish precise semantics and require full conversion at boundaries; reject leftover illegal operations and unresolved casts. LLVM target/backend A real custom ISA needs ABI, instruction selection, scheduling, register allocation, object emission, assembly/disassembly, and relocation support. Data layout and calling convention; instruction/register descriptions; legalization; scheduling model; MC encoder/decoder; object and round-trip tests. Do not add a core LLVM IR instruction just to represent one accelerator feature. Prefer intrinsics, target-specific nodes, or a higher-level dialect unless universal semantics justify the change. StableHLO + XLA FFI A portable HLO graph needs a bounded target-specific escape hatch with typed runtime binding. Versioned StableHLO; namespaced custom_call ; typed handler; shape/rank, dtype, backend attributes, aliasing, side-effect, and ABI metadata; compatibility tests. Custom calls weaken portability. The current XLA FFI API/ABI is documented as experimental, so pin versions and qualify supported combinations. PJRT plugin The whole accelerator should appear to frameworks through a uniform device interface rather than a single external operation. Client and device discovery; buffers/transfers; compile and loaded executable; execution/events/errors; topology; packaging; framework smoke test. Version the framework binding, PJRT API, portable artifact, compiler, runtime, driver, and hardware capability as one tested matrix. Internal customization policy

entries.heading: Make the fork burden visible
entries.text: Write an extension-seam decision record covering ownership, fallback, performance, portability, integration cost, and expected lifetime. Pin the upstream commit and toolchain; make builds reproducible; record patches, licenses, security response, and supported host platforms. Isolate vendor dialects, targets, runtime modules, and feature flags. Keep unavoidable core patches small and review whether generic fixes can go upstream. Budget rebases; test both the pinned baseline and candidate upgrades; retain IR reproducers for pass crashes and changed optimization decisions. Qualify old and new model artifacts, compiler/runtime/driver versions, devices, and cached executables before an internal release. Acceptance suite

entries.heading: Test decisions, not only generated answers
entries.text: Golden import and IR snapshots, round trips, verifier negatives, pass determinism, and source-location preservation. Differential operator/model results across boundary shapes, layouts, dtypes, quantization, dynamic dimensions, and hardware revisions. Visible partition/fallback reasons, cost-model decisions, host/device copies, cache keys, compile time, and unsupported-input diagnostics. Artifact load/reject behavior, buffer lifetime, stream ordering, cancellation, asynchronous errors, faults, and recovery. Stable profiling IDs connecting framework node → IR operation → command → counter/trace event → device result. Owner Core responsibilities Inspectable artifact Typical failure Frontend graph optimizer Import, type and shape inference; canonicalization, folding, CSE/DCE; fusion; layout and precision propagation; capability-aware partitioning. Versioned input, before/after IR, pass statistics, semantic differential, and support, rejection, or fallback log. A topology-only pattern ignores extra consumers, effects, dtypes, or dynamic cases; over-fusion increases live ranges, spills, and transfers. Frontend lowering and scheduler Decompose, legalize, and convert types; lower operators to target or kernel IR; choose tiles, layouts, memory spaces, liveness/reuse, bufferization, and DMA overlap. Legality matrix, lowering snapshots, memory plan and live ranges, traffic/capacity estimate, and edge/tail tests. Lowering loses broadcast, padding, reduction, or numerical semantics; early bufferization can freeze alias/reuse decisions, introduce allocations or copies, and prevent later tensor-level fusion. Frontend ↔ backend IR contract Version operations, types, possible shapes, layouts, precision, effects, memory-space intent, target capabilities, rejection reasons, and source/profile provenance. Machine-readable capability and IR schemas, verifier and negative vectors, supported/unsupported decision logs, and two-revision consumer tests. An implicit semantic or legality rule causes a code-generation mismatch, silent fallback, lost provenance, or wrong result. Backend compiler and code generation Enforce target legality; map and schedule target operations; select kernels or instructions; allocate registers and scratch resources; emit, link, and relocate code. Code object or disassembly, resource report, symbol/relocation map, backend diagnostics, and source-to-kernel profile map. Frontend-legal work is physically infeasible, or backend layout, buffer-order, numerical, or resource decisions erase the predicted gain. Backend ↔ runtime executable contract Version code objects, entry points, argument bindings, constants, layouts, alignment, ownership/lifetimes, workspace, dependencies/events, target/ISA/firmware/driver compatibility, cache identity, and debug maps. Executable manifest and ABI schema, loader conformance and negative vectors, compatibility matrix, cache-key tests, and two-revision load/execute tests. A changed binding, lifetime, workspace, event, compatibility, or cache rule causes load rejection, stale execution, corruption, a leak, or a race. Runtime Discover devices/topology; validate, load, and cache artifacts; manage quotas, pools, buffers, and transfers; submit queues/events; synchronize; dispatch; recover; profile. Lifecycle trace, cache key, allocation high-water mark and fragmentation, queue timeline, structured errors, and device capability record. Hidden copies, premature reclamation, asynchronous timing without a fence, stale cache, fragmentation, or command overhead dominates execution. Joint performance loop Separate compile, load, allocate, copy, queue, device, and synchronization time; correlate stable IDs; classify the bottleneck; assign an owner and test one change. Aligned graph/IR/kernel/runtime/counter trace, before/after distributions and counters, correctness/quality result, and cost-model update. A microkernel improves while end-to-end or p99 worsens; an estimate is reported as measured data; learning never reaches the compiler or architecture model. Boundary diagnosis rule: preserve stable identity from framework node → graph IR → lowered operation → backend kernel/command → runtime event → device counter . First label a case unsupported , legal but not selected , or selected and failed . Then split latency into compile, load, allocation, copy, queue, device, and synchronization time; inspect reformats, spills, fragmentation, launches, fallback, and utilization. Change one factor, recheck correctness or task quality plus p50/p99, throughput, and peak memory, then feed the result into capability, cost, and architecture models. Example accelerator DSL contract Illustrative, not executable syntax kernel qgemm(A: i8[M,K], B: i8[K,N], a_scale: f32, b_scale: f32[N], c_scale: f32, C: i8[M,N]) requires K % 32 == 0 and K <= 65535 and a_scale > 0 and all(b_scale > 0) and c_scale > 0 and aligned(A, 64) and aligned(B, 64) numerics { zero_points: A = 0, B = 0, C = 0 accumulator: acc[m,n] = sum_k(i32(A[m,k]) * i32(B[k,n])) real_scale: r[n] = a_scale * b_scale[n] / c_scale output: C[m,n] = saturate_i8(round_nearest_even(acc[m,n] * r[n])) } schedule non_semantic { tile M by 64, N by 64, K by 32 double_buffer A, B in scratchpad map [M, N] to matrix_engine } lowers_to @npu.gemm_v1 fallback @reference.qgemm DSL design review

entries.heading: Specify meaning before syntax
entries.text: Purpose: name the user and abstraction boundary. Separate algorithmic semantics from a retargetable schedule. Types: define shapes, dynamic dimensions, layouts, precision/scales, memory spaces, ownership, aliases, effects, and synchronization. Numerics: define accumulation, reduction order, overflow, saturation, rounding, NaNs, determinism, and approximation tolerance. Legality: implement verifiers with source-located diagnostics and invalid-program tests; do not defer every error to code generation. Lowering: retain before/after IR for semantic NPU → tiled accelerator → buffer/command → LLVM IR or custom ISA stages. Evolution: version operations and artifacts, preserve profiling identity, provide a bounded escape hatch, and document deprecation. Capstone proof: compile one fused graph through StableHLO or Relax → graph optimization → semantic NPU DSL → scheduled/bufferized IR → backend target code → executable + metadata → runtime → mock driver/device . Retain partition and lowering decisions, every IR stage, reference diffs, interface and artifact compatibility, buffer/event traces, unsupported cases, and a correlated latency breakdown of compile, load, allocation, transfer, queue, device, and synchronization time. Companion: TVM path Companion: scheduling and memory planning Companion: runtime and queues Foundation: LLVM and MLIR Performance verification

entries.heading: Build a ladder of models and measure the error between adjacent rungs
entries.text: A fast analytical model explores a large design space; a detailed timing model explains contention; RTL proves implementation behavior; FPGA and silicon reveal physical effects. None is a universal oracle. Level 0 Golden semantics Reference math, legal ranges, numerical and fault behavior Level 1 Analytical bounds Operations, compulsory bytes, Roofline, capacity, sensitivity Level 2 Functional / TLM Commands, resources, latency annotations, queues, contention Level 3 RTL / emulation Cycle behavior, protocol assertions, coverage, long regressions Level 4 FPGA / silicon Clock, power, thermal, DRAM, OS, firmware, real counters Verification layer Required tests Required outputs Gate Operator Directed corners, seeded random shapes, dtype/layout/quantization/mask cases, negative constraints. Reference diff, tolerance policy, first mismatch, reproducible seed. Every legal case matches; every illegal case returns the specified error without unsafe side effects. ISA / commands Encode/decode round trips, legal and illegal streams, dependency cycles, misalignment, reset and fault injection. Architectural state diff, command trace, coverage of fields and faults. Functional simulator and RTL retire the same visible state or a documented exception. Microarchitecture Compute, memory, NoC, queue, arbitration and backpressure saturation sweeps. Cycles, bytes, utilization, stalls, occupancy, service distributions. Counters reconcile with events and modeled conservation rules; no unexplained cycles or bytes. Networks Representative models/shapes, concurrency, cold/warm start, fallback, sustained thermal load. p50/p90/p99, throughput, energy/inference, accuracy, memory high-water mark. Scenario-level product targets pass, including pre/post-processing and boundary transfers. Correlation Same artifact, input, clock, memory parameters, software versions, and trace IDs on adjacent models. Absolute/relative error, bias by workload class, confidence interval, root-cause tags. Error stays within an agreed envelope; calibration never hides an unmodeled mechanism. Benchmark hygiene

entries.heading: Fix the measurement boundary
entries.text: State warm-up, repetitions, clocks, temperature, batch and arrival process, included transfers, compile/load time, and percentile calculation. Counter hygiene

entries.heading: Reconcile rather than decorate
entries.text: Check active + stall + idle against elapsed cycles; requested versus delivered bytes; issued versus retired work; overflow and multiplexing behavior. Claim hygiene

entries.heading: Carry correctness with speed
entries.text: A performance result is invalid if operator semantics, model accuracy, precision, fallback, preprocessing, or concurrency changed outside the declared experiment. Cross-functional architecture requirements

entries.heading: One feature must remain traceable from product intent to a passing test
entries.text: Compiler, RTL, firmware, driver, runtime, validation, and product teams should review the same behavioral contract. A requirement is ready only when it is measurable, owned, observable, and testable. Use case Customer outcome Scenario, workload, accuracy, latency, lifecycle Compiler Legal lowering Shapes, layout, precision, tiling, fallback, artifact ISA / ABI Visible command Encoding, ordering, faults, version, telemetry RTL / firmware Execution behavior Resources, scheduling, progress, counters, reset Driver / runtime System behavior Buffers, IOVA, queues, fences, timeout, recovery Verification Acceptance evidence Golden, negative, stress, performance, correlation Shared artifact Compiler question RTL question Driver/runtime question Capability manifest Which op/shape/dtype/layout combinations are legal and profitable? Which target revision and resource limits implement each capability? How are revision, firmware, memory, and concurrency limits queried? ISA and descriptor schema How are tiles, addresses, dependencies, relocations, and debug IDs emitted? What is normative at decode/retire, and what malformed state is rejected? What must be validated before submit, and how are errors returned? Memory contract Which tensors alias, spill, persist, or require layout conversion? What alignment, burst, bank, coherency, and page-fault behavior exists? Who allocates/maps/unmaps, owns fences, synchronizes CPU access, and recovers faults? Trace and counters Which graph/source ID maps to each command and estimated cost? Which events and stalls are counted, at what clock and overflow rule? How are sessions, buffers, timestamps, permissions, and schema versions managed? Compatibility matrix Which compiler emits each artifact/ISA version? Which hardware/firmware revisions accept it? Which driver/runtime combinations negotiate, reject, or translate it? Feature requirement template Review before implementation ID: PERF-ATTN-017 Scenario: decoder, batch 1..8, context 1k..16k Target: p99 next-token latency <= X ms at Y W Semantics: ONNX Attention rules + stated cache extension Supported: dtype/layout/head/mask/sequence predicates Compiler: fusion, tiling, artifact fields, fallback rule Hardware: engines, SRAM, DMA, queue and progress behavior Driver: buffers, IOVA, fences, timeout, reset, telemetry Errors: unsupported, OOM, page fault, timeout, engine fault Evidence: golden vectors, stress, counters, model correlation Owners: product / compiler / RTL / firmware / driver / DV Compatibility: capability bit, ABI version, rollback behavior

entries.heading: Review questions that prevent late surprises
entries.text: What exact shapes and arrival patterns represent the product, including the tails? Which behavior is normative, which is a performance hint, and which may change by revision? Who owns every buffer, state transition, timeout, error, counter, and compatibility decision? How does unsupported work fail or fall back, and what is its end-to-end cost? What can be observed before silicon, and what evidence closes the requirement after silicon? Which version combinations are supported, rejected, translated, rolled back, and tested in CI? Product development and commercialization

entries.heading: Design the hardware and software interface for years of use, not one demo
entries.text: A commercially useful NPU meets customer workloads within system cost and power while remaining integrable, secure, diagnosable, recoverable, upgradeable, and supportable across hardware and software revisions. Value

entries.heading: End-to-end workload fit
entries.text: Define customer models, quality, latency distributions, throughput, concurrency, cold start, memory, power, thermal, and fallback—not a single peak metric. Economics

entries.heading: PPA and system cost
entries.text: Trade compute, SRAM, NoC, DRAM bandwidth, die/package area, IP, yield, board memory, cooling, and engineering schedule against the actual workload mix. Adoption

entries.heading: Compiler and SDK coverage
entries.text: Make supported semantics discoverable, failures actionable, examples executable, results reproducible, and migration possible across target revisions. Compatibility

entries.heading: Version every boundary
entries.text: Negotiate capabilities and size-versioned messages; test old/new compiler, artifact, runtime, driver, firmware, and hardware combinations. Trust

entries.heading: Isolation and safe failure
entries.text: Validate descriptors, enforce IOMMU/context ownership, prevent cross-process leakage, bound execution, recover from hangs, and report partial effects. Operations

entries.heading: Field diagnostics and lifecycle
entries.text: Provide health counters, trace/crash capture, firmware update and rollback, manufacturing tests, failure triage, deprecation policy, and support documentation. Commercialization perspective: a fabless accelerator team typically owns product definition, architecture, RTL, software, verification, validation, and the customer result while coordinating external manufacturing and ecosystem partners, including outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT). Outsourcing wafer fabrication does not outsource technical accountability: process, memories and PHY IP, package, thermal limits, test access and automated test equipment (ATE), yield, board design, compiler coverage, bring-up, and customer qualification must enter architecture decisions early. 01 · Discover Product and customer Workloads, scenarios, quality, PPA, cost, SKU, schedule, acceptance 02 · Co-design Architecture and software Model, ISA/ABI, node, memory/IP, package, compiler, runtime, debug 03 · Close RTL to tape-out DV/formal, emulation, DFT/ATE readiness, P&R, timing, power, IR/EM, DRC/LVS 04 · Produce Wafer, package, and test Mask release, fabrication, wafer probe, package assembly, final test, yield 05 · Correlate First silicon Boot, SRAM/DMA/DRAM, PVT, counters, ATE, model/RTL delta, errata 06 · Sustain SDK and customer release Qualification, yield/binning, model matrix, support, RMA, updates, respin Fabless stage Required outputs Critical interfaces Review question Product discovery Target customers and workload envelope; latency/throughput/quality/power/cost limits; process/package assumptions; SKU, schedule, benchmark, and acceptance criteria. Product, customers, ML applications, architecture, finance, sales, supply chain. Is the product objective measurable end to end, and does its volume/value justify the silicon and software schedule? Architecture co-design Executable golden model; performance/power model; architecture; ISA/ABI; memory map; operator and precision matrix; compiler/runtime/driver, debug, and profiling plan. Architecture, compiler, runtime, driver, firmware, RTL/DV, physical design, foundry, EDA and IP vendors, package team. Which external assumption—process, SRAM, PHY, package, bandwidth, IP, license, or tool—can invalidate the architecture? RTL to tape-out Requirements-to-tests trace; formal/DV coverage; emulation; DFT/scan/BIST; synthesis/P&R; STA; power; IR/EM; CDC/RDC; DRC/LVS; package SI/PI; firmware smoke image. RTL, DV, DFT, physical design, firmware, EDA support, foundry, package and OSAT/test partners. Can every sign-off exception be traced to an owner, risk, containment, first-silicon test, and schedule decision? Fabrication, package, and test Mask release and manufacturing data; front-end wafer fabrication; wafer sort/probe; package assembly; final test; lot, bin, test, and yield-learning records; reviewed handoffs. Foundry, mask operations, OSAT, package, product/test engineering, quality, physical design, DFT, supply chain. Are foundry-to-probe-to-package-to-final-test data, ownership, excursion response, sample traceability, and yield feedback unambiguous? First silicon Power/clock/reset and boot plan; register/ISA known-answer tests; SRAM/DMA/DRAM; interrupts; PVT characterization; counter/model/RTL correlation; ATE correlation; errata/workarounds. Lab, firmware, driver, compiler/runtime, DV, board, test/product engineering, foundry and package/test partners. Can the team isolate power, signal/package, RTL, firmware, driver, compiler, model, test, and workload causes with existing observability? Qualification, volume, and sustaining Reliability/qualification; yield and binning; cost; security; SDK/model support matrix; customer enablement; telemetry/RMA diagnostics; revision, deprecation, and respin criteria. Quality, manufacturing/test, software release, security, field applications, customers, sales and supply chain. Can shipped systems be supported safely across device, board, firmware, driver, compiler, framework, model, and OS revisions?

entries.heading: Artifacts that show fabless accelerator experience
entries.text: Measurable PRD and workload, precision, and operator support matrix tied to architecture and software milestones. Versioned ISA, ABI, firmware, and driver contracts plus requirements-to-tests traceability and a responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed (RACI) ownership matrix. PPA and system-cost model with foundry, IP, package, memory, EDA, license, supply, software, and schedule risks. Tape-out, bring-up, ATE correlation, qualification, SDK and customer-release, errata, and sustaining checklists.

entries.heading: First-silicon debugging order
entries.text: Prove safe power, clocks, reset, scan/JTAG access, boot, register reads, and controlled shutdown. Run SRAM, DMA, external-memory, interrupt, address-translation, and fault-path known-answer tests. Execute one command from a fixed artifact; compare golden, simulator, RTL, firmware, driver, and silicon IDs. Reconcile cycles, bytes, clocks, voltage, temperature, and ATE/lab measurements before tuning the model. Record erratum, impact, containment, software workaround, qualification evidence, and respin criterion. Release gate Minimum evidence Question for sign-off Architecture freeze Workload census, sensitivity sweeps, PPA estimate, memory/NoC proof, software contract draft, observable counters. Which target fails first if workload mix, bandwidth, or SRAM assumption moves by 25%? RTL freeze ISA/ABI conformance, performance-model correlation, fault/recovery coverage, compiler schedule proof, trace/counter validation. Can software diagnose every target miss without a new signal or register? Tape-out release DV/formal and coverage closure; DFT/ATE readiness; physical and package sign-off; approved waivers; mask/foundry/OSAT handoffs; bring-up vectors, firmware, boards, owners, and containment plans. Is every residual risk accepted with a detectable first-silicon symptom, owner, containment, and schedule impact? First-silicon / qualification release Power/boot and subsystem bring-up; model/RTL/ATE correlation; PVT, reliability, yield/binning, security and recovery evidence; errata/workarounds; SDK and board readiness. Does measured silicon meet the qualified operating envelope, and are every deviation and customer-visible workaround controlled? SDK beta Representative model coverage, deterministic packaging, examples, profiler, negative diagnostics, compatibility matrix. Can an external team reproduce success and distinguish unsupported input from a product defect? Production Scenario benchmarks, accuracy, sustained power/thermal, security, reset/recovery, update/rollback, manufacturing and field diagnostics. Can the device fail safely, produce a supportable record, and return to service? Lifecycle Telemetry policy, regression corpus, vulnerability response, revision migration, deprecation dates, fleet rollback and data retention. How will a five-year-old application behave after a compiler, firmware, OS, or silicon revision changes? SystemC/TLM and simulator development

entries.heading: Choose fidelity explicitly, then validate every timing claim
entries.text: SystemC supplies an event-driven C++ simulation kernel. TLM-2.0 standardizes transaction interfaces. Neither makes a model cycle-accurate automatically: timing points, contention, arbitration, pipelines, and calibration are deliberate modeling choices. Untimed Functional model Semantics, software enablement, golden state; highest speed Register-accurate Programmer view MMIO, descriptors, interrupts, faults, firmware and driver flow Loosely timed TLM b_transport Coarse annotated delays, temporal decoupling, architecture sweeps Approximately timed TLM nb_transport Multiple phases, overlap, backpressure, arbitration and contention Cycle-aware Detailed model / RTL Pipelines, cycle events and validated timing; lowest speed LT Loosely timed Fast software and design exploration AT Approximately timed Phases, overlap, and backpressure Δ Correlation Make model error visible Blocking transport

entries.heading: Use LT to boot software early and sweep architecture parameters quickly
entries.text: An initiator calls b_transport(payload, delay) . The target executes the transaction in one blocking call and annotates coarse delay. A quantum keeper can let processes run ahead locally before synchronizing, improving simulation speed. Model Registers, memories, commands, functional engines, interrupts, coarse DMA/compute latency, counters, errors. Do not claim Cycle-level arbitration, exact queue overlap, pipeline bubbles, or tail latency unless those mechanisms are explicitly represented and correlated. Non-blocking transport

entries.heading: Use AT where request/response phases and contention change the answer
entries.text: The base protocol uses nb_transport_fw / nb_transport_bw and four timing points: BEGIN_REQ, END_REQ, BEGIN_RESP, and END_RESP. Multiple transactions may be in flight, so payload lifetime, phase transitions, exclusion rules, and backpressure must be correct. Add detail Queue depth, accept interval, service latency, arbitration, NoC/DRAM contention, DMA overlap, response ordering. Pay the cost More scheduler interaction, protocol state, validation effort, slower simulation, and harder debugging. Error is a metric

entries.heading: Correlate shared events, not unrelated summary numbers
entries.text: Run the same artifact and input under the same clocks, memory parameters, firmware policy, and measurement boundary. Preserve command/engine IDs across TLM, RTL, FPGA, and silicon traces. Compare per-command cycles and bytes before comparing only total latency. Report Absolute and relative error, bias by operator/shape, confidence, unmatched events, modeled and unmodeled causes. Regress Freeze calibrated cases, retain raw traces/configuration, and alert when a change improves one class while degrading another. Minimal LT target shape SystemC / TLM-2.0 sketch struct npu_target : sc_core::sc_module { tlm_utils::simple_target_socket<npu_target> socket{"socket"}; SC_CTOR(npu_target) { socket.register_b_transport(this, &npu_target::b_transport); } void b_transport(tlm::tlm_generic_payload& tx, sc_core::sc_time& delay) { const auto address = tx.get_address(); auto* data = tx.get_data_ptr(); if (!data || tx.get_data_length() != 4) { tx.set_response_status(tlm::TLM_BURST_ERROR_RESPONSE); return; } if (tx.is_write() && address == kDoorbell) { const auto command = read_u32(data); const auto arrival_delay = delay + sc_core::sc_time(20, sc_core::SC_NS); // A PEQ/event accepts work at the annotated arrival time; // it must not mutate visible state early. schedule_command(command, arrival_delay); delay = arrival_delay; tx.set_response_status(tlm::TLM_OK_RESPONSE); return; } tx.set_response_status(tlm::TLM_ADDRESS_ERROR_RESPONSE); } };

entries.heading: Virtual-platform build order
entries.text: Implement command semantics and deterministic golden state without time. Add register map, memory targets, descriptors, interrupts, errors, and a driver-like test. Annotate compute and DMA latency; expose cycles, bytes, queue occupancy, and stalls. Add contention/backpressure only where sensitivity analysis shows it can change a decision. Replay seeded workloads against functional model and RTL; retain first-divergence traces. Calibrate with documented parameters, report error envelopes, and lock correlation regressions. Also understand generic payload ownership, DMI and invalidation, debug transport, byte enables, streaming width, endianness, delta cycles, SC_THREAD/SC_METHOD behavior, and deterministic event ordering. Companion: C++/SystemC/RTL model correlation Companion: runtime, queue, and driver flow Eight-week build path

entries.heading: Finish with a mini-NPU full-stack evidence package
entries.text: Use INT8 GEMM plus one mapped Conv or attention case. Each week produces a reviewable artifact; the final result should let another engineer reproduce correctness, performance, compatibility, and model limitations. 0 / 8 complete Week 1 · Workload census Twelve representative Conv/GEMM/Attention cases with semantics, shapes, precision, operations, bytes, targets, and accuracy tolerance. Week 2 · Roofline and sensitivity model Compute/bandwidth/capacity bounds, three candidate configurations, bottleneck predictions, and ±25% parameter sweeps. Week 3 · Operator mapping Blocked GEMM and one Conv or attention implementation with reference parity, traffic estimates, tile sweeps, and edge cases. Week 4 · Architecture and ISA Compute/memory/NoC/control design, versioned command schema, numerical semantics, faults, counters, and conformance vectors. Week 5 · SystemC/TLM platform CPU initiator, interconnect, memories, NPU target, driver-like sequence, annotated timing, queues, interrupts, and counters. Week 6 · Cross-team feature RFC Trace one feature through product, compiler, ISA, RTL, firmware, driver/runtime, telemetry, tests, owners, and compatibility. Week 7 · Verification and correlation Seeded random streams, functional/timing/RTL comparison, fault injection, counter reconciliation, error envelope, and regressions. Week 8 · Product-readiness review Scenario results, PPA/system cost, security, recovery, version matrix, diagnostics, update/rollback, limits, and launch decision. Five-lab compiler and product extension

entries.heading: Turn the added requirements into one portfolio-grade accelerator path
entries.text: Complete this after, or alongside, the core eight-week lab. Reuse one model slice and one target contract so the evidence connects from workload and precision through DSL/compiler/runtime to a fabless release decision. 0 / 5 complete Lab 1 · Model signature and precision sweep Trace one dense LLM plus one DiT, MoE, SSM, multimodal, or recommendation case. Inventory shapes, work, bytes, state, dynamic behavior, and service goals; compare BF16, FP8-emulated, INT8, and groupwise INT4 for task quality, footprint, metadata, transfers, and fallback. Emulation validates numerics only; measure latency on native supported kernels and never infer speed from emulation. Lab 2 · Frontend compiler and backend interface First justify the extension seam, pin a reproducible build, and record patch surface, rebase cost, and upstream-versus-fork policy. Then implement one capability-aware graph optimization and one operator-level lowering in TVM Relax, MLIR/StableHLO, or XLA HLO; use LLVM only for the backend/code-generation portion. Add a dataflow and memory-hierarchy schedule, emit a versioned backend interface schema, and retain before/after IR, legality and rejection decisions, negative/fallback tests, kernel count, transfers, peak live bytes, and end-to-end latency. Lab 3 · Accelerator DSL and lowering Define two semantic operations with types, shapes, layouts, precision, memory/effects, rounding and invalid cases. Add parser/printer, verifier, canonicalization, source diagnostics, and a staged semantic → scheduled → buffer/command → target lowering trace. Lab 4 · Runtime execution and correlated profiling Load, validate, and cache a versioned executable; discover capabilities; manage memory pools, quotas, buffers, queues, events, and asynchronous lifetimes; add structured errors and recovery; preserve stable profile IDs. Report cold/warm and p99 results with load, allocation, copy, queue, device, and synchronization time separated. Lab 5 · Fabless tape-out and first-silicon capstone Run a go/no-go tabletop covering PRD traceability, PPA/system cost, DV/formal, DFT, physical sign-off, foundry/IP/package/test dependencies, software readiness, bring-up known-answer tests, ATE/model correlation, errata, qualification, SDK/customer release, and respin criteria. Final evidence chain: reviewed model artifact → workload/precision report → extension decision → DSL and IR snapshots → executable manifest → runtime/driver trace → reference/simulator/RTL comparison → tape-out and first-silicon review. A reviewer should be able to reproduce the result and identify every unsupported or unproven claim. Interview and portfolio evidence

entries.heading: Explain decisions with a compact evidence chain
entries.text: Architecture

entries.heading: Workload → resource
entries.text: Show how shape/utilization, operations, bytes, latency, power, and cost selected array, SRAM, NoC, precision, and control parameters. Evidence: assumptions, sweeps, rejected alternatives, and the trigger that would reopen the decision. ISA

entries.heading: Contract → implementation freedom
entries.text: Separate normative operands, numerical behavior, ordering, faults, state, and versioning from an internal pipeline or schedule. Evidence: schema, pseudocode, encoder/decoder, simulator, illegal cases, and differential tests. Operators

entries.heading: Bottleneck → optimization
entries.text: Derive work/traffic, name the hierarchy, classify the limit, predict a counter change, implement the lever, and retain correctness. Evidence: before/after traces, counters, distributions, reference diff, and regression guard. Co-design

entries.heading: Feature → traceability
entries.text: Connect product scenario to compiler legality, command, RTL resource, firmware policy, driver lifecycle, observable event, and test. Evidence: reviewed RFC, owner matrix, compatibility impact, adversarial cases, and sign-off result. Product

entries.heading: Demo → lifecycle
entries.text: Discuss coverage, system cost, security, multi-process behavior, recovery, field diagnostics, updates, rollback, and support boundaries. Evidence: readiness gates, failure drills, old/new version matrix, known limits, and rollout plan. Modeling

entries.heading: Fidelity → correlation
entries.text: Explain why LT or AT was sufficient, which mechanisms were omitted, how timing was calibrated, and where prediction error remains. Evidence: shared traces, per-class error, raw configuration, first-divergence report, and correlation CI. Fabless delivery

entries.heading: Requirement → shipped silicon
entries.text: Connect customer goals to architecture/software milestones, partner dependencies, tape-out sign-off, first-silicon correlation, qualification, SDK release, and sustaining. Evidence: stage-gate RACI, risk register, bring-up plan, errata/workaround record, and customer acceptance result. Frontend compiler stack

entries.heading: Extension seam → verified IR handoff
entries.text: Justify the maintained TVM, MLIR, XLA, or LLVM/backend extension boundary, then explain the graph transformation, operator lowering, dataflow/memory schedule, IR invariant, and versioned interface that let the backend generate correct target code. Evidence: pinned build, patch/rebase/upstream policy, before/after IR, semantic and legality checks, capability decisions, memory plan, interface schema, target artifact, source map, and end-to-end result. Runtime

entries.heading: Artifact → correlated execution
entries.text: Trace validation and caching, device capabilities, resource ownership and lifetimes, transfers, queues/events, driver calls, profiling, asynchronous errors, and recovery. Evidence: versioned manifest, allocation and buffer/event trace, stable profile IDs, error injection, compatibility matrix, and full latency breakdown. Models & precision

entries.heading: Workload signature → numerical contract
entries.text: Relate current model families to operations, state, control, traffic, service goals, and mixed BF16/FP8/INT8/INT4 choices. Evidence: workload census, calibration record, bit-accurate tests, task-quality results, kernel coverage, bytes, and end-to-end speed. Accelerator DSL

entries.heading: Semantics → staged lowering
entries.text: Separate domain meaning from target schedule while specifying types, shapes, layout, precision, memory, effects, legality, diagnostics, versioning, and escape hatches. Evidence: language spec, valid/invalid corpus, IR snapshots, source maps, complete conversion, and target execution. Primary specifications and original work

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: Backend engineers must know which semantics survive capture
entries.text: Eager execution, automatic differentiation, graph capture, ahead-of-time export, and backend lowering are different mechanisms. A graph compiler receives only the behavior that the selected capture path represents. 1 PyTorch eager Dispatcher and autograd 2 PyTorch compile/export Dynamo, AOTAutograd, Inductor 3 TensorFlow graph path Eager, tf.function, AutoGraph 4 NPU backend contract What capture must hand off Dynamic execution

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: PyTorch eager: Python call to dispatched kernel
entries.text: A tensor operation reaches the dispatcher, which selects behavior for backend and cross-cutting features such as autograd, autocast, or functionalization. Autograd records a reverse-mode graph of Function objects as the forward computation executes. Reason about Dispatch keys, ATen operator schema, tensor metadata, views/aliasing, mutation, saved tensors, grad mode. Backend implication An NPU kernel registration is not enough if autograd, fake/meta, autocast, serialization, or profiling paths are missing. Failure signature Wrong dispatch key, missing kernel, device mismatch, alias violation, unsupported layout, or backward error. Evidence Operator registration tests, gradcheck where applicable, fake-tensor shape tests, profiler events, CPU differential vectors. Captured execution

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: PyTorch compile and export are related but not interchangeable
entries.text: torch.compile uses TorchDynamo to capture Python frames, AOTAutograd to capture forward/backward work, and a backend such as TorchInductor to generate code. Guards and graph breaks preserve dynamic Python behavior. torch.export targets an ahead-of-time, full-graph ExportedProgram with explicit input constraints. Dynamo Captures traceable regions and guards assumptions; unsupported behavior can create graph breaks or recompilation. AOTAutograd Functionalizes and captures forward/backward graphs so compilers can optimize beyond eager autograd execution. Inductor / backend Consumes captured graphs, performs fusion/scheduling, and generates target code or delegates to another backend. Export Represents an AOT program plus constraints; deployment must validate shapes and unsupported Python side effects. Trace and cache

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: TensorFlow: eager code becomes one or more concrete graphs
entries.text: tf.function traces TensorFlow operations into graphs and caches concrete functions for compatible inputs. AutoGraph converts supported Python control flow into graph-building code. Python side effects happen during tracing, not as ordinary work on every graph execution. Reason about Trace keys, TensorSpec signatures, polymorphic shapes, retracing, captured variables, resources, control flow. Optimization path Graph optimizers and optional XLA compilation operate after capture; target clusters must preserve resource and control dependencies. Failure signature Excess retracing, Python value frozen at trace time, unsupported op, resource placement, shape specialization, graph/eager mismatch. Evidence Concrete-function inventory, GraphDef inspection, signature tests, eager/graph parity, target cluster and fallback report. Compiler boundary

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: The NPU backend must publish a semantic acceptance contract
entries.text: Supported operator names are insufficient. Support depends on rank, shape bounds, dtype, layout, quantization scheme, attributes, aliasing, mutation, dynamic control flow, memory limit, and target revision. Capability Machine-readable predicates plus a human diagnostic for every rejection or fallback. Partition Maximize useful offload while accounting for boundary copies, conversions, synchronization, and cold-start cost. Correctness Reference outputs, tolerance policy, deterministic modes, shape guards, and state/resource behavior. Observability Graph-break or fallback reason, compile report, source map, target counters, and first-divergence capture. Question PyTorch TensorFlow NPU engineering consequence Eager path Dispatcher selects ATen kernels and cross-cutting behavior. Eager runtime executes TensorFlow ops immediately. Device integration needs operator, memory, error, profiler, and lifecycle support, not only a compiler. Autodiff Dynamic reverse graph of autograd Function objects. GradientTape records operations for differentiation. Inference-only backends must reject training paths clearly; training backends need backward and state semantics. Capture Dynamo regions with guards and graph breaks; export offers AOT full-graph capture. tf.function traces and caches concrete graphs. Compile cache keys must include all specialization assumptions that affect generated code. Dynamic shapes Guards, symbolic dimensions, specialization, possible recompilation. Input signatures and trace compatibility control concrete-function reuse. Choose bounded dynamic kernels, shape classes, or compile-on-demand with visible cache behavior. Debug unit Python frame, FX/ATen graph, compiled region, generated kernel. Python function, ConcreteFunction/GraphDef, cluster, executable. Preserve IDs through each level so a device fault maps back to source behavior. ONNX network analysis

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: Inspect the graph before optimizing it
entries.text: ONNX separately versions the IR, operator sets, and model. Shape inference is useful but intentionally incomplete for some dynamic behavior. A production analyzer records unknowns instead of inventing shapes. 1 Validate IR, opsets, schemas, topology, external data 2 Infer Types, ranks, static and symbolic dimensions 3 Inventory Ops, attributes, constants, subgraphs, state 4 Diagnose Target predicates, dynamic regions, fallback islands 5 Transform Ordered passes with local proof obligations 6 Verify Structural checks, numerical parity, performance delta ONNX forensic inventory Python from collections import Counter import math import numpy as np import onnx from onnx import checker, helper, shape_inference model = onnx.load("model.onnx", load_external_data=True) checker.check_model(model, full_check=True) typed = shape_inference.infer_shapes(model, strict_mode=False) graph = typed.graph def shape_of(value): tensor = value.type.tensor_type if not tensor.HasField("shape"): return "unknown-rank" dims = [] for dim in tensor.shape.dim: dims.append(dim.dim_value or dim.dim_param or "?") return dims print("IR:", typed.ir_version) print("Opsets:", [(item.domain or "ai.onnx", item.version) for item in typed.opset_import]) print("Operators:", Counter(node.op_type for node in graph.node)) print("Inputs:", [(value.name, shape_of(value)) for value in graph.input]) print("Outputs:", [(value.name, shape_of(value)) for value in graph.output]) def logical_bytes(tensor): if tensor.data_type == onnx.TensorProto.STRING: return sum(len(value) for value in tensor.string_data) dtype = np.dtype(helper.tensor_dtype_to_np_dtype(tensor.data_type)) return math.prod(tensor.dims) * dtype.itemsize weight_bytes = sum(logical_bytes(item) for item in graph.initializer) print("Initializers:", len(graph.initializer), weight_bytes, "logical bytes") for index, node in enumerate(graph.node): domain = node.domain or "ai.onnx" print(index, domain, node.op_type, list(node.input), list(node.output))

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: Analyzer outputs worth keeping in CI
entries.text: IR and opset versions, model and external-data digests, producer metadata. Input/output signatures with symbolic dimensions and bounded-shape policy. Operator, domain, attribute, initializer, sparse tensor, function, and subgraph inventory. Target support result for every node, with reason and estimated boundary transfer cost. Quantization representation: QDQ, integer operators, scales, zero points, granularity, axis. Reference vectors and per-output tolerances tied to preprocessing and postprocessing versions. Peak live tensor estimate, constant bytes, dynamic allocation sites, and fallback memory. Pass order Transformation Proof obligation before the next stage 1. Validate/version Reject malformed graphs; convert opsets only with defined adapters. Every node resolves to known semantics for its imported domain and version. 2. Type/shape analysis Propagate known facts and record unresolved symbols. No pass assumes a static dimension that analysis has not proved or guarded. 3. Normalize Canonicalize equivalent forms and make implicit broadcasts/layouts explicit where needed. Reference output remains equal; source and quantization metadata survive. 4. Simplify Constant fold, eliminate dead/identity work, simplify control and shape subgraphs. Folding respects dtype, overflow, NaN, rounding, and external-data policy. 5. Capability/partition Assign maximal legal regions to NPU or fallback providers. Each region satisfies target predicates; boundary conversions are explicit and costed. 6. Target transforms Fuse, choose layouts, quantize/lower, schedule, and plan memory inside owned regions. Numerical, memory, and resource constraints pass independent verifiers. 7. Package/compare Emit executable and run framework/ONNX/target parity plus performance measurements. Artifact provenance, tolerances, target versions, and regression result are retained. Partition timing matters. ONNX Runtime performs provider-independent optimizations before partitioning and provider-specific work afterward. Its current documentation recommends a plugin execution provider for new integrations starting with ONNX Runtime 1.23. A vendor backend should verify which layer owns each rewrite so two optimizers do not erase one another's patterns or apply incompatible layouts. Applied TVM architecture

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: Use TVM as two connected optimization levels plus a runtime
entries.text: The site already introduces TVM beside MLIR. This section focuses on the current practical mapping: Relax for graph/dataflow structure, TensorIR for primitive tensor programs, scheduling for implementation choices, and runtime modules for deployment. Front end Model import Build an IRModule with Relax functions Relax Graph transforms Legalize, fuse, plan buffers, preserve shapes TensorIR Primitive functions Loop nests, buffers, loads/stores, tensor intrinsics Schedule Implementation Tile, reorder, vectorize, bind, tensorize, search Codegen Target module LLVM or source code plus external kernels Runtime Execute VM bytecode, compiled functions, PackedFunc, allocators Extension point NPU use Acceptance evidence Relax import / rewrite Represent target composite patterns, quantized forms, shape constraints, and offload regions. Before/after IR, structural matcher tests, numerical parity, rejection diagnostics. Operator legalization Lower high-level ops to target primitives, TIR, or external PackedFunc calls. Semantic tests across dtype, shape boundary, attributes, and dynamic dimensions. TensorIR Represent local buffers, data movement, loop structure, and hardware tensor intrinsics. Generated access bounds, race analysis, bit parity, resource estimates. Schedule / MetaSchedule Search tile, layout, memory scope, parallelization, and tensorization choices. Reproducible workload key, search budget, measured target result, held-out validation. Codegen / module Emit NPU command binaries, firmware code, target source, or runtime-call wrappers. Versioned module metadata, load tests, disassembly/descriptor inspection, compatibility checks. Runtime / VM Load modules, resolve functions, allocate devices, execute graph control, call compiled kernels. Lifecycle, concurrency, serialization, allocator, error, and remote-device tests. RISC-V and NPU accelerator ISA

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: The key decision is how software submits work, not whether an opcode looks elegant
entries.text: RISC-V reserves custom encoding spaces for vendor-specific extensions. An accelerator may instead use MMIO, memory-resident command queues, a standard device interface, or a combination. Workload granularity and system isolation usually matter more than instruction count. Integration style Best fit Main cost Compiler/runtime consequence Custom scalar/vector instruction Fine-grain tightly coupled operations with registers or local state. Toolchain, context state, exceptions, virtualization, and memory-model integration. Intrinsic/builtin lowering, assembler/disassembler, ABI and scheduler awareness. MMIO control Simple control/status, boot, reset, capability, and low-rate commands. High per-command CPU overhead; ordering and posted writes require care. Driver API and register generation; rarely suitable for every tensor tile. Memory command queue Coarse asynchronous kernels, DMA descriptors, multiple in-flight jobs. Descriptor validation, coherency, fences, queue wrap, reset and fault recovery. Compiler emits command graph; runtime owns buffers, dependencies, submission, events. Firmware RPC Complex scheduling, stable host API across changing hardware internals. Firmware latency, version negotiation, watchdogs, diagnosability. Artifact carries firmware-facing operations; host remains insulated from microarchitecture. Illustrative queue descriptor C ABI contract #include <stdint.h> struct npu_command_v1 { uint16_t size_bytes; /* permits compatible extension */ uint16_t opcode; uint32_t flags; uint64_t command_id; uint64_t executable_id; uint64_t input_iova; uint64_t output_iova; uint32_t input_bytes; uint32_t output_bytes; uint32_t dependency_count; uint32_t completion_slot; }; /* Producer protocol: * 1. Validate ownership and bounds. * 2. Write descriptor and dependency records. * 3. Publish with the required release ordering. * 4. Update producer index and ring the doorbell. */

entries.chapterTitle: Frontend compiler, IR, and code generation
entries.heading: ISA and ABI review checklist
entries.text: Define architectural state, privilege, context-switch cost, and reset value. Specify operand widths, alignment, endianness, rounding, saturation, and exception behavior. Separate virtual, physical, and I/O virtual addresses; state IOMMU and coherency assumptions. Name memory ordering for descriptors, MMIO, DMA, completion, and CPU visibility. Define malformed command, page fault, watchdog, engine fault, retry, and partial-write behavior. Reserve feature bits and size-versioned messages; test old/new driver and firmware combinations. Generate encoders, decoders, docs, simulator tables, and disassembly from one source of truth. Run differential ISA tests plus whole-command random sequences through model and RTL. RISC-V uses a relaxed memory model and explicit fences for required ordering. A queue protocol must translate that architectural rule into concrete producer/consumer barriers and device coherency operations. "Write the descriptor, then ring the doorbell" is incomplete until visibility and ordering are specified for every agent. Low-power and high-performance optimization

Production engineering reference | updated 2026-07-11 NPU and SoC Software Architecture A contract-first view of the software that turns a model into work on an edge NPU.
