Trace the complete stack Inspect interface contracts Build the portfolio labs Compile Freeze graph, schedule, memory, and ABI decisions Dispatch Move buffers and commands through stable queues Correlate Keep model, command, cycle, and wall-clock identities aligned Qualify Gate correctness, performance, power, and compatibility Coverage boundary

entries.heading: This page adds system contracts instead of repeating existing lessons
entries.text: The current site already covers accelerator taxonomy, LLVM/MLIR fundamentals, graph optimization, tiling, quantization, C, Git, and Analog CIM. Use the foundation chapters first, then treat the Analog CIM material as an optional specialization. This document begins where those introductions stop. Accelerator comparison NPU, GPU, TPU, VPU, and LPU tradeoffs already exist. Use existing processor study LLVM and MLIR foundations SSA, dialects, progressive lowering, and backend concepts already exist. Use existing compiler foundation Graph, tiling, and quantization Core rewrites, layouts, memory levels, TVM, and quantization already exist. Use existing NPU practice New: executable contracts Artifact schema, target manifest, ABI compatibility, and reproducibility. Study compiler-to-runtime boundaries New: production control plane SDK, runtime, driver, firmware, queues, synchronization, and recovery. Study runtime ownership New: model-to-silicon evidence C++ models, cycle correlation, power and bandwidth metrics, debugger, and CI gates. Study verification and profiling End-to-end architecture

entries.heading: The stack has two products: an executable artifact and a controlled device
entries.text: Data-plane work carries tensors and commands. Control-plane work owns discovery, allocation, power, faults, version negotiation, and observability. A robust design makes both planes explicit. Model plane Application Inputs, outputs, preprocessing, latency policy Framework / ONNX Graph semantics, shapes, dtypes, constants Deployment profile Target, precision, memory, fallback, power mode Build plane Importer and analyzer Validate, infer, normalize, diagnose support NPU compiler Partition, schedule, plan memory, lower kernels Artifact packager Code, constants, commands, metadata, ABI versions Offline build boundary Host control SDK C/C++ API, Python tools, examples, diagnostics User runtime Sessions, buffers, queues, events, execution Kernel driver Isolation, DMA mapping, interrupts, power, reset User / kernel / device trust boundaries Device control Firmware scheduler Validate descriptors, sequence engines, report faults SoC services IOMMU, DMA, NoC, clocks, power domains, timers Trace and counters Correlation IDs, cycles, bytes, stalls, errors NPU data plane Command processors Queues, microcode, dependencies, events Compute engines Matrix, vector, scalar, activation, reduction Memory system SRAM banks, caches, DRAM, fabric, coherency The deployable artifact is the architectural hinge. It should identify the target and ABI, define constants and mutable buffers, carry command or kernel payloads, preserve graph-to-command debug maps, and include enough provenance to reproduce the compile. A binary blob without that contract is difficult to validate, debug, cache, or evolve. Responsibility catalog

entries.heading: What every component consumes, produces, owns, and must reveal
entries.text: The compact map shows placement. The catalog below shows engineering ownership. A layer is complete only when its input contract, output contract, decisions, telemetry, and failure behavior are all explicit. 01

entries.heading: Model plane
entries.text: Defines application meaning and deployment intent before target-specific lowering begins. Application Data + control Converts a product request, sensor frame, or media stream into model inputs and turns model outputs into product behavior. It owns the user-visible latency and correctness contract, not only tensor I/O. Consumes Raw requests or sensor data, application configuration, model identity, and service-level policy. Produces Typed tensor bindings, shape metadata, deadlines, priorities, correlation IDs, and interpreted outputs. Owns Preprocessing and postprocessing versions, batching and admission policy, fallback, cancellation, and accuracy/latency tradeoffs. Must expose Request shape, preprocessing time, queue delay, inference time, postprocessing time, fallback reason, and final status. Failure pattern: training used RGB normalization and NHWC tensors, while deployment silently sends BGR or NCHW; the accelerator is correct but the product result is wrong. Framework / ONNX Semantic data Represents the portable computation contract. A graph is more than operator names: opset versions, attributes, control flow, broadcasting, aliasing, layouts, quantization metadata, and shape constraints determine the result that every backend must preserve. Consumes Trained checkpoint or framework module, exporter configuration, example inputs, and external constant files. Produces A versioned graph with nodes, tensors, constants, symbolic dimensions, dtypes, quantization parameters, and named outputs. Owns Framework-level semantics and export fidelity; it does not own target scheduling, physical addresses, or device command order. Must expose Exporter revision, opset imports, source-node mapping, unresolved shape constraints, model digest, and framework golden outputs. Failure pattern: an exporter decomposes one operation differently after an upgrade, or leaves preprocessing outside the graph, and the importer accepts a graph whose meaning no longer matches the validated model. Deployment profile Control policy Separates model semantics from deployment choices. The same graph may need different precision, memory, fallback, and power decisions for a camera, battery device, automotive SoC, or throughput server. Consumes Model analysis, hardware capability manifest, accuracy tolerance, latency target, memory budget, thermal limits, and fleet policy. Produces An immutable compile profile naming target revision, shape classes, precision policy, calibration data, fallback rules, and optimization objective. Owns Allowed approximations, dynamic-shape bounds, SRAM/DRAM limits, power mode, digital fallback, and compatibility floor. Must expose Profile digest, policy source, rejected constraints, selected objective weights, calibration-set identity, and target capability version. Failure pattern: important target flags live only in shell scripts or engineer memory, so two builds of the same model produce different artifacts with no reproducible explanation. 02

entries.heading: Build plane
entries.text: Proves semantics, makes target decisions, and freezes them into a deployable contract. Importer and analyzer Semantic gate Turns an external graph into a canonical internal representation while preserving source identity. It should fail early on ambiguity and provide a support report before expensive target compilation. Consumes Framework graph, constants, deployment profile, calibration metadata, importer schema, and target support manifest. Produces Validated typed IR, inferred shape constraints, canonical operators, source maps, support classification, and actionable diagnostics. Owns Schema and opset checks, shape/type inference, constant integrity, semantic normalization, capability diagnosis, and minimal failing subgraphs. Must expose Unsupported node path, source location, inferred versus declared shape, fallback reason, warning severity, and normalization history. Failure pattern: unsupported behavior is discovered after many compiler passes and reported as an internal lowering error, leaving the user unable to identify the original node or repair the model. NPU compiler Program construction Converts validated IR into a legal and efficient command program. Partitioning, layout, quantization, tiling, scheduling, and memory allocation are coupled decisions because each changes traffic, lifetime, engine occupancy, and numerical behavior. Consumes Canonical IR, deployment profile, target ISA and capabilities, kernel library, calibration data, and measured cost models. Produces Partitions, lowered kernels or microcode, command DAG, DMA plan, static buffer offsets, constants, relocations, and debug maps. Owns Legalization, fusion, precision and layout choice, tiling, resource scheduling, memory lifetimes, spill decisions, and fallback boundaries. Must expose Pass pipeline, IR checkpoints, cost breakdown, rejected alternatives, peak memory, expected cycles/bytes, and every graph-to-command mapping. Failure pattern: a locally faster fusion increases live memory, forces DRAM spills, and makes the complete graph slower because schedule and allocation were optimized independently. Artifact packager Offline/runtime hinge Serializes compiler decisions into a bounded, versioned object that a runtime can validate and load without reconstructing compiler intent. The format is a product ABI, even when only one compiler emits it. Consumes Code and microcode, constants, command templates, buffer plan, relocations, entry points, ABI schemas, debug map, and build provenance. Produces A deterministic artifact with aligned sections, manifest, feature requirements, integrity data, signatures when required, and a stable build ID. Owns Section layout, bounds, compression, relocation records, target/ABI compatibility ranges, hashes, schema evolution, and reproducible serialization. Must expose Human-readable manifest, section inventory and hashes, compiler/pass revision, model and profile digests, required resources, and debug-symbol availability. Failure pattern: the runtime accepts an opaque blob for the wrong firmware ABI or hardware stepping, then fails after allocation or submission with no safe compatibility diagnosis. 03

entries.heading: Host control
entries.text: Turns an artifact and application request into isolated, asynchronous device work. SDK Supported interface Provides the supported developer path through compilation, packaging, loading, execution, profiling, and diagnosis. Its job is to make correct lifetime and synchronization behavior easier than unsafe shortcuts. Consumes Compiler and runtime capabilities, artifact schemas, support matrix, target discovery data, and diagnostic interfaces. Produces Stable C ABI, C++ RAII wrappers, Python tools, CLI output, examples, headers, packages, compatibility documentation, and reports. Owns Public handle semantics, ownership rules, error taxonomy, thread-safety contract, binding parity, deprecation policy, and example quality. Must expose SDK/runtime/driver/firmware versions, target features, artifact inspection, machine-readable errors, trace export, and minimal reproducer tools. Failure pattern: samples bypass the runtime or rely on hidden global state, so customer applications copy patterns that leak buffers, serialize asynchronous work, or break on upgrades. User runtime Execution owner Owns user-space object lifetime and asynchronous truth. It discovers devices, loads artifacts, manages sessions and buffers, submits work, resolves events, and converts lower-level failures into stable API results. Consumes Validated artifact, application tensor bindings, dynamic shapes, queue policy, driver capabilities, and device telemetry. Produces Executable/session handles, buffer and mapping objects, submissions, dependency events, completions, output bindings, and diagnostics. Owns Artifact cache and load policy, runtime allocation, imports/exports, queue ordering, batching, event lifetime, timeout, fallback, cancellation, and device-loss recovery. Must expose Session/queue/command IDs, hidden-copy count, allocation and cache statistics, queue delay, submit/complete timestamps, fallback, timeout, and terminal device state. Failure pattern: a buffer is destroyed while commands still reference it, or a convenience call performs a hidden device-wide synchronization that destroys pipeline overlap. Kernel driver Privilege boundary Converts untrusted user requests into isolated hardware resources. It is the authority for process ownership, DMA-visible memory, queue access, interrupt delivery, firmware lifecycle, power, and reset. Consumes System calls or ioctls, object handles, buffer import requests, validated submission descriptors, fences, and administrator policy. Produces Contexts, IOMMU mappings, pinned or imported buffers, queue slots, doorbell access, completion fences, fault reports, and reset results. Owns Isolation, handle validation, DMA mapping lifetime, cache maintenance, interrupt routing, scheduler admission, firmware loading, power transitions, and reset escalation. Must expose Process/context identity, mapped bytes, submissions and interrupts, IOMMU faults, firmware health, power state, reset generation, and stable kernel error codes. Failure pattern: a stale handle or mapping survives context teardown and lets later work DMA into released memory, creating both a correctness fault and a security boundary violation. 04

entries.heading: Device control
entries.text: Validates host intent, schedules finite resources, manages the SoC, and reports device truth. Firmware scheduler Device authority Receives queue work after the kernel boundary and turns it into legal engine sequences. It protects the device from malformed descriptors, arbitrates shared resources, watches progress, and owns first-stage recovery. Consumes Command-ring descriptors, dependency tokens, buffer mappings, queue/context metadata, deadlines, and negotiated feature bits. Produces Engine dispatches, DMA sequences, resource reservations, completion records, performance snapshots, and structured fault reports. Owns Descriptor validation, dependency scheduling, fairness, preemption points, SRAM/DMA/engine reservations, watchdogs, queue quarantine, and warm-reset policy. Must expose Queue and command generation, scheduler state, wait reason, resource occupancy, heartbeat, last completed unit, faulting descriptor, and recovery action. Failure pattern: reset leaves a stale producer generation or dependency token visible, so new commands wait on work that belonged to the previous firmware epoch. SoC services Shared infrastructure Supplies address translation, data movement, communication, time, clocks, resets, and power domains to the NPU. These services determine whether an otherwise correct accelerator can operate predictably inside the SoC. Consumes Device virtual addresses, transfer descriptors, NoC routes and priorities, clock requests, power votes, reset requests, and timer operations. Produces IOMMU translations, DMA completions, coherent or explicitly synchronized data, NoC delivery, stable clocks, powered domains, timestamps, and fault interrupts. Owns Initialization order, translation context, burst and alignment limits, coherency protocol, bandwidth/QoS policy, DVFS sequencing, clock gating, and reset dependencies. Must expose Bytes and latency per path, page faults, NoC congestion, DMA utilization, clock frequency, voltage/power state, temperature, throttling, and reset cause. Failure pattern: a compiler schedule assumes bandwidth that the shared NoC cannot provide under camera or ISP traffic, causing deadline misses that never appear in isolated NPU tests. Trace and counters Observability plane Preserves identity and time across graph nodes, artifacts, queues, firmware commands, engines, memory, and host APIs. Counters without units, scope, correlation, and loss accounting are not actionable telemetry. Consumes Compiler debug IDs, runtime correlation IDs, firmware events, engine counters, DMA/NoC events, power changes, faults, and clock-sync samples. Produces A versioned bounded-overhead event stream, counter samples, host/device time conversion, layer timeline, fault bundle, and profiler database. Owns ID propagation, timestamp width and wrap, clock-domain alignment, event schema, units, sampling and trigger policy, buffer overflow behavior, and privacy controls. Must expose Lost-event count, sampling interval, counter scope, conversion uncertainty, frequency epoch, schema version, source engine, and trace buffer pressure. Failure pattern: a layer is slow, but command, DMA, and engine records cannot be joined because each layer generated unrelated IDs and used a different clock without synchronization metadata. 05

entries.heading: NPU data plane
entries.text: Fetches the frozen program, performs numerical work, and moves tensors through the memory hierarchy. Command processors Dispatch data path Fetches and decodes validated command buffers or microcode, resolves dependencies, programs engines, and emits completion events. It is the hardware realization of the compiler and firmware command model. Consumes Command buffers, microcode, queue pointers, dependency tokens, tensor descriptors, addresses, engine masks, and execution modes. Produces Register or descriptor writes to engines, DMA launches, barriers, event updates, completion status, and precise command faults. Owns Fetch/decode, queue arbitration, branch or loop semantics, barrier ordering, dependency-scoreboard behavior, legal opcode handling, and forward progress. Must expose Current queue/opcode, commands retired, dependency wait cycles, decode faults, issue stalls, event state, and last known forward-progress point. Failure pattern: a malformed length or unsupported opcode advances the queue incorrectly, turning one bad command into an unrecoverable device hang rather than a bounded fault. Compute engines Numerical data path Performs matrix, vector, scalar, activation, reduction, conversion, and optional sparse operations. The contract includes exact numeric behavior for every precision mode, not just nominal throughput. Consumes Input tensor tiles, weights, accumulator state, tensor views, masks, strides, precision mode, rounding mode, saturation policy, and kernel parameters. Produces Output tiles, partial sums or reductions, exception/status bits, dependency events, utilization counters, and numerical debug checkpoints. Owns Operation semantics, accumulator width, rounding and saturation, NaN/Inf policy where relevant, tail handling, sparse metadata, pipeline hazards, and deterministic modes. Must expose Active and issued cycles, lane utilization, operand starvation, pipeline stalls, overflow/saturation count, sparse skips, and per-mode error status. Failure pattern: the main matrix shape passes, but tail channels use a different rounding or mask rule, creating small layer errors that accumulate only on production tensor shapes. Memory system Storage + movement Delivers constants, activations, commands, and intermediate state through local SRAM, caches, DRAM, and the fabric. Capacity, bank topology, alignment, ordering, and contention shape the achievable schedule. Consumes Compiler buffer plan, engine load/store traffic, DMA requests, cache operations, physical or device virtual addresses, priorities, and coherency actions. Produces Data with defined visibility and ordering, allocation capacity, bandwidth and latency service, cache responses, fabric transactions, and memory faults. Owns Address spaces, SRAM bank mapping, cacheability, replacement and write policy, DRAM channels, arbitration/QoS, coherency, ECC, and memory protection. Must expose Bytes per level, hit/miss rate, bank conflicts, queue occupancy, DRAM and NoC stalls, peak live memory, ECC events, page faults, and spill traffic. Failure pattern: tensors fit in total SRAM capacity but collide in the same banks during concurrent compute and DMA, so the realized throughput is far below the compiler estimate. Deployable artifact anatomy

entries.heading: The runtime should load decisions, not rediscover them
entries.text: The artifact carries the compiler-to-runtime contract across machines, releases, and trust boundaries. Each section needs explicit bounds, alignment, integrity, compatibility, and ownership rules. Artifact section Required contents Loader validation question Identity and compatibility Magic, format version, target family/revision, required feature bits, runtime and firmware ABI ranges, endianness, build ID. Can this runtime, firmware, and hardware revision execute every required feature without reinterpretation? Entry points and tensor ABI Named entry points, tensor count, shape classes or bounds, dtype, layout, quantization, stride/alignment, mutability, binding index. Do application bindings match the compiled interface before any device work is submitted? Code and microcode Engine payloads, kernel IDs, ISA revision, command templates, patch locations, execution permissions, required scratch state. Are all opcodes, payload sizes, alignments, and executable regions legal for the negotiated target? Constants Weights, lookup tables, scales, zero points, compression/encryption flags, placement hints, alignment, content hashes. Are constant bytes intact, trusted when policy requires it, and mapped into legal address classes? Mutable buffers Static arena size, offsets, lifetimes, alias groups, access permissions, bank/address class, host visibility, dynamic allocation requirements. Can every buffer be materialized without overlap, overflow, illegal aliasing, or an unsupported memory class? Command and dependency graph DMA operations, engine commands, barriers, event/token IDs, queue requirements, patchable tensor addresses, timeout classes. Are dependencies acyclic and bounded, descriptors well formed, and all referenced resources declared? Relocations and resources Symbols, addends, section references, address widths, SRAM banks, DMA channels, queue count, firmware scratch, counter requirements. Can relocation arithmetic be checked without truncation, out-of-range access, or resource overcommit? Debug, provenance, and trust Graph-to-partition/kernel/command map, tensor checkpoints, compiler revision, pass configuration, model/profile digests, section hashes, optional signature. Can the build be reproduced, faults mapped back to the graph, and every loaded byte authenticated according to policy? 1 Parse Check header, sizes, offsets, integer arithmetic, required and optional sections 2 Negotiate Match target revision, feature bits, runtime ABI, firmware ABI, and policy 3 Verify Validate hashes or signatures, permissions, tensor ABI, commands, and dependency bounds 4 Materialize Allocate arenas, map constants, apply checked relocations, and patch runtime bindings 5 Register Create executable handle, publish debug IDs, and make submission atomically visible Failure must be atomic: a rejected artifact must not leave executable memory, DMA mappings, queue state, or partially registered debug identities behind. Loading either produces one valid executable object or rolls back every resource. Interface explorer

entries.heading: Every boundary needs ownership, invariants, observability, and versioning
entries.text: 1 Model to compiler Semantic import contract 2 Compiler to runtime Executable artifact contract 3 Runtime to driver Resource and submission ABI 4 Driver to firmware Queue and fault protocol 5 Firmware to engines Micro-operation contract 6 Trace to tools Time and identity contract Semantic boundary

entries.heading: Model to compiler
entries.text: The importer must distinguish what the graph states, what it implies, and what remains dynamic. Operator names alone are not a contract: opset, attributes, layouts, quantization metadata, control flow, aliasing, and preprocessing assumptions all matter. Inputs Model IR, opset imports, shape constraints, constants, calibration profile, target policy. Owned by Exporter and importer jointly; neither side may silently reinterpret semantics. Invariants Graph validates, dtypes and ranks are legal, outputs match a framework reference within declared tolerance. Diagnostics Unsupported node path, source location, shape state, fallback reason, and minimal reproducer. Deployable boundary

entries.heading: Compiler to runtime
entries.text: The compiler freezes decisions that the runtime must execute without reconstructing compiler intent. Treat the artifact format as a versioned product, not an internal serialization accident. Payload Target code, command templates, constants, relocations, buffer plan, entry points, debug map. Compatibility Format version, runtime ABI, firmware ABI, target ID, feature bits, endianness, alignment. Security Bounds, signatures or hashes, section validation, integer-overflow checks, untrusted model policy. Reproducibility Compiler revision, pass configuration, model digest, target profile, deterministic build identifier. Privilege boundary

entries.heading: Runtime to kernel driver
entries.text: User space asks for capabilities, memory, queues, and synchronization. The kernel validates ownership and lifetime, maps memory for DMA, controls reset and power, and prevents one process from corrupting another. Objects Device, context, buffer, mapping, queue, fence/event, executable handle, telemetry stream. Submission Validated descriptors, dependency fences, completion event, timeout, cancellation and reset policy. Memory CPU virtual, physical, and device-visible DMA addresses remain distinct; mapping lifetime is explicit. Errors Stable codes separate invalid input, out-of-memory, timeout, page fault, firmware fault, and device loss. Asynchronous boundary

entries.heading: Driver to firmware
entries.text: A ring, doorbell, and interrupt look simple until wraparound, reset, partial writes, stale generations, and malformed descriptors occur. Define producer and consumer indices, ownership transfer, memory ordering, and recovery together. Transport Shared command/completion rings, MMIO doorbells, generation counters, interrupt or polling mode. Ordering Descriptor bytes become visible before the producer index; completion data becomes visible before signaling. Watchdog Per-command deadline, heartbeat, fault snapshot, queue quarantine, warm reset, full reset escalation. Upgrade Feature negotiation and backward-compatible message sizes protect driver/firmware combinations. Hardware boundary

entries.heading: Firmware to NPU engines
entries.text: The scheduler translates a command graph into engine work while preserving dependencies and resource limits. Register writes are only one part; descriptors, local-memory ownership, preemption points, and fault semantics complete the contract. Work unit Kernel or micro-op ID, tensor views, addresses, strides, tile counts, precision, dependency tokens. Resources Engine slots, SRAM banks, DMA channels, NoC credits, scratch registers, power/clock state. Completion Architectural write visibility, status code, performance counters, timestamp, fault address. Model parity Bit-accurate result, bounded cycle estimate, and named differences from RTL or silicon. Observability boundary

entries.heading: Trace producer to debugger and profiler
entries.text: Every layer, partition, command, DMA, interrupt, and counter sample needs a correlation path. Clock-domain conversion must carry source frequency, wrap width, synchronization samples, and uncertainty. Identity Model digest, graph node, fused region, executable, queue, command, engine, buffer, process. Time Host monotonic time plus device cycles, conversion epochs, wrap handling, and calibration error. Events Begin/end slices, counters, flows, faults, allocations, frequency and power-state changes. Schema Versioned fields, stable units, optional extensions, bounded overhead, loss accounting. Edge NPU framework and SDK

entries.heading: An SDK is the supported path through the architecture
entries.text: Headers and bindings are only the surface. A production SDK also defines packaging, target discovery, diagnostics, examples, compatibility policy, telemetry, and the boundary between compile time and run time. 1 Inspect Validate model, shapes, operators, precision, target support 2 Compile Apply target policy and produce a reproducible artifact 3 Package Bundle artifact, labels, preprocessing, version manifest 4 Load Negotiate target and allocate session resources 5 Run Bind buffers, submit asynchronously, synchronize explicitly 6 Diagnose Export trace, counters, tensor checkpoints, and errors SDK surface Required contract Failure that good design prevents C ABI Opaque handles, explicit ownership, size-versioned structs, stable error codes, no C++ ABI leakage. Applications breaking when compiler, STL, or internal object layouts change. C++ API RAII wrappers, typed views, move semantics, futures/events, exception or status policy, thread-safety statement. Leaked contexts, double frees, hidden synchronization, and ambiguous buffer lifetime. Python tools Model inspection, compilation orchestration, reports, reproducible config, clear native-error propagation. Python becoming an undocumented second runtime or hiding target failures. CLI Machine-readable output, deterministic exit codes, config files, artifact hashes, quiet and verbose modes. CI scripts scraping human prose and silently accepting partial success. Examples Minimal sync, async, zero-copy, dynamic-shape, multi-model, profiling, custom-op, and recovery paths. A sample that works only on a golden model and teaches unsafe lifetime patterns. Compatibility Documented support matrix across SDK, artifact, driver, firmware, hardware revision, and model opset. Field failures that appear only after independent component upgrades. NPU runtime software

entries.heading: The runtime owns object lifetime and asynchronous truth
entries.text: Session state

entries.heading: Create, load, bind, submit, retire, destroy
entries.text: Each transition has preconditions. Destroy waits for or cancels in-flight work by policy; a failed device transitions the session to a terminal state instead of pretending later calls can succeed. Queue semantics

entries.heading: Ordering must be named
entries.text: Define in-order versus out-of-order execution, cross-queue dependencies, host visibility, event reuse, callback context, timeout behavior, and whether cancellation is best effort or guaranteed. Memory objects

entries.heading: Ownership is separate from visibility
entries.text: A buffer can be alive but not coherent, mapped but not device-visible, or device-visible but not writable. State transitions should name mapping, cache maintenance, import/export, and fence ownership. Concern C++ production path Python engineering path Hot execution Queue submission, buffer management, synchronization, callbacks, low-overhead tracing. Usually wraps native code; avoid per-layer Python dispatch in latency-sensitive paths. Compiler control Pass implementations, IR ownership, serializers, target backends, runtime ABI. Experiment orchestration, pass configuration, model analysis, test generation, reports. Hardware models Bit/cycle models, SystemC/TLM, Verilator harnesses, deterministic simulation. Stimulus generation, differential comparison, sweep automation, visualization. Tests Unit, concurrency, sanitizers, ABI, fault injection, performance microbenchmarks. Model corpus, property tests, tolerance analysis, CI summaries, triage automation. Compiler architecture beyond basic rewrites

entries.heading: Scheduling and memory planning solve one coupled resource problem
entries.text: Graph fusion, tiling, layouts, and quantization are already covered in NPU Practice . Here the focus is pass contracts, constrained scheduling, and offset assignment for a real target. Import Prove semantics Validate versions, infer types/shapes, preserve source map Legalize Expose target forms Normalize ops without losing quantization intent Partition Choose ownership Price fallback boundaries and transfer cost Schedule Order resources Engines, DMA, dependencies, buffers, deadlines Allocate Assign storage Lifetimes, banks, alignment, aliasing, spill Package Freeze contract Code, commands, constants, manifest, debug map Critical-path list scheduling

entries.heading: Prioritize ready work by downstream urgency
entries.text: Compute an earliest/latest schedule or remaining critical-path length. At each decision, choose a ready operation whose engine and buffers are available. Add transfer and bank-conflict cost to avoid a compute-only optimum. Modulo or pipeline scheduling

entries.heading: Overlap repeated tiles and frames
entries.text: Pick an initiation interval constrained by engine occupancy, DMA throughput, dependencies, and buffer reuse. Prologue, steady state, and epilogue schedules need separate validation. Search and exact methods

entries.heading: Use costlier solvers on bounded regions
entries.text: Dynamic programming, beam search, ILP, or constraint programming can optimize small fused regions. Production compilers usually combine exact local decisions with scalable heuristics and measured cost models. Static arena planning Lifetime and alignment aware buffers = sort_by(size_descending, temporary_buffers) active = interval_index(buffers.live_range) arena = empty_free_list() for buffer in buffers: legal = gaps_not_overlapping(active, buffer.live_range) legal = enforce_alignment_bank_and_address_class(legal, buffer) offset = best_fit_with_fragmentation_cost(legal, buffer.size) if offset is NONE: offset = grow_arena_or_spill(buffer) assign(buffer, offset) reserve_for_lifetime(arena, buffer.live_range, offset, buffer.size) verify_no_illegal_aliases(arena) emit_offsets_and_peak_usage(arena)

entries.heading: Allocator proof obligations
entries.text: Buffers overlap in address only when lifetimes do not overlap or an in-place alias is explicitly legal. Sub-byte and packed formats still satisfy engine and DMA alignment requirements. Bank selection respects concurrent access patterns, not only total capacity. Dynamic dimensions have bounded arenas, shape classes, or a runtime allocation path. Spills include transfer commands, synchronization, and performance cost in the schedule. The emitted peak is independently recomputed by a verifier before packaging. Hardware C++ modeling and integration

entries.heading: One model cannot be fast, bit-exact, cycle-exact, and easy to change at once
entries.text: Use a model ladder with named fidelity. SystemC/TLM supports architectural exploration and virtual platforms; Verilator compiles SystemVerilog into executable C++ or SystemC models for closer RTL correlation. L0 Functional Tensor semantics and shapes; fastest reference for graph tests L1 Bit accurate Integer widths, rounding, saturation, special values, deterministic parity L2 Transaction level DMA, NoC, memory contention, command latency, approximate timing L3 Cycle model Pipelines, queues, hazards, stalls, counters, firmware-visible behavior L4 RTL / silicon Waveforms, exact protocols, measured counters, final correlation authority Model contract Required definition Correlation evidence Functional Supported op or micro-op semantics, tensor layout, numeric mode, exception behavior. Golden vectors and randomized differential tests against framework/reference kernels. Temporal Cycle start/end convention, pipeline occupancy, queue depth, arbitration, backpressure. Cycle-by-cycle event comparison for directed traces plus aggregate error on model corpus. Memory Address spaces, transaction size, burst, alignment, banks, cache/coherency assumptions. Bytes and transactions by engine, bank conflicts, peak occupancy, RTL counter parity. Integration Register map, descriptors, interrupts, reset, power states, version and feature discovery. Same driver/firmware tests run against model, FPGA/emulation, and silicon where possible. Known gaps Deliberately omitted behavior and the expected direction/magnitude of resulting error. Versioned correlation report; no unexplained tuning constant is accepted as architecture. Integration rule: do not let the performance model become a second undocumented ISA. Reuse the same generated register, descriptor, opcode, and trace definitions across compiler, runtime, firmware, model, and debugger whenever the build system permits it. Hardware metric profiling

entries.heading: Power, cycles, latency, and bandwidth need a shared measurement frame
entries.text: "Clock latency" is ambiguous. Report device cycles, clock frequency, queue delay, execution duration, and end-to-end wall time separately. Correlate each value to shape, batch, precision, power mode, and temperature. End-to-end latency T = Tqueue + Thost + Tdma + Texec + Tsync Expose overlap; do not add mutually concurrent intervals twice. Engine utilization U = busy cycles / available cycles Define available cycles after clock and power gating. Memory bandwidth BW = transferred bytes / measured time State payload versus fabric bytes and read/write direction. Energy per inference E = integral(P(t) dt) / completed runs Subtract or report idle baseline and include steady thermal state. Host queue submit wait DMA read weights input Matrix engine conv 12 conv 13 Vector engine activation requant Fault / stall bank stall Metric Collect Control variables Common mistake Latency Host monotonic timestamps, device start/end cycles, queue events. Warm/cold, batch, shape, frequency, thermal state, concurrent load. Mixing compile/setup time with steady execution or reporting only an average. Power Board rail samples, on-chip monitors, PMIC telemetry, state transitions. Sample rate, rails included, idle baseline, DVFS, temperature, workload duty cycle. Dividing a slow power average by a short burst without time alignment. Memory BW Controller/NoC counters, DMA descriptors, trace bytes, duration. Read/write, compression, cache hits, payload/overhead, all traffic generators. Comparing payload bandwidth directly with a raw peak bus figure. Clock and cycles Cycle counters plus frequency-change events and clock-domain IDs. DVFS epochs, gating, counter wrap, asynchronous domains, timestamp uncertainty. Converting all cycles using one nominal frequency. Network layer step debugger

entries.heading: "Next layer" is a mapping problem, not a hardware primitive
entries.text: Compilers fuse, split, reorder, tile, and overlap graph operations. A debugger should expose several step granularities and preserve the many-to-many map between source nodes, compiled regions, commands, and engines. Logical step

entries.heading: Framework or ONNX node
entries.text: Best for model authors. The debugger materializes a semantically meaningful output even when the implementation fused it away, which may require an instrumented recompile. Compiled step

entries.heading: Partition or fused region
entries.text: Best for compiler triage. It compares region inputs/outputs, target support, layouts, precision, and reference execution without exposing every tile. Device step

entries.heading: Command, kernel, or micro-op
entries.text: Best for runtime, firmware, and hardware work. It exposes queue dependencies, addresses, cycles, engine state, counters, and fault snapshots. Map Source map Node to region to command identities Replay Deterministic run Inputs, artifact, state, seeds, clocks Capture Checkpoints Tensor, layout, quantization, memory view Compare Reference diff Abs/rel/ULP, saturation, first divergence Correlate Timeline Commands, DMA, engines, counters, faults Debugger pane Data model Engineering question Graph map Source node, fused region, target/fallback assignment, command IDs. Where did this operation go, and which boundary added conversion cost? Tensor diff Shape, dtype, layout, quantization parameters, reference/target values, error histogram. Where is the first numerical divergence, and does it match the declared tolerance? Memory map Buffer lifetime, offset, bank, producer/consumer, alias set, residency. Was data overwritten, misaligned, stale, or transferred unnecessarily? Timeline Host, driver, firmware, DMA, engine, power, and fault tracks with flows. Is latency caused by dispatch, dependencies, memory, compute, or recovery? Replay package Inputs, model/artifact hashes, component versions, device state, trace and logs. Can another engineer reproduce the same failure without the original machine? Git and CI/CD for NPU stacks

entries.heading: Gate contracts at the cheapest level that can disprove them
entries.text: Git fundamentals already exist in Git Practice . This section focuses on the compiler/runtime/model/hardware release system built on top of version control. Gate 1 Static Format, lint, schema, generated-file drift, ABI checks Gate 2 Host unit Passes, allocator, queue state machine, fault injection, sanitizers Gate 3 Model Differential vectors, bit parity, cycle bounds, trace schema Gate 4 RTL / device Co-simulation, hardware-in-loop, resets, concurrency, compatibility Gate 5 Qualification Model corpus, performance, power, thermal, endurance, release matrix Pipeline dimension Fast pull request lane Scheduled / release lane Toolchains Primary supported compiler and one sanitizer build. Supported host OS, compiler, architecture, and packaging matrix. Targets Functional model and one representative hardware revision. All supported firmware/hardware revisions and compatibility edges. Models Small operator set plus compact end-to-end smoke models. Versioned model zoo across shapes, precision modes, dynamic behavior, and fallbacks. Performance Microbenchmark guardrails with noise budget; fail only on clear regressions. Dedicated quiet devices, repeated distributions, thermal steady state, baseline approval. Artifacts Failed traces, diffs, logs, executable manifest, exact command line. Signed packages, SBOM/provenance, qualification report, dashboards, retained baselines. GitHub Actions distinguishes dependency caches from workflow artifacts: caches accelerate reproducible work, while artifacts retain outputs such as binaries, logs, traces, coverage, and reports. A failed NPU test should upload the replay package as an artifact, not hide it inside an ephemeral runner log. Portfolio build

entries.heading: Six artifacts that demonstrate the architecture
entries.text: 0 / 6 complete Versioned executable manifest Define sections, ABI fields, target features, hashes, debug map, and a strict validator. Static memory planner Allocate interval lifetimes with alignment and bank constraints; verify aliases and report peak use. Asynchronous runtime simulator Implement contexts, queues, buffers, events, dependency ordering, timeout, and device-loss tests. C++ hardware model ladder Correlate a bit-accurate kernel and a queued cycle model against shared golden vectors. Correlated trace and layer debugger Emit model/region/command IDs, device cycles, flows, counters, tensor checkpoints, and first-divergence reports. CI qualification lanes Run unit, differential, simulator, performance, compatibility, and artifact-retention jobs. Hardware implementation companion: continue with the Analog CIM board bring-up guide for a concrete PCIe BAR map, UMD/KMD split, Linux probe path, DMA and MSI-X sequence, firmware scheduler, analog program/calibration lifecycle, YOLO dataflow, recovery, and qualification plan. entries.heading: Accelerator Repository Blueprint
entries.text: Turn architecture and software interfaces into a product-ready repository, validation strategy, and commercialization workflow. TT-Metal repository study | snapshot 2026-07-11 Accelerator Repository Blueprint Build a repository that can grow from one simulated matrix operation into a maintained compiler, runtime, SDK, firmware, driver, model library, and hardware qualification system. TT-Metal supplies the concrete reference; this page extracts the boundaries and test discipline that also apply to an Analog CIM machine. Open the repository tree Build the minimal example Follow the test ladder Profile host and device Open the debug playbook Contracts first One source for ABI, command, target, and artifact schemas Host first Compiler and runtime behavior testable without scarce hardware Vertical slices Each milestone ends in an executable path and evidence Layered gates Fast PR feedback plus deeper hardware and nightly coverage Observed in TT-Metal

entries.heading: The repository is an engineering system, not a large source folder
entries.text: The current TT-Metal repository separates the Metalium programming layer, TT-NN, models, tests, documentation, tools, scripts, build infrastructure, and GitHub automation. The exact names and scale are Tenstorrent-specific; the separation of ownership is the useful pattern. Product code tt_metal/ Host API, hardware kernels, low-level runtime, device implementation, examples, tests, and architecture descriptors. Operator and Python layer ttnn/ C++ implementation, Python package, public API, examples, tutorials, and component tests. Workload evidence models/ Demos, reusable model utilities, reference paths, performance support, datasets, and model CI tiers. Cross-stack tests tests/ Metalium, TT-NN, end-to-end, sweeps, performance, nightly, stress, distributed, and shared test infrastructure. Debug and profiling tools/ Hardware debug, triage, tracing, profiling, power support, inspection, and test utilities. Automation scripts/ Build, test, API checks, profiling, CI helpers, code health, and generated-data maintenance. Build and configuration cmake/ Toolchains, dependencies, sanitizers, packaging, compiler checks, caching, and version construction. Project contract docs/ .github/ contributing/ Documentation, workflows, time budgets, ownership, pull-request rules, and engineering practices. The current test tree is purpose-oriented: tests/tt_metal/ covers low-level subsystems and microbenchmarks; tests/ttnn/ includes unit, integration, performance, profiling, statistical, stress, and nightly paths; tests/end_to_end_tests/ crosses stack boundaries; tests/sweep_framework/ explores parameter spaces; and tests/nightly/ groups deeper hardware configurations. This is the model for the proposed test ladder later on this page. Copy the architecture of responsibility, not the repository size. A new ACiM stack should begin with one contract path, one simulator backend, one runtime path, and one operator. Create a directory only when it has a clear owner, dependency direction, test lane, and generated artifact. TT-Metal pattern General lesson ACiM translation C++ core plus Python product layer Keep performance-sensitive and ABI-sensitive code below a usable high-level API. C++ compiler/runtime/HAL with Python bindings, model tools, calibration tools, and framework integration. Tests at root and inside components Local tests protect implementation details; root tests protect cross-component behavior. Place private compiler/runtime tests beside their components and complete system lanes under tests/ . GoogleTest and pytest Use each framework where its language, fixtures, and failure diagnostics are strongest. GoogleTest for C++ contracts and state machines; pytest for Python APIs, parametrized operators, models, and lab scheduling. Dedicated tools tree Debugging and profiling are products with stable inputs and outputs. Ship artifact inspection, IR dumps, command traces, calibration inspection, first-divergence analysis, triage bundles, and profilers. Fast and deep CI lanes A pull request cannot run every expensive accelerator test, so routing and post-commit coverage must be explicit. Use host-only PR gates, selected hardware smoke, merge integration, nightly sweeps/performance, and release qualification. Repository terminology

entries.heading: Terms used throughout the blueprint
entries.text: ABI: Application Binary Interface The binary-level contract for calling functions or exchanging structures across independently built components. HAL: Hardware Abstraction Layer An internal device-neutral interface implemented by simulator, fake-device, and real-hardware backends. SDK: Software Development Kit The supported APIs, libraries, tools, examples, documentation, packages, and diagnostics used by application developers. UMD / KMD User-Mode Driver and Kernel-Mode Driver. UMD integrates the runtime; KMD owns privileged OS resources such as DMA, interrupts, isolation and reset. CI: Continuous Integration Automated build, static analysis, test, packaging, and evidence collection triggered by code changes or schedules. CTest CMake's test runner and test registry. It can launch GoogleTest executables and label or group native test targets. Smoke test The shortest complete health path: discover, open, execute one known operation, compare, close, and leave the device usable. Sweep test A parameterized exploration across shapes, dtypes, layouts, precision, faults, calibration, or other supported dimensions. Soak test A long-running stress test intended to reveal leaks, state accumulation, thermal behavior, rare races, and recovery failures. Golden test A deterministic comparison against an approved IR, artifact, command sequence, tensor, or report. Updates require an explained semantic change. PVT: Process, Voltage, Temperature The manufacturing and operating corners used to characterize timing, power, numerical variation, and reliability. ADR: Architecture Decision Record A short document preserving the context, alternatives, chosen design, consequences, migration, tests, and owner of a durable decision. SKU: Stock Keeping Unit A specific product or board configuration that may differ in devices, memory, topology, clocks, power, firmware, or supported features. Sanitizer Compiler instrumentation such as AddressSanitizer or UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer that detects classes of memory and language errors at runtime. Tracy A real-time frame profiler used here for host C++ zones, frames, messages, plots, threads, locks, memory, and operating-system activity. Zone A named interval with a begin and end timestamp. Nested zones divide a host request or device command into attributable phases. Device cycle counter A monotonically increasing hardware timer read by firmware. Its clock domain and frequency must accompany the captured value. Clock domain Logic driven by one clock source. Host, controller, array sequencer, converter, DSP, and multiple devices may not share a timestamp origin or rate. Correlation ID A stable identifier carried through API call, queue command, firmware descriptor, device trace, interrupt, and result so records from different planes can be joined. Probe effect The latency, memory, bandwidth, scheduling, or power change caused by observation itself. Profiled and official uninstrumented measurements must be compared. Recommended repository

entries.heading: A smaller tree with production boundaries from the beginning
entries.text: The tree below is a proposed starting architecture for an accelerator stack named acim-stack . Rename it for the product, but keep the ownership and dependency rules. schemas/ generates C++, Python, and firmware readers. Never maintain three handwritten definitions of a command or artifact. Rule 2 Public API is narrow include/acim/ exposes supported interfaces. Private implementation headers remain below src/ . Rule 3 Hardware is a backend The runtime targets a HAL implemented by functional simulation, queued fake device, and hardware. Compiler tests do not require a board. Rule 4 Tests state their scope A developer can tell whether a test needs no device, one device, a topology, calibration data, or a qualification lab from its path and markers. Rule 5 Models are consumers Model demos may use the public SDK; they must not reach into compiler internals, physical addresses, or private driver APIs. Rule 6 Tools consume stable evidence Inspectors and profilers read versioned artifacts and traces. They do not scrape human log text as their primary interface. Rule 7 Configuration is validated data Target, test-matrix, model, and threshold files have schemas, units, version fields, examples, and validation tests. Rule 8 Generated output is reproducible Generated files record generator version and source hash; CI fails when committed output differs from regeneration. Dependency direction

entries.heading: The directory tree matters only when dependencies follow it
entries.text: Keep stable data contracts at the bottom, device-neutral behavior in the middle, and user-facing integrations at the top. Hardware implementations satisfy interfaces; they do not redefine them. Foundation Schemas and types Status codes, target, artifact, command, calibration, and trace contracts Mechanism Compiler and HAL Lowering, mapping, code generation, buffers, queues, events, and device interface Execution Runtime Compatibility, allocation, binding, submission, synchronization, recovery, telemetry Language C API and bindings Stable ABI plus C++ and Python convenience layers Integration Framework and SDK ONNX Runtime, PyTorch tools, CLI, packaging, examples Product proof Models and applications Real preprocessing, fallback, execution, postprocessing, accuracy, and performance Boundary May depend on Must not depend on Enforcement schemas/ Schema compiler and primitive types Runtime, framework, board, or model code Standalone generation target and compatibility tests src/compiler/ IR, target descriptors, operation/cost models, artifact writer Live device handles, kernel-driver calls, serial-specific state Link boundaries plus host-only compiler tests src/runtime/ Public contracts, HAL, artifact reader, telemetry Framework graph classes or compiler-private passes Runtime target links only approved libraries src/hal/ Device-neutral interfaces and backend-specific implementation Model semantics, graph partition policy, Python objects Backend conformance suite python/acim/ Public C ABI or supported bindings Private C++ symbols and raw MMIO Wheel test against installed headers and libraries models/ Installed SDK, public framework plugin, test utilities Source-tree implementation imports Run selected demos from a packaged installation Native build toolchain

entries.heading: Turn one ACiM source file into a repeatable binary and test result
entries.text: A build stack is a chain of different tools. CMake describes targets and generates a build graph; Ninja or Make executes that graph; GCC, Clang, or MSVC compiles C/C++; an archiver and linker create libraries and executables; CTest runs the native tests. Treating all of this as "the compiler" makes failures difficult to locate. 1. Select Preset and toolchain Host OS, compiler, build type, features, target/sysroot 2. Configure CMake Detect capabilities, resolve packages, create explicit targets 3. Generate Ninja build graph Commands, dependencies, generated files and output paths 4. Compile GCC / Clang / MSVC Preprocess, parse, optimize, generate objects and diagnostics 5. Link Archiver and linker Static/shared libraries, executables, symbols, ABI and runtime paths 6. Prove CTest and install Unit, smoke, labels, package layout and saved build manifest

entries.heading: Know which tool owns each failure
entries.text: Tool Responsibility Recommended ACiM use Typical failure or evidence CMake Meta-build system: declares targets, requirements, generated files, installation, tests and package discovery. One target per compiler/runtime/HAL boundary; checked-in presets; target-scoped options instead of global flags. Configure log, compiler ID/version, cache, target graph, package resolution, generated Ninja files. Ninja Executes the generated dependency graph with fast incremental and parallel builds. Default local and CI generator. Let CMake generate build.ninja ; do not hand-author it. Exact failed command, missing generated dependency, stale output, unexpected rebuild or parallel race. GNU Make Alternative build executor and the basis of Linux Kbuild. Accept as a CMake generator when needed; use the kernel's Make/Kbuild flow for the Linux KMD. Make target, dependency/rule expansion, kernel build output. GCC / G++ GNU C/C++ compiler driver, frontend, optimizer and code generator; invokes assembler and linker. Linux baseline for host compiler, runtime, simulator and SDK release builds with libstdc++ . Standards/warning diagnostics, generated objects, optimization report, GNU ABI and runtime dependencies. Clang / Clang++ LLVM C/C++ compiler driver with independent diagnostics and sanitizer integration. Second compiler in CI, developer diagnostics, AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and future LLVM/MLIR integration. Independent compile result, sanitizer trace, optimization remarks, LLVM IR when explicitly requested. MSVC / clang-cl Windows-native C/C++ toolchains using the Microsoft command-line and ABI conventions. Host-only Windows simulator/SDK confidence. Keep the production Linux PCIe/KMD lane separate. MSVC ABI, CRT selection, PDB debug symbols, DLL import/export and Windows packaging behavior. Assembler Turns compiler-generated assembly into architecture-specific object files. Normally driven by the compiler; direct use appears in firmware startup, interrupt stubs and ISA kernels. Object sections, relocation records, instruction encoding and target ISA mismatch. Archiver Packages object files into static libraries such as .a or .lib . Create narrow compiler, artifact, runtime and simulator libraries; inspect symbol ownership when links fail. Archive member list, duplicate/missing symbols and unexpected private implementation exposure. GNU ld / LLD / link.exe Resolves symbols and relocations into shared libraries and executables. Start with the compiler's default linker; add LLD only as a measured build-time optimization or target requirement. Link map, unresolved/duplicate symbol, section size, RPATH, SONAME, import library and ABI mismatch. CTest CMake's native test registry and runner with labels, fixtures, timeouts and presets. Common entry point for dependency-free unit tests, GoogleTest discovery, smoke tests and install checks. Test name, label, command, timeout, exit code, output and per-lane summary. GoogleTest C++ test framework with typed assertions, fixtures, parameterized tests and CMake discovery. Use for compiler passes, schemas, allocators, runtime state machines and backend contracts after the minimal offline tests work. Focused assertion, parameter, fixture lifecycle and --gtest_filter reproducer. clang-format / clang-tidy Mechanical formatting plus AST-based diagnostics and refactoring checks. Format automatically; run selected analyzer, bug-prone, performance and portability checks on owned targets. Formatting diff or source-located diagnostic. Do not apply project warnings to third-party code. Sanitizers Compiler instrumentation for memory errors, undefined behavior, races or uninitialized reads. Clang ASan+UBSan PR lane; separate TSan lane for queue/runtime concurrency; never use sanitizer timing as performance data. Symbolized stack, allocation/free history, undefined operation or race report. gcov / llvm-cov Compiler instrumentation and reporting for function, line, region and branch coverage. Measure owned host code after tests are stable; keep GCC and Clang coverage artifacts in separate lanes. Instrumented binary, raw/indexed profile, source report and uncovered branch list. Coverage percentage is not correctness. ccache / sccache Caches compiler outputs keyed by source, compiler and command inputs. Add after the uncached build is correct; report hit rate and include compiler/config hashes in CI cache keys. Hit/miss statistics, cache-key mismatch and stale/non-reproducible input diagnosis. Package/dependency tools find_package , package managers, dependency providers, pkg-config and optional FetchContent . Prefer installed/pinned packages for release builds. Keep network fetching opt-in and hash-pinned. Resolved package version, include/library path, dependency lock and provenance manifest. Schema/code generators Tools such as flatc , protoc or TableGen turn one contract source into language-specific code. Generate C++, Python and firmware readers into the build tree; verify committed generated output only when distribution requires it. Generator version, schema hash, generated diff, compatibility test and dependency edge in Ninja. Python wheel and bindings pyproject.toml build backend plus pybind11/nanobind or a C ABI wrapper creates an installable Python extension. Add after the C++ install tree is stable; build wheels against the supported Python/OS/architecture matrix. Wheel contents, extension ABI, imported shared-library paths, Python tag and installed-package smoke test. Doxygen / Sphinx Generates C/C++ API documentation and narrative SDK documentation as explicit build targets. Run warnings-as-errors for public API comments, examples and cross-links without putting docs in the default native compile target. Generated HTML, missing-symbol/comment warnings, broken links and versioned API reference. Cross compiler and sysroot Builds host runtime or firmware for a target ISA/OS using target headers, libraries and ABI. CMake toolchain file for AArch64 host runtim

entries.heading: Recommended choices for the first repository
entries.text: Decision Start with Add when needed Avoid in the first loop Language ISO C++20 through target_compile_features ; C ABI only at the supported SDK boundary C17 for firmware/KMD boundaries and target-specific assembly where the ABI requires it Compiler-specific language extensions in public headers Linux compiler GCC baseline plus Clang as an independent CI compiler Versioned release matrix and target cross-compilers Supporting many old compilers before a product/toolchain requirement exists Windows compiler MSVC for host simulator and SDK portability clang-cl if Windows LLVM diagnostics or compatibility is valuable Claiming Windows device support from a host-only simulator build Generator CMake plus Ninja Unix Makefiles or IDE generators as secondary paths Handwritten per-platform build scripts that duplicate the target graph Linker Compiler default LLD after measuring link time, memory or cross-target requirements Mixing C++ standard libraries or CRT modes inside one ABI without an explicit boundary Dependencies No dependency for the first smoke/unit path; find_package for installed packages Pinned provider/package manager; hash-pinned FetchContent for developer convenience Downloading LLVM, MLIR or GoogleTest on every default configure LLVM / MLIR Disabled in the minimal build Prebuilt, version-pinned package behind ACIM_ENABLE_MLIR Making a full LLVM source build a prerequisite for the first MVM smoke test Device firmware Host model of descriptors and state machines Separate cross-toolchain, linker script, startup and hardware/RTL tests after ISA/ABI freeze Linking host C++ runtime libraries into freestanding firmware by accident Linux driver Fake HAL and userspace tests Kbuild module, kernel-version matrix and PCIe lab after UAPI/resource ownership is defined Hiding driver commands inside general CMake targets or unit tests
