entries.heading: Deep Learning
entries.text: Questions for neural network fundamentals, CNNs, transformers, training, and deployment.

entries.heading: Foundations
entries.text: Deep Learning 5 questions

entries.heading: What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter?
entries.text: A parameter is learned from data, such as a weight or bias. A hyperparameter is chosen outside training, such as learning rate, batch size, optimizer, model depth, dropout probability, or weight decay.

entries.heading: Why do neural networks need nonlinear activation functions?
entries.text: Without nonlinear activations, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear transformation. Nonlinearities such as ReLU let the model represent complex decision boundaries and hierarchical features.

entries.heading: What does backpropagation compute?
entries.text: Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss back through the computation graph to compute gradients for trainable parameters. Optimizers then use those gradients to update parameters.

entries.heading: What is the role of a loss function?
entries.text: The loss converts prediction quality into a scalar training objective. For example, cross entropy is common for classification and mean squared error is common for regression.

entries.heading: Why do we separate training, validation, and test sets?
entries.text: Training data fits parameters, validation data guides model selection and hyperparameters, and test data estimates final generalization. Mixing them causes optimistic results and possible data leakage.

entries.heading: Optimization and Regularization
entries.text: Deep Learning 5 questions

entries.heading: Why can a learning rate be too high or too low?
entries.text: Too high can make optimization diverge or bounce around minima. Too low can make training painfully slow or get stuck before reaching a useful solution.

entries.heading: What is the difference between SGD, momentum, and Adam?
entries.text: SGD follows the current gradient. Momentum smooths updates using velocity. Adam adapts step sizes using running estimates of first and second moments, often making early training easier.

entries.heading: What does weight decay do?
entries.text: Weight decay penalizes large weights, usually by adding an L2-style term or decoupled decay in the optimizer. It can reduce overfitting and improve generalization.

entries.heading: Why use dropout?
entries.text: Dropout randomly disables activations during training so the network cannot depend too heavily on exact co-adapted paths. It is a regularizer, and it is disabled or converted to deterministic scaling during evaluation.

entries.heading: What is gradient clipping useful for?
entries.text: Gradient clipping limits very large gradients, which is especially useful in recurrent models, transformers, and unstable training runs where exploding gradients can destroy updates.

entries.heading: CNN and Computer Vision
entries.text: Deep Learning 5 questions

entries.heading: Why are convolutions useful for images?
entries.text: Convolutions exploit local spatial structure and weight sharing. The same filter is applied across positions, reducing parameters and learning translation-friendly features.

entries.heading: What do stride and padding control in convolution?
entries.text: Stride controls how far the filter moves between positions. Padding controls border handling and output size. Together they affect spatial resolution, compute, and receptive field placement.

entries.heading: Why does a 1x1 convolution matter?
entries.text: A 1x1 convolution mixes channels at each spatial position. It can reduce or expand channel count, implement projections, and make bottleneck residual blocks efficient.

entries.heading: What is batch normalization doing at a high level?
entries.text: Batch normalization normalizes intermediate activations using batch statistics during training and running statistics during inference, often stabilizing and accelerating deep network training.

entries.heading: Why are residual connections important?
entries.text: Residual connections give gradients and information shorter paths through deep networks. They make very deep models easier to optimize by learning corrections around an identity-like path.

entries.heading: Transformers and LLMs
entries.text: Deep Learning 5 questions

entries.heading: What problem does self-attention solve?
entries.text: Self-attention lets each token combine information from other tokens in the sequence using learned query, key, and value projections. It handles long-range dependencies more directly than purely local operations.

entries.heading: What are Q, K, and V in attention?
entries.text: Queries ask what a token is looking for, keys describe what each token offers, and values are the information mixed into the output. Scores come from query-key similarity and weight the values.

entries.heading: Why is attention scaled by sqrt(d)?
entries.text: Scaling keeps dot-product logits from growing too large as the key/query dimension increases. That helps softmax avoid saturation and improves gradient behavior.

entries.heading: What is the KV cache in autoregressive decoding?
entries.text: The KV cache stores past key and value tensors so each new token does not recompute attention projections for all previous tokens. It saves compute but consumes memory proportional to sequence length and layers.

entries.heading: Why are tokenizers important in LLM systems?
entries.text: Tokenizers map text to model IDs and back. They affect vocabulary coverage, sequence length, latency, multilingual behavior, and how prompts or special tokens are represented.

entries.heading: Training Debugging
entries.text: Deep Learning 5 questions

entries.heading: What is a good first check when training loss does not decrease?
entries.text: Overfit a tiny batch. If the model cannot drive loss very low on a few examples, suspect bugs in labels, loss, optimizer, gradients, data preprocessing, or model wiring.

entries.heading: How do you detect data leakage?
entries.text: Look for features derived from labels, train/test duplicates, future information in time series, preprocessing fitted on all data, or validation performance that is unrealistically high.

entries.heading: Why can validation loss rise while training loss falls?
entries.text: The model is overfitting: it keeps improving on training examples while generalization worsens. Regularization, more data, augmentation, early stopping, or a smaller model may help.

entries.heading: What is mixed precision training?
entries.text: Mixed precision uses lower precision such as FP16/BF16 for many tensor operations while preserving stability with techniques such as master weights, loss scaling, or higher-precision accumulations.

entries.heading: Why should evaluation use model.eval() in PyTorch?
entries.text: Evaluation mode changes layers such as dropout and batch normalization to inference behavior. Without it, validation metrics can be noisy or wrong.

entries.heading: Deployment and Performance
entries.text: Deep Learning 5 questions

entries.heading: What is quantization?
entries.text: Quantization represents weights or activations with lower precision, commonly INT8, to reduce memory and accelerate inference. It needs calibration, quantization-aware training, or careful error analysis.

entries.heading: What is operator fusion?
entries.text: Fusion combines adjacent operations, such as convolution plus bias plus activation, to reduce memory traffic and kernel launch overhead. It often matters as much as raw arithmetic throughput.

entries.heading: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
entries.text: Latency is time for one request. Throughput is requests or tokens per second over a workload. Batching often improves throughput but can increase per-request latency.

entries.heading: Why export a model to ONNX?
entries.text: ONNX gives a portable graph representation that many runtimes and compilers can consume. Export requires checking operator support, dynamic shapes, numerical parity, and postprocessing assumptions.

entries.heading: What is a good deployment validation loop?
entries.text: Compare framework output, exported model output, and runtime/compiler output on representative inputs. Track accuracy, latency, memory, unsupported ops, dtype changes, and preprocessing parity.

entries.heading: Operating Systems
entries.text: Questions for Linux-style process, memory, synchronization, filesystem, and debugging interviews.

entries.heading: Processes and Threads
entries.text: Operating Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What does fork() create?
entries.text: fork() creates a child process by duplicating the calling process. Parent and child run in separate address spaces, and Linux commonly uses copy-on-write pages to avoid copying all memory immediately.

entries.heading: What is the difference between fork() and exec()?
entries.text: fork() creates a new process. exec() replaces the current process image with a new program. Shells commonly fork, then the child execs the requested command.

entries.heading: How are processes and threads different?
entries.text: Processes have separate address spaces. Threads in the same process share address space and resources such as file descriptors, but each thread has its own stack and execution context.

entries.heading: What is a context switch?
entries.text: A context switch saves the state of one running task and restores another. It enables multitasking but has overhead from scheduler work, register state, cache/TLB effects, and possible kernel transitions.

entries.heading: What is a zombie process?
entries.text: A zombie is a terminated child whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent with wait-like calls. It no longer runs but still has a process table entry.

entries.heading: Scheduling and CPU
entries.text: Operating Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What does the scheduler decide?
entries.text: The scheduler decides which runnable task gets CPU time, balancing responsiveness, fairness, priorities, affinity, deadlines, and system policy.

entries.heading: What is preemption?
entries.text: Preemption means the OS can interrupt a running task and switch to another runnable task, usually due to timer interrupts, priority changes, or wakeups.

entries.heading: What is starvation?
entries.text: Starvation happens when a runnable task waits indefinitely or too long because other tasks keep receiving resources. Aging, fair scheduling, and priority rules can reduce it.

entries.heading: What is priority inversion?
entries.text: Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task while medium-priority work prevents the low-priority task from running. Priority inheritance is a common fix.

entries.heading: Why does CPU affinity matter?
entries.text: Affinity can improve cache locality and reduce migration overhead. But overly strict affinity can hurt load balancing if some CPUs are overloaded.

entries.heading: Synchronization
entries.text: Operating Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What is a race condition?
entries.text: A race condition happens when correctness depends on timing between concurrent operations. Shared mutable data needs synchronization or ownership discipline.

entries.heading: When would you use a mutex?
entries.text: Use a mutex to protect a critical section so only one thread at a time accesses shared state. Keep the protected region small and avoid blocking calls while holding it when possible.

entries.heading: How is a semaphore different from a mutex?
entries.text: A mutex protects ownership of a resource and is released by its owner. A semaphore is a counter used to signal resource availability or events; it does not necessarily imply ownership.

entries.heading: Why do condition variables need a predicate loop?
entries.text: Threads can wake spuriously or after another thread consumes the condition. The standard pattern is lock, while predicate is false wait, then proceed.

entries.heading: What are common deadlock conditions?
entries.text: Deadlock usually requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Avoid it with lock ordering, timeouts, try-locks, or reducing shared locks.

entries.heading: Virtual Memory
entries.text: Operating Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What is virtual memory?
entries.text: Virtual memory gives each process an address space abstraction. The OS and MMU map virtual pages to physical frames and enforce protection and sharing.

entries.heading: What is a page fault?
entries.text: A page fault occurs when a virtual address cannot be translated with current permissions or mappings. It may load a page, allocate memory, grow a stack, or terminate the process if invalid.

entries.heading: What is copy-on-write?
entries.text: Copy-on-write lets parent and child initially share physical pages after fork. A real copy is made only when one process writes to a shared page.

entries.heading: What does the TLB cache?
entries.text: The translation lookaside buffer caches virtual-to-physical page translations. TLB misses require page-table walks and can be expensive.

entries.heading: Why can mmap be useful?
entries.text: mmap maps files or anonymous memory into a process address space. It can support file-backed I/O, shared memory, lazy loading, and zero-copy-style workflows.

entries.heading: Filesystems and I/O
entries.text: Operating Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What is the difference between a file descriptor and an open file description?
entries.text: A file descriptor is a per-process handle. Multiple descriptors can refer to the same open file description, sharing offset and status flags.

entries.heading: Why can buffered I/O and direct I/O behave differently?
entries.text: Buffered I/O goes through the page cache and can merge or defer writes. Direct I/O tries to bypass page cache, often requiring alignment and careful application buffering.

entries.heading: What is epoll used for?
entries.text: epoll lets a program wait efficiently for readiness events on many file descriptors, useful for high-concurrency network servers.

entries.heading: What is fsync for?
entries.text: fsync asks the OS to flush file data and metadata needed for persistence to stable storage. It is important for durability but can be expensive.

entries.heading: What does zero-copy mean in I/O discussions?
entries.text: Zero-copy means avoiding unnecessary copies between kernel and user buffers or between intermediate buffers. The exact mechanism depends on APIs such as mmap, sendfile, splice, or DMA paths.

entries.heading: Debugging and Real-Time
entries.text: Operating Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: When would you use strace?
entries.text: Use strace to observe system calls, arguments, errors, signals, and blocking behavior. It is very useful for diagnosing file, process, and permission problems.

entries.heading: When would you use perf?
entries.text: Use perf to sample CPU hotspots, call stacks, cache misses, context switches, and other performance counters. It helps distinguish compute, kernel, and scheduling costs.

entries.heading: What is a real-time scheduling concern?
entries.text: Real-time systems care about bounded latency and predictability, not just average throughput. Paging, unbounded locks, interrupt storms, and priority inversion are common hazards.

entries.heading: Why might mlock be used in real-time programs?
entries.text: mlock can keep memory resident to avoid page faults during time-critical execution. It must be used carefully because locked memory reduces flexibility for the rest of the system.

entries.heading: How do you debug a hung multithreaded process?
entries.text: Collect stack traces for all threads, inspect locks and futex waits, check CPU usage, use strace or gdb, and look for deadlocks, missed condition signals, or blocking I/O.

entries.heading: Embedded Systems
entries.text: Questions for C/C++, interrupts, RTOS, hardware interfaces, linker scripts, and firmware debugging.

entries.heading: C/C++ and Memory
entries.text: Embedded Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What does volatile mean in embedded C?
entries.text: volatile tells the compiler that a value can change outside normal program flow, such as a memory-mapped register or ISR-updated flag. It prevents certain optimizations but is not a lock or memory barrier by itself.

entries.heading: Why is alignment important?
entries.text: Many MCUs and buses require or strongly prefer aligned accesses. Misalignment can cause faults, extra cycles, or multiple bus transactions.

entries.heading: What is the difference between stack and heap in firmware?
entries.text: The stack is automatic storage for calls and locals, usually fixed and fast. The heap supports dynamic allocation but can fragment and is often avoided or tightly controlled in embedded systems.

entries.heading: Why avoid malloc in hard real-time code?
entries.text: Dynamic allocation can have unpredictable latency, fragmentation, failure modes, and ownership complexity. Static allocation or pools are often preferred.

entries.heading: What is a memory-mapped register?
entries.text: A peripheral register exposed at a specific memory address. Firmware reads and writes that address to control hardware such as GPIO, UART, timers, or DMA.

entries.heading: Interrupts and Peripherals
entries.text: Embedded Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What should an ISR generally do?
entries.text: An ISR should handle the urgent hardware event, clear or acknowledge the interrupt, capture minimal data, and defer heavier work to a task, queue, or bottom-half mechanism.

entries.heading: Why keep ISRs short?
entries.text: Long ISRs increase interrupt latency, block lower-priority work, and can make real-time behavior unpredictable. They can also complicate locking and shared-state handling.

entries.heading: What is interrupt priority?
entries.text: Interrupt priority determines which exception can preempt another. On Cortex-M systems, priority configuration and grouping affect nesting and latency.

entries.heading: What is debouncing?
entries.text: Debouncing filters mechanical switch bounce so one physical press is not interpreted as many transitions. It can be done with hardware, timers, or state machines.

entries.heading: What is DMA useful for?
entries.text: DMA moves data between peripherals and memory without CPU copying each byte. It reduces CPU load but requires cache coherency, buffer ownership, and completion/error handling.

entries.heading: RTOS Concepts
entries.text: Embedded Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What is a task in an RTOS?
entries.text: A task is an independently scheduled thread of execution with its own stack and priority. Tasks communicate through queues, semaphores, notifications, or shared protected data.

entries.heading: What is a FreeRTOS queue good for?
entries.text: A queue transfers fixed-size items between tasks or from ISR-safe APIs to tasks. It provides synchronization and data movement with optional blocking timeouts.

entries.heading: When use a mutex instead of a binary semaphore?
entries.text: Use a mutex for mutual exclusion around a shared resource, especially when priority inheritance is needed. Use a binary semaphore more often for signaling events.

entries.heading: What is priority inversion in RTOS code?
entries.text: A high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task while medium-priority tasks run. Mutex priority inheritance can reduce the inversion.

entries.heading: What is a tickless idle mode?
entries.text: Tickless idle suppresses periodic scheduler ticks during idle periods to save power, programming a timer to wake the system at the next deadline or interrupt.

entries.heading: Boot and Linker
entries.text: Embedded Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What happens during embedded startup code?
entries.text: Startup code sets the stack pointer, initializes data from flash to RAM, zeros BSS, configures low-level runtime state, then calls main or the RTOS entry path.

entries.heading: What does a linker script define?
entries.text: A linker script maps code and data sections into target memory regions such as flash, SRAM, tightly coupled memory, bootloader areas, or special peripheral regions.

entries.heading: What are .text, .data, and .bss?
entries.text: .text holds code and constants, .data holds initialized writable data copied to RAM at startup, and .bss holds zero-initialized writable data cleared at startup.

entries.heading: Why inspect a map file?
entries.text: A linker map shows where symbols and sections landed, how much memory they use, and whether unexpected objects or libraries are inflating firmware size.

entries.heading: What is a vector table?
entries.text: A vector table contains initial stack pointer and exception/interrupt handler addresses. On Cortex-M it is central to reset and interrupt dispatch.

entries.heading: Interfaces and Timing
entries.text: Embedded Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: How do UART, SPI, and I2C differ?
entries.text: UART is asynchronous point-to-point serial. SPI is synchronous and fast with separate clock and chip-select lines. I2C is synchronous two-wire shared bus with addressing and pull-ups.

entries.heading: What is a watchdog timer?
entries.text: A watchdog resets or interrupts the system if firmware fails to service it in time. It helps recover from hangs but should be paired with root-cause logging if possible.

entries.heading: What is jitter?
entries.text: Jitter is variation in timing, such as task wakeup or control-loop period variation. In control systems, too much jitter can reduce stability and accuracy.

entries.heading: Why use fixed-point arithmetic?
entries.text: Fixed-point can be faster, smaller, or more deterministic on hardware without floating-point support. It requires careful scale, overflow, rounding, and saturation design.

entries.heading: What is cache coherency in DMA?
entries.text: If CPU caches and DMA buffers are not coherent, the CPU may read stale data or DMA may see old data. Firmware may need cache clean/invalidate operations or uncached buffers.

entries.heading: Debug and Safety
entries.text: Embedded Systems 5 questions

entries.heading: What is JTAG or SWD used for?
entries.text: JTAG/SWD provides low-level debug access: halt, step, inspect registers/memory, program flash, and sometimes trace execution.

entries.heading: How do you debug a hard fault?
entries.text: Capture fault status registers, stacked PC/LR/xPSR, stack pointer, and memory access status. Then map the PC to symbols and inspect the failing instruction and call path.

entries.heading: What is brownout detection?
entries.text: Brownout detection resets or protects the MCU when supply voltage drops below a safe threshold, preventing undefined behavior from low voltage.

entries.heading: Why design firmware state machines?
entries.text: State machines make event-driven behavior explicit, testable, and less dependent on fragile delays. They are useful for protocols, peripherals, UI, and control flows.

entries.heading: What makes firmware update design hard?
entries.text: Updates must handle power loss, corrupted images, version compatibility, rollback, authentication, storage limits, and safe bootloader handoff.

entries.heading: AiCM, AIMC, AiMC, and analog CIM
entries.text: The research literature most often says analog in-memory computing (AIMC or AiMC) . Analog compute-in-memory (analog CIM or ACIM) expresses the same central idea. This study treats AiCM as the user's name for that family. It is different from digital CIM, which performs exact bit operations inside or beside a memory array. The physical primitive

entries.text: The ideal equation is compact. Every production challenge enters through the assumptions hidden underneath it. entries.text: Real I-V curves, source resistance, wire drop, coupling, and sneak paths make a large array input dependent. Ideal assumption

entries.text: Programming spread, defects, relaxation, drift, temperature, and aging change the effective conductance. Ideal assumption

entries.heading: Readout preserves information
entries.text: ADC range, offset, noise, resolution, and saturation place a ceiling on useful end-to-end precision. From tensor operation to physical math

entries.heading: A framework MatMul becomes repeated analog matrix-vector operations
entries.text: Software usually presents a matrix-matrix operation. A conductance array naturally evaluates one input vector against a resident weight matrix. Batch rows, oversized dimensions, signs, and additional bits are handled through repeated firings, parallel arrays, and digital reconstruction. GEMM : matrix by matrix MVM : one vector by resident weights MAC : one product added to a sum Row driver : presents an activation to array rows Column readout : senses a dot-product result Partial sum : one contribution to a larger output Sequencer : hardware that times drivers, sampling, and conversion

entries.heading: Short answer: where does the MatMul happen?
entries.text: For C[B,N] = A[B,K] x W[K,N] , the compiler places blocks of W into conductance arrays. For each batch row A[b,:] , input circuitry drives a vector onto array rows. Each memory cell performs the physical product V i G ij ; each column wire and sensing circuit accumulates those products; the ADC creates digital partial results; and nearby digital logic subtracts signed paths, combines bit planes and array partitions, applies scale and bias, and stores or routes C[b,:] . The RISC-V controller schedules this work; it does not execute the bulk analog MACs. Input A[B,K] B activation vectors, each with K elements Resident weights W[K,N] K physical rows by N logical outputs before tiling Array primitive a b [K] x W[K,N] One logical MVM per batch row, possibly split across arrays and bit phases Result C[B,N] Stack or stream the reconstructed N -element output vectors Layout convention: these diagrams use the mathematical form A[B,K] x W[K,N] . A framework may store a linear-layer weight as W[N,K] and request an implicit transpose. The importer and compiler must normalize that storage convention before physical mapping. Deployment or model change Weight path is rare and stateful Quantized weights → Physical mapping → Program + verify → Resident conductance handle Programming may require write pulses, verify reads, remapping, and calibration. It is not repeated for every inference. Every inference or token Activation path is streamed Input tensor → DMA / NoC → Local SRAM → Array + ADC → Digital result Activations, partial sums, and outputs move. Correct mapping tries to keep the much larger weight population stationary. No instruction is issued for each individual multiply. Accumulate Column wire and sensing circuit Currents or charge contributions combine by circuit behavior before conversion. Quantize ADC or comparator The analog result becomes a bounded digital code and may require multiple conversion cycles. Reconstruct SIMD, DSP, or fixed digital logic Signed paths, bit planes, partitions, scale, bias, and activation become the final tensor value. Signed weights W ∝ G + - G - Many arrays cannot represent negative conductance. Positive and negative lines or an offset representation are measured separately and combined digitally. Multi-bit activation x = Σ p 2 p x (p) A full DAC may present a multi-level signal, or several bit/pulse phases may be fired and shifted into alignment afterward. Multi-cell or sliced weight W = Σ s 2 s W (s) Several conductances or arrays can encode one logical weight; their ADC codes require weighted digital accumulation. Oversized K dimension C n = Σ k P k,n Each K shard produces a partial output vector. A digital accumulator combines those vectors before the layer is complete. Mythic evidence boundary: the public M1076 brief documents the ACE, RISC-V nano-processor, SIMD processor, SRAM, and NoC router, while the Hot Chips presentation documents flash-resistor MVM, digital input approximation, and ADC readout. Public material does not specify the internal ACE command registers, exact sequencer, firmware ABI, per-cycle schedule, or which digital block owns every reconstruction step. entries.heading: Three control timescales turn one graph operation into array pulses
entries.text: Software chooses what should run. Firmware coordinates when resources are ready. Dedicated hardware produces the precise electrical timing. Compile time Graph compiler Chooses array tiles, signed/bit representation, K/N partitions, buffer addresses, routes, digital fallback, scales, and command templates. Command time Runtime and tile controller Validate the executable and device state, bind tensor addresses, wait for dependencies, configure resources, start work, and report completion or faults. Cycle time ACE-local hardware sequencer Times row drive, settling, sample/integrate, ADC phases, register capture, and backpressure. Software should not toggle every switch directly. Sequence for one already-programmed weight tile Weight programming and calibration happen before this steady-state path. Performs math? What must be explicit in software Graph compiler Convert graph semantics into array placement, schedule, buffers, routes, and a device artifact. No runtime transfer Constant folding and reference analysis only Shapes, precision, tiling, partition reductions, capability and fallback decisions. Host runtime / driver Discover the device, load artifacts, bind buffers, enqueue work, synchronize, handle faults and reset. Requests DMA; may copy at external boundaries CPU fallback and preprocessing when assigned Buffer lifetime, queues, events, timeout, ABI and device-state compatibility. Tile RISC-V / controller Sequence coarse tile operations, dependencies, descriptors, local resource setup, and completion. Commands movers; may perform scalar loads/stores Small scalar/control work, not the bulk MVM Command format, synchronization, firmware ownership, counters, fault and recovery behavior. DMA / NoC router Transfer activations, partial sums, commands, and outputs between host, memory, and tiles. Yes No neural-network arithmetic Address spaces, alignment, routes, bandwidth, multicast, ordering, barriers, and backpressure. Local SRAM / registers Hold activation blocks, output slots, descriptors, temporary partial sums, and digital state. Storage endpoint No Bank ownership, capacity, lifetime, double buffering, layout, and producer/consumer credits. ACE-local sequencer Generate deterministic row-drive, settling, sensing, conversion, and capture timing. Feeds local registers and readout Controls the circuits that perform math Precision modes, phase counts, resource hazards, timeout, saturation, retry and telemetry contract. Conductance array Store weights and evaluate many cell products and column sums in parallel. Weights remain in place Bulk analog multiply and accumulate Array dimensions, conductance encoding, signed mapping, defects, operating range and nonideality model. ADC / readout Sense, integrate or compare column results and produce bounded digital codes. Creates the analog-to-digital boundary Quantization and sometimes threshold/nonlinearity Sharing, range, resolution, latency, energy, calibration, saturation and output format. Reads/writes local buffers Digital accumulation and epilogue math ISA or kernel API, accumulator width, rounding, saturation, fusion, and fallback cost. Design rule: the control processor should issue compact work descriptors and handle exceptional control. A dedicated sequencer should own repetitive cycle-level analog timing. If firmware must micromanage every input phase, ADC lane, and transfer, controller utilization and NoC traffic can erase the array's theoretical advantage. TT-Metal-style ownership

entries.heading: Name the controller and the working engine for every data transformation
entries.text: TT-Metal is easy to reason about because its architecture names both sides of each action: a baby RISC-V dispatches work, while a NoC, unpacker, FPU/SFPU, or packer performs it. An implementable ACiM architecture needs the same precision instead of grouping everything under "the analog tile."

entries.heading: Controller versus working engine
entries.text: Tenstorrent documents five baby RISC-V roles per Tensix: Data Movement 0, Data Movement 1, Unpack, Math, and Pack. These processors mainly dispatch and synchronize dedicated peripherals. Likewise, an ACiM tile should distinguish the firmware or state machine that issues an action from the DMA, formatter, row driver, memory array, ADC, or SIMD engine that actually transforms the data. entries.heading: Array dimensions determine which results concatenate and which must be added
entries.text: The compiler must distinguish four independent decompositions. Confusing an N shard with a K shard produces the wrong graph even when every local MVM is correct. Split N: output columns Concatenate Each array stores a different group of output columns and receives the same activation slice. Outputs represent distinct channels and are joined side by side. Split K: reduction rows Add partial vectors Each array stores a different K range for the same output channels. Its result is incomplete until a digital accumulator adds every K contribution. Split B: batch or tokens Repeat or replicate Reuse one resident weight mapping over time, or duplicate weights onto additional arrays to process independent vectors concurrently. Split precision Shift, scale, and add Spatial weight slices or temporal input phases produce weighted fragments. Digital reconstruction aligns each fragment before summation. Example: A[2,3072] x W[3072,4096] Hypothetical logical array capacity: 1024 rows by 1024 columns W blocks N0 N1 N2 N3 K0 W00 W01 W02 W03 K1 W10 W11 W12 W13 K2 W20 W21 W22 W23 1 Tile the weight matrix ceil(3072/1024) x ceil(4096/1024) = 3 x 4 = 12 logical weight blocks, before sign and bit-slice expansion. 2 Slice and broadcast one input row Split A[b,:] into K0, K1, and K2. Broadcast each slice to the four arrays in its K row. 3 Run twelve local MVMs With enough independent hardware they can run in parallel; otherwise schedule waves under ADC, NoC, SRAM, power, and thermal constraints. 4 Reduce along K For each N group, add P0n + P1n + P2n into one 1024-element output block. 5 Concatenate along N Join the four reduced blocks to form one 4096-element row of C . 6 Handle B=2 Repeat for the second row or use a replicated weight mapping. Then stack both result rows into C[2,4096] . Input slices x[K0], x[K1], x[K2] Per-inference data 12 resident blocks W[k,n] Array-local MVMs K reductions y[n] = Σ k P[k,n] Four digital partial-sum accumulators N concatenate y = [y0 | y1 | y2 | y3] One 4096-element output vector Convolution

entries.heading: Filters become matrix columns
entries.text: Flatten each receptive-field patch across kernel height, kernel width, and input channels into a K-vector. Map output-channel filters to N columns. Stream patches as repeated MVM inputs, then reshape output vectors back to spatial feature maps. Transformer

entries.heading: Linear projections dominate the analog-friendly part
entries.text: Q, K, V, output, and MLP projections are dense MatMuls and can use the same decomposition. Attention score MatMul, softmax, normalization, dynamic KV-cache access, and control generally require the digital companion or another engine. Mythic's mapping patent describes partitioning coefficients across multiple arrays, applying inputs, combining outputs, positive/negative paths, multi-row inputs, and serial multi-step input handling. NeuRRAM independently demonstrates the same system need: layers larger than an array are segmented across cores, with intermediate buffers and partial-sum accumulation outside the array in the reported prototype. Mythic mapping patent | NeuRRAM measured-silicon paper Communication limits and asynchronous execution

entries.heading: More array tiles can reduce performance after the NoC saturates
entries.text: Resident weights remove repeated weight fetches, but activations, ADC codes, partial sums, outputs, commands, and synchronization still move. The compiler must therefore treat NoC links, router ports, SRAM banks, and consumers as bounded resources rather than assuming that every mapped array can fire simultaneously. NoC : packet fabric connecting on-chip blocks DMA : transfer engine that moves blocks without CPU copies VC : logical queue sharing a physical NoC link Backpressure : a full downstream resource makes upstream senders wait Credit : permission proving that destination capacity is available Barrier / event : ordering or completion condition between asynchronous operations

entries.heading: Short answer: async hides latency; it does not create bandwidth
entries.text: Let R offered be activation fan-out, partial-sum, output, command, and event traffic injected per second. When it approaches the effective rate of the busiest link, router output, SRAM port, or consumer, queues grow. Once buffers fill, backpressure stalls DMA and tile controllers. Double buffering can absorb a temporary mismatch, but a sustained R offered ≥ R service remains a bandwidth problem. Split M: independent rows or tokens Usually the least cross-core communication Each shard computes different output rows. This is attractive when batch or token parallelism exists, but autoregressive LLM decode often has only one current token per sequence. Split N: output columns Activation fan-out Every N shard needs the same K activation slice. Multicast reduces repeated source injection, although replicated traffic still consumes branch links and receiver bandwidth. Split K: reduction rows Partial-sum traffic Every K shard emits an incomplete result for the same output channels. Those vectors must meet at local accumulators, a reduction tree, or a shared digital engine. Split precision More phases and fragments Input bits, signed paths, or weight slices can generate several ADC result fragments. Reconstruct them near the array or pay extra NoC traffic and synchronization. Traffic created by a P K x P N weight mapping N partitioning fans one activation slice outward; K partitioning brings partial results back together. Source SRAM x[K0], x[K1], x[K2] One input vector → Multicast each K slice across N Arrays N0 N1 N2 N3 K0 W00 W01 W02 W03 K1 W10 W11 W12 W13 K2 W20 W21 W22 W23 → Reduce partials along K Digital reduction y[n] = P0n + P1n + P2n Four final N blocks A useful first-order model is traffic = activation fan-out + K-partial reductions + final outputs + protocol overhead . Small tiles increase headers, descriptors, events, and barriers per useful byte; poor placement adds long shared routes and hotspots. How congestion becomes an array stall A correct bounded design normally slows producers instead of dropping tensor data. 1 Many producers issue traffic DMA reads, multicast, partial sums, outputs, commands 2 A shared resource saturates NoC link, router output, destination SRAM port, ADC or reducer 3 Queues and circular buffers fill Outstanding requests can no longer retire at the issue rate 4 Backpressure moves upstream Writers lose credits; DMA and dispatch wait 5 The compute pipeline bubbles Array is input-starved or output-blocked; latency and energy rise Safe overlap

entries.heading: Bound every asynchronous pipeline with ownership, completion, and credits
entries.text: Desired steady-state overlap Different tiles occupy independent engines at the same time. Engine t0 t1 t2 t3 Input DMA Tile 0 Tile 1 Tile 2 Tile 3 MVM + ADC Tile 0 Tile 1 Tile 2 SIMD / reduce Tile 0 Tile 1 Output DMA Tile 0 T tile ≥ max(T input , T MVM+ADC , T digital , T output ) only when those stages use sufficiently independent resources. Shared NoC links couple input and output time. One bounded producer-consumer transaction Publish validity only after payload completion. 1 Reserve destination slot Consumer credit proves SRAM capacity exists. 2 Issue async DMA / NoC transfer Keep the source and destination buffers alive. 3 Wait or record completion A transfer barrier orders the payload before its ready event. 4 Publish tile-ready The array sequencer may now consume the slot. 5 Complete MVM, ADC, and digital work Record consumer-done after the last read or write. 6 Release and reuse Return the credit; only now overwrite the ping-pong slot. Problem What goes wrong Observable symptom Implementation control Activation fan-out Repeated unicast injects the same K slice once per N shard. Source link or SRAM-read port saturates while receivers remain unevenly utilized. Multicast once, place receivers along short routes, and reserve every receiver before transmission. K-partial convergence Many arrays send vectors to one reducer or output SRAM bank. Reducer busy, destination-bank conflicts, output-blocked array cycles. Reduce locally, use a tree, distribute accumulators, and fuse scale or epilogue before egress. Too many small tiles Headers, descriptors, events, and barriers dominate useful payload. High command rate and low payload bandwidth despite busy routers. Coalesce transfers, enlarge useful work per launch, cache command templates, and avoid unnecessary precision fragments. Burst synchronization All cores inject at the same phase and contend for the same links. Periodic queue-depth spikes and long tail latency. Schedule waves, stagger launches, cap in-flight work, or map traffic across independent routes. Early consumption The controller starts MVM before an asynchronous transfer completes. Nondeterministic wrong outputs or stale activation data. Wait on a completion event; order payload writes before publishing tile-ready. Premature reuse A producer overwrites a ping-pong slot still owned by DMA or compute. Intermittent corruption that changes with timing or profiling. Reserve/publish/wait/release semantics, bounded credits, and explicit buffer lifetimes. Cross-path reordering Data and notification use NoCs or virtual channels without a common ordering guarantee. Ready flag observed before payload arrival. Use documented same-path ordering where valid; otherwise add explicit NoC barriers and device events. Cyclic wait Producers hold one resource while waiting for credits owned by one another. No forward progress, timeout, or watchdog reset. Use a global acquisition order, separate traffic classes, bounded queues, timeout diagnostics, and reset recovery. Excess synchronization A barrier is placed after every operation, serializing independent engines. Correct results but little DMA/MVM/output overlap. Synchronize at ownership boundaries and true hazards, then verify overlap with timestamped counters. Compiler Model communication, not just MAC count Estimate bytes and routes for N fan-out, K reductions, precision fragments, outputs, and protocol overhead. Reject mappings whose busiest link or destination exceeds a measured utilization budget. Runtime and firmware Keep async work bounded Use command-queue limits, credits, dependency events, transfer barriers, cancellation, timeouts, and deterministic recovery instead of allowing unlimited outstanding descriptors. Hardware Expose traffic classes and telemetry Provide multicast, adequate virtual channels, distributed reducers, bank-aware SRAM access, queue-depth and stall counters, and independent paths where overlap is expected. Profiler Identify the resource that stopped progress Correlate NoC bytes, link utilization, queue high-water marks, DMA busy, input-starved, output-blocked, reducer busy, and array-active cycles under one execution ID. Evidence boundary: Tenstorrent publicly documents asynchronous NoC operations, program order for requests on the same NoC and the same virtual channel, no ordering guarantee across different NoCs or virtual channels, and a semaphore-based multicast MatMul pattern in which receivers reserve space before the sender transmits. Applying those mechanisms to ACiM is a design inference: the exact Mythic or iHW queue, route, barrier, and virtual-channel implementation is not public. entries.heading: Is the Analog CIM Accuracy Problem Solved?
entries.text: Separate measured evidence from claims and study accuracy, variation, endurance, and calibration limits. Evidence review 2026-07-11 Is the Analog CIM Accuracy Problem Solved? No, not as a universal claim. Measured chips now reach software-comparable accuracy on meaningful workloads. They do so through cross-layer co-design, and each result has a defined baseline, hardware boundary, model scale, mitigation cost, and time horizon. Inspect the papers Study failure modes Study hardware/software solutions Demonstrated Scoped inference accuracy on fabricated chips Conditional Calibration, retraining, expansion, or mixed precision Not universal Results do not cover every model, chip, time, or corner Still active 2026 reviews retain accuracy and reliability roadmaps Verdict

entries.heading: The precise answer has three parts
1. The demonstrations are real
entries.text: NeuRRAM, IBM's PCM chips, and the 2025 mixed memristor/SRAM processor report measured results close to low-precision or floating-point software references on complete named tasks. This is much stronger evidence than early device-characterization simulations. 2. Accuracy moved up the stack

entries.heading: Co-design contains the error
entries.text: Write-verify, calibration, hardware-aware training, weight expansion, mixed precision, and digital execution turn imperfect MVMs into accurate applications. 3. The cost remains

entries.heading: Correction consumes something

entries.heading: "Fault-free" solves static matrix representation, not every analog error
What is new and important
entries.text: The June 2026 Nature Electronics paper factors a target matrix into two adjustable submatrices. Their product can represent the target even when many physical cells are stuck, because optimization steers the factors around those defects. The paper reports more than 99.999% cosine similarity for a DFT matrix despite a 39% device fault rate and a large wireless bit-error-rate improvement.

entries.heading: What the title does not mean
entries.text: It does not make analog hardware physically fault-free. Random read noise, ADC and driver error, nonlinear I-V behavior, parasitic resistance, drift, endurance, and full DNN system accuracy remain separate questions. The method also uses two matrix stages and may add compensation layers or refresh. The most accurate interpretation is: a general and impressive representation method for bypassing static device faults , with demonstrated signal-processing applications. It is one major component of an accuracy stack, not proof that the complete field is finished. Failure modes and mitigations

entries.heading: Accuracy is becoming an engineering budget
entries.text: The field has progressed from "can an array classify MNIST?" to measured multicore speech, ImageNet, transformer, and mixed-precision systems. That is a real change. The winning pattern is not a perfect analog cell; it is a measured error model plus co-designed device, circuit, architecture, compiler, algorithm, and calibration policy . The unresolved question is whether that complete stack keeps its density, energy, cost, yield, and lifetime advantages at production and frontier-model scale.

entries.heading: Solving Analog CIM Problems in Hardware and Software
entries.text: Partition responsibilities across arrays, digital logic, compiler, runtime, firmware, and model adaptation. Paper-to-engineering study | research snapshot 2026-07-11 Solving Analog CIM Problems in Hardware and Software Analog compute-in-memory is not one architecture and accuracy is not one problem. SRAM charge-domain macros, RRAM crossbars, PCM tiles, embedded-flash arrays, and heterogeneous processors fail differently. The strongest papers recover useful accuracy by co-designing devices, circuits, converters, digital units, compilers, training, calibration, runtime maintenance, and validation. Trace Analog CIM execution Compare architectures Inspect paper solutions Build the software stack Characterize Measure real error distributions and corners Contain Fix high-cost errors near the device and converter Adapt Train, map, and calibrate for the measured target Maintain Track per-chip state, drift, faults, and fallback Research verdict

entries.heading: The papers show scoped solutions, not a universal accuracy cure
entries.text: Analog accuracy is now engineerable for selected models and operating conditions. NeuRRAM, IBM PCM systems, heterogeneous memristor/SRAM processors, and full-stack memristor platforms demonstrate that cross-layer mitigation can approach a declared software baseline. The 2026 reviews still identify variability, nonlinearity, drift, endurance, converters, parasitics, and mitigation overhead as active deployment barriers. A valid claim must name the workload, baseline, hardware boundary, calibration state, time horizon, chip population, and cost of every correction. Hardware alone Necessary, not sufficient Better cells and ADCs cannot choose model partitioning or create noise robustness. Training alone Necessary for weak regimes Noise injection cannot repair saturation, catastrophic faults, missing dynamic range, or a broken ABI. Compiler alone Allocates the error budget Mapping and fallback work only when the target exposes measured capabilities and calibration state. Runtime alone Preserves the deployed state Calibration and refresh cannot recover a model that was never trained or mapped for the hardware.
