entries.heading: What the previous pages explained, and what was still missing for implementation
entries.text: The existing pages remain useful for physics, evidence, co-design, and reuse decisions. The changes below remove ambiguous ownership and add the contracts needed to write and test code. Priority Review finding Why it blocks real code Resolution in this guide P1 Model calibration, silicon characterization, and per-device calibration were discussed under one name. They have different producers, update schedules, security requirements, and consumers. Three separate schemas and lifecycle owners are defined. P1 The executable and serial-number-specific device state were treated as one artifact. That prevents portable AOT compilation and creates a rebuild for every replacement device. A device-class executable is bound to a separate device-state bundle at load time. P1 No stable SDK API, handle ownership, queue, event, buffer, or error contract was specified. Compiler, runtime, simulator, applications, and tests cannot evolve independently. A versioned C ABI, C++ HAL, and Python workflow are provided. P1 Accuracy simulation and performance simulation were not separated strongly enough. AIHWKit and CrossSim can model numerical non-idealities, but they are not a product cycle/energy model. Functional, statistical, cycle/resource, and hardware backends have distinct acceptance criteria. P2 PyTorch, ONNX, StableHLO, ORT, and PJRT appeared as equivalent starting points. Supporting several frontends before one executable path works multiplies semantic and build risk. The MVP starts with ONNX; ORT and PJRT are staged integrations. P2 The compiler pipeline had no repository ownership or executable acceptance test. A list of passes does not show which library owns state or when a feature is complete. Modules, CLI commands, CI lanes, and vertical-slice exit tests are defined. P2 Firmware validation and recovery were described but not represented as a command protocol. Raw or weakly checked descriptors can damage state, hang queues, or use stale calibration. A bounded command set, state machine, validation rules, and recovery policy are specified. P3 Patent evidence and implementation design occupied the same long page. Readers could confuse a proposed software design with a vendor-disclosed implementation. The patent page now labels its software mapping as proposed, links here, and makes this page the authoritative build specification. Architecture recommendation: build a simulator-first inference stack around one stable executable contract. Keep framework adapters above the compiler, physical device state below the artifact, and vendor-specific hardware behind a HAL. Do not begin by forking TTMetal, implementing PJRT, or supporting a complete model before one statically shaped MatMul compiles and runs end to end. Product boundaries

entries.heading: Toolchain, SDK, runtime, HAL, driver, and firmware are different products

Physical addresses, queue descriptors, kernel-driver calls, or device secrets ML engineers and compiler CI Compiler toolchain Import, legalize, quantize, partition, map, schedule, lower, package, inspect, and verify. Live device ownership, asynchronous request state, or field recovery decisions Build systems, framework plugins, release engineering Public SDK Expose device discovery, executable loading, buffers, sessions, queues, events, telemetry, and errors. Compiler implementation classes, direct register access, or unstable C++ internals Applications, frameworks, tests, samples Runtime Validate compatibility, bind device state, manage memory, submit work, synchronize, and apply recovery policy. Framework graph semantics or unrestricted firmware commands SDK bindings and execution providers HAL Provide one internal device interface implemented by simulation and silicon backends. User-facing ABI promises or model-level graph transformations Runtime, bring-up tests, emulators Driver Isolation, DMA/IOMMU, interrupts, mapping, reset, power, and firmware transport. Model partitioning, quantization policy, or source-level debug meaning HAL hardware backend and system software Firmware Validate bounded descriptors, schedule engines, own programming/calibration sequences, report faults, and recover. Untrusted host pointers, arbitrary array voltages, or policy hidden from telemetry Driver, runtime, manufacturing tools Corrected calibration model

entries.heading: Three kinds of calibration create three different artifacts
entries.text: Artifact Producer and input Contents Update trigger Consumer Model calibration .qcal ML/compiler team; representative model inputs Activation histograms, clipping, group scales, outlier policy, sensitivity, dataset hash Model, preprocessing, dataset, or quantization policy changes Quantization and partition passes Target characterization .achar Silicon/algorithm team; measured chip populations and PVT sweeps Array distributions, transfer models, ADC/DAC behavior, IR drop, drift, faults, timing, energy coefficients, confidence Device revision, process, firmware, characterization method, or qualification changes Compiler operation model and statistical/cycle simulators Device state .acal Manufacturing or firmware; one device serial number Gain/offset trims, usable-array bitmap, remaps, weak cells, sensor references, calibration age, signature Factory test, replacement, boot check, thermal event, aging threshold, recalibration, or repair Runtime, firmware, and hardware backend Proposed file extensions are illustrative. The important contract is ownership. A model build may depend on a target class and characterization version, but it should not embed mutable calibration from a particular serial number. The runtime binds an accepted .acal bundle and rejects stale or incompatible state.

entries.heading: Keep the portable executable separate from device binding
entries.text: Target descriptor .atarget Static device class, revision, arrays, memory, commands, formats, and ABI capabilities. Model executable .acx Portable within declared target requirements; graph, constants, plans, commands, kernels, and debug maps. Device binding .acal Serial-specific calibration, remap, health, age, and signature loaded independently. Execution evidence .atrace Correlation IDs, timings, bytes, phases, saturation, faults, fallback, and calibration identity. Deterministic cache key Everything that can change generated behavior compile_cache_key = hash( normalized_model, model_calibration, target_descriptor, characterization_version, compiler_version, compiler_options, artifact_schema_major ) load_binding_key = hash( executable_target_requirements, device_revision, firmware_abi, device_state_schema, device_state_calibration_id ) End-to-end flow

entries.heading: Characterize the target, build the executable, then bind and run
entries.text: Plane A Target characterization Runs in lab and manufacturing infrastructure, not on every application build. A1 Measure silicon Arrays, ADC/DAC, wires, programming, PVT, drift, timing, energy A2 Fit models Distributions, correlations, guard bands, confidence, device classes A3 Validate predictors Hold-out chips and workloads; numerical and cycle correlation A4 Sign target data Versioned .atarget and .achar artifacts A5 Publish compatibility Compiler, firmware, simulator, and qualification matrix target class becomes a compiler input Plane B Offline model build Runs in CI, an SDK tool, or a framework execution-provider compile callback. B1 Check and import ONNX checker, shape inference, source locations, reference tensors B2 Calibrate model Representative inputs, ranges, clipping, scales, sensitivity B3 Plan graph Support, quantization, analog/digital partition, fusion, fallback B4 Map physical work Digits, arrays, faults, ADC ranges, phases, buffers, schedule B5 Lower and package Commands, digital kernels, program recipe, ABI, debug map B6 Verify artifact Functional, statistical, cycle, version, schema, and reproducibility gates portable executable is delivered Plane C Load and execution Runs through the public SDK, runtime, HAL, driver, firmware, and device. C1 Discover device Revision, firmware ABI, memory, health, supported modes C2 Bind device state Validate calibration signature, age, temperature, and remaps C3 Load executable Check target requirements, allocate resources, program/verify weights C4 Submit requests Bind buffers, enqueue, return event, overlap transfer and compute C5 Execute and observe Pulse, MVM, convert, reconstruct, digital work, telemetry C6 Recover or complete Repeat, remap, recalibrate, refresh, fallback, reset, or return Closed feedback loop Silicon trace and model accuracy → correlation report → characterization or compiler update → new versioned artifacts → staged qualification SDK sequence diagram

entries.heading: One executable moves through five ownership boundaries
entries.text: The compile path may run once per model release. Device binding and load run per deployment or boot. Submit and completion repeat per request. Application Python, C, C++ Framework/CLI ONNX or plugin Compiler MLIR and packager Runtime/HAL Buffers and queues Firmware/device Physical execution Offline compile Model + deployment policy + representative-data identity Normalized graph + target/characterization versions Import → analyze → partition → map → schedule → lower → verify .acx + support, accuracy, mapping, and cost reports Device binding and load Open device + load executable Query revision, firmware ABI, health, and .acal Validated calibration/remap identity and resource availability Program recipe + bounded write/verify commands Ready session + compatibility and load report Repeated asynchronous request Bind buffers + submit queue + request policy Return event immediately DMA → pulse/MVM → ADC → reconstruct → digital work Completion + counters + saturation/fault status Output + event status + trace correlation ID Software architecture

entries.heading: Use a thin stable public API over replaceable compiler and device internals
entries.text: Module Suggested library Owns Dependency rule ONNX frontend libacim_frontend_onnx Checker, shape inference, semantic import, source locations, constants May depend on ONNX and MLIR; must not depend on runtime or driver Compiler core libacim_compiler Dialects, analyses, passes, target operation model, reports Depends on MLIR and schema libraries; hardware access is forbidden Artifact support libacim_artifact Schema, serialization, hashes, signatures, inspect, compatibility rules Shared by compiler and runtime; may not depend on either implementation Public runtime ABI libacim C handles, status codes, discovery, sessions, buffers, queues, events, traces Only stable exported surface; hides C++ classes and backend choice Runtime core libacim_runtime Compatibility, memory plan, load, binding, queueing, recovery policy Depends on artifact and HAL interfaces, never on a framework HAL interfaces libacim_hal Backend, device, buffer, executable, command queue, event, telemetry interfaces No vendor headers in public interfaces; backends are loadable or link-time modules Simulation backends acim_hal_functional , _analog , _cycle Exact numerics, non-ideal distributions, timing/resources Implement the same HAL and artifact semantics as hardware Hardware backend acim_hal_device Driver calls, DMA, command submission, firmware events, reset, telemetry Only module allowed to include driver or firmware transport headers Framework plugins acim_ort_ep , later acim_pjrt Framework capabilities, graph handoff, buffer adaptation, fallback integration Call compiler and public runtime APIs; do not duplicate backend logic Python package acim_sdk Ergonomic compiler/runtime wrappers, reports, examples, notebooks Thin bindings over stable C ABI plus optional compiler Python API Repository structure One ownership boundary per top-level directory acim-stack/ include/acim/ stable C API and versioned public structs api/cpp/ header-only RAII wrapper over the C ABI python/acim_sdk/ Python compiler and runtime bindings compiler/ frontend/onnx/ ONNX validation and import dialect/plan/ logical ACiM planning operations and attributes dialect/physical/ arrays, slices, converters, calibration requirements dialect/command/ firmware-visible command graph analysis/ shape, range, sensitivity, legality, cost, liveness transforms/ quantize, partition, map, schedule, lower, verify target/ target and characterization schema readers artifact/ FlatBuffer schema, serializer, verifier, inspector runtime/ sessions, buffers, queues, events, load, recovery hal/ backend interfaces and backend registry backends/{functional,analog,cycle,device}/ driver/ OS integration; separate release and privilege boundary firmware/ descriptor parser, scheduler, health, reset, calibration integrations/{onnxruntime,pjrt}/ tools/ acim-compile, inspect, run, profile, characterize tests/{unit,ir,golden,differential,hardware,models}/ examples/{matmul,onnx_ep,async_pipeline}/ Detailed repository guide: the accelerator repository blueprint expands this compact ownership sketch into schemas, generated code, C++ and Python packages, GoogleTest and pytest lanes, smoke through qualification tests, CI routing, contribution rules, performance methodology, and a full debug evidence bundle. Its minimal ACiM native example provides the first working CMake/Ninja, compiler, CTest, installation, and functional MVM path. Compiler implementation

entries.heading: Start with upstream IR, then introduce hardware meaning in three small dialects
entries.text: MLIR's declarative ODS and dialect-conversion infrastructure provide generated operation classes, verifiers, parsing, printing, and legality-driven lowering. Use them for infrastructure; do not import Tenstorrent target semantics into an ACiM backend. IR stage Recommended representation Allowed knowledge Verifier examples Imported graph Upstream func , tensor , arith , linalg , quant , or a small normalized frontend layer Tensor semantics, shapes, constants, source names, QDQ scales Ranks known where required, contraction dimensions agree, quantized zero is representable acim_plan Logical MVM/Conv regions plus candidate precision, scale domain, fallback, and error budget Target capabilities and measured operation-model estimates, not physical addresses Every op has a legal implementation; scale and accumulator types are complete acim_physical Arrays, rows/columns, digit slices, sign paths, ADC grades, phases, buffers, and calibration class Target geometry, characterization, fault-reserve policy, and static schedule resources No overlap, current and range limits pass, all slices reconstruct, resources fit acim_command Bounded commands, dependencies, events, DMA, program/verify, execute, telemetry, and recovery points Firmware ABI and driver-visible memory handles No raw pointers, all buffer ranges valid, dependency graph acyclic, firmware supports opcode/version Starter ODS shape Logical MVM is pure; programming and command operations are not def ACIMPlan_MvmOp : ACIMPlan_Op<"mvm", [Pure]> { let summary = "Logical matrix-vector operation eligible for ACiM planning"; let arguments = (ins AnyRankedTensor:$activation, AnyRankedTensor:$weight, ACIM_PrecisionAttr:$precision, ACIM_ErrorBudgetAttr:$error_budget, ACIM_FallbackAttr:$fallback); let results = (outs AnyRankedTensor:$result); let hasVerifier = 1; } def ACIMCmd_ProgramArrayOp : ACIMCmd_Op<"program_array"> { let summary = "Request a bounded firmware-owned program and verify sequence"; let arguments = (ins ACIM_ArrayRefType:$array, ACIM_ProgramImageType:$image, ACIM_CalibrationClassAttr:$calibration_class, ACIM_EventType:$dependency); let results = (outs ACIM_EventType:$completion); let hasVerifier = 1; }

entries.heading: Implement passes in dependency order and save every boundary
entries.text: Order Pass/library Implementation responsibility Minimum test 1 onnx-check-import Run ONNX checking and shape inference; import only MatMul/Gemm first; preserve source location and constants. Valid model imports; invalid rank/K dimension returns a stable diagnostic. 2 canonicalize-contracts Normalize transpose, bias, broadcast, and contraction forms into one MVM semantic contract. Equivalent ONNX forms produce identical normalized IR. 3 attach-quant-contract Consume QDQ or .qcal ; materialize scale, zero point, clipping, rounding, and accumulator type. Integer software reference exactly matches expected output and saturation. 4 analyze-capability Generate reason-coded analog, digital, and host candidates from target capabilities. Unsupported shapes are rejected or receive an explicit fallback candidate. 5 partition-and-fuse Choose regions using boundary conversion and transfer cost, not operation support alone. A forced analog/digital override produces a report and valid graph. 6 decompose-weights Generate radix/sign slices and reconstruction coefficients; preserve logical-to-physical debug mapping. Reconstructed logical weights exactly equal the quantized reference. 7 place-arrays Tile matrices, reserve spares, constrain current, pack slices, and emit calibration-class requirements. No overlap; capacity and current constraints are checked by an independent verifier. 8 plan-adc-phases Select ranges, converter sharing, phase count, repeat policy, and saturation/fallback guard. Every candidate reports predicted error, phases, saturation margin, and confidence. 9 plan-memory-schedule Allocate static arenas and overlap DMA, input encoding, MVM, ADC, reconstruction, and digital work. Lifetime intervals do not overlap illegally; cycle model accepts the schedule. 10 lower-command-abi Emit versioned bounded commands and events; insert firmware validation and recovery checkpoints. Command schema round-trips and malformed descriptors fail before execution. 11 serialize-acx Package target requirements, programs, constants, plans, commands, reports, and debug maps. Artifact is deterministic, inspectable, schema-conformant, and rejects wrong target major versions. 12 differential-verify Run exact reference and selected backends; compare checkpoints and release thresholds. First divergent op, expected tolerance, seed, profile versions, and tensors are retained.

entries.heading: Candidate selection needs measured coefficients and uncertainty
entries.text: Candidate record and constrained objective Persist this data in compiler reports candidate = { implementation: analog | digital | host, layout: {tiles, groups, buffers, sharding}, numerics: {weight_digits, activation_bits, adc_grade, accumulator}, physical: {arrays, phases, spares, calibration_class}, estimates: {latency_ns, energy_pj, error_distribution, confidence}, boundaries: {copies, conversions, synchronization}, fallback: {trigger, implementation, recovery_cost} } minimize latency_weight * latency_p99 + energy_weight * energy + risk_weight * accuracy_risk + boundary_weight * transfer_and_conversion + wear_weight * programming_and_refresh subject to error_budget, SRAM, current, ADC range, capacity, firmware ABI, calibration class, and service policy. Do not use an accuracy simulator as a latency oracle. CrossSim explicitly states that it does not model accelerator energy, area, or speed. Use AIHWKit or CrossSim adapters for numerical studies, then maintain a separately correlated cycle/resource model for queues, SRAM, NoC, converters, firmware, and digital work. Public SDK

entries.heading: Stabilize a C ABI, then build C++ and Python ergonomics on top
entries.text: Opaque handles prevent ABI exposure of STL, compiler, and driver classes. Every public struct starts with its size and API version so newer libraries can accept older callers safely. C ABI v0 starter header Compile-ready shape; the API remains a proposed design #ifndef ACIM_SDK_H_ #define ACIM_SDK_H_ #include <stddef.h> #include <stdint.h> #if defined(_WIN32) # if defined(ACIM_SDK_EXPORTS) # define ACIM_API __declspec(dllexport) # else # define ACIM_API __declspec(dllimport) # endif #elif defined(__GNUC__) # define ACIM_API __attribute__((visibility("default"))) #else # define ACIM_API #endif #define ACIM_API_VERSION 1u #define ACIM_MAX_RANK 8u #ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { #endif typedef struct acim_context acim_context_t; typedef struct acim_device acim_device_t; typedef struct acim_executable acim_executable_t; typedef struct acim_session acim_session_t; typedef struct acim_queue acim_queue_t; typedef struct acim_buffer acim_buffer_t; typedef struct acim_event acim_event_t; typedef enum acim_status { ACIM_STATUS_OK = 0, ACIM_STATUS_INVALID_ARGUMENT, ACIM_STATUS_UNSUPPORTED, ACIM_STATUS_INCOMPATIBLE_ARTIFACT, ACIM_STATUS_STALE_CALIBRATION, ACIM_STATUS_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, ACIM_STATUS_BUSY, ACIM_STATUS_TIMEOUT, ACIM_STATUS_CANCELED, ACIM_STATUS_DEVICE_FAULT, ACIM_STATUS_INTERNAL } acim_status_t; typedef enum acim_io_kind { ACIM_IO_INPUT = 0, ACIM_IO_OUTPUT = 1 } acim_io_kind_t; typedef enum acim_element_type { ACIM_ELEMENT_I8 = 0, ACIM_ELEMENT_I32, ACIM_ELEMENT_F16, ACIM_ELEMENT_F32 } acim_element_type_t; typedef enum acim_memory_flags { ACIM_MEMORY_HOST_VISIBLE = 1u << 0, ACIM_MEMORY_HOST_PINNED = 1u << 1, ACIM_MEMORY_DEVICE_LOCAL = 1u << 2 } acim_memory_flags_t; typedef struct acim_context_options { uint32_t struct_size; uint32_t api_version; const char* backend_name; /* functional, analog, cycle, device */ const char* backend_options; /* validated JSON or key/value text */ } acim_context_options_t; typedef struct acim_tensor_desc { uint32_t struct_size; uint32_t api_version; const char* name; /* executable-owned; valid until release */ acim_element_type_t element_type; uint32_t rank; int64_t dimensions[ACIM_MAX_RANK]; size_t byte_size; } acim_tensor_desc_t; typedef struct acim_buffer_binding { uint32_t struct_size; uint32_t api_version; uint32_t tensor_index; acim_buffer_t* buffer; size_t offset; size_t size; } acim_buffer_binding_t; typedef struct acim_error_info { uint32_t struct_size; uint32_t api_version; acim_status_t status; uint32_t subsystem; int64_t device_code; uint64_t trace_id; char message[256]; } acim_error_info_t; ACIM_API uint32_t acim_api_version(void); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_context_create( const acim_context_options_t*, acim_context_t**); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_context_get_last_error( acim_context_t*, acim_error_info_t*); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_device_count(acim_context_t*, uint32_t*); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_device_open(acim_context_t*, uint32_t, acim_device_t**); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_device_get_capabilities( acim_device_t*, char* json, size_t* inout_size); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_device_bind_state( acim_device_t*, const void* bytes, size_t size); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_executable_load( acim_device_t*, const void* bytes, size_t size, acim_executable_t**); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_executable_get_tensor_desc( acim_executable_t*, acim_io_kind_t, uint32_t index, acim_tensor_desc_t*); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_session_create( acim_device_t*, acim_executable_t*, acim_session_t**); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_queue_create( acim_session_t*, uint32_t queue_flags, acim_queue_t**); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_buffer_allocate( acim_device_t*, size_t bytes, uint32_t memory_flags, acim_buffer_t**); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_buffer_write( acim_buffer_t*, size_t offset, const void* source, size_t size); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_buffer_read( acim_buffer_t*, size_t offset, void* destination, size_t size); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_queue_submit( acim_queue_t*, const acim_buffer_binding_t* inputs, size_t input_count, const acim_buffer_binding_t* outputs, size_t output_count, acim_event_t**); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_event_wait(acim_event_t*, uint64_t timeout_ns); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_event_cancel(acim_event_t*); ACIM_API acim_status_t acim_event_get_result(acim_event_t*, acim_error_info_t*); ACIM_API void acim_event_release(acim_event_t*); ACIM_API void acim_buffer_release(acim_buffer_t*); ACIM_API void acim_queue_release(acim_queue_t*); ACIM_API void acim_session_release(acim_session_t*); ACIM_API void acim_executable_release(acim_executable_t*); ACIM_API void acim_device_release(acim_device_t*); ACIM_API void acim_context_release(acim_context_t*); #ifdef __cplusplus } /* extern "C" */ #endif #endif /* ACIM_SDK_H_ */ API rule Required behavior Test Ownership Every successful create/open/load/allocate returns one owned reference. Parents outlive children; queues are drained or canceled before release; release is called exactly once. Sanitizer and fault-injection tests cover success, partial construction, outstanding events, and every failure path. Thread safety Context/device queries are concurrent; a queue is ordered; independent queues may overlap; session concurrency is reported by capabilities, never assumed. Multi-threaded submit and teardown with deterministic per-queue order and allowed cross-queue overlap. Asynchrony Submit returns an event without waiting; buffer lifetime extends through event completion. Two queues overlap transfers and execution in the cycle and hardware backends. Errors Status codes are stable categories. Synchronous details are thread-local to the context; event results carry structured subsystem, device code, trace ID, and bounded message text. Firmware fault, timeout, stale calibration, cancellation, and incompatibility map consistently across backends. Versioning The caller initializes struct_size and api_version ; the library copies input strings and ignores compatible unknown trailing fields.

entries.heading: Python should expose the same lifecycle without hiding events or reports
entries.text: Python compile and run One obvious path from ONNX to a simulator or device from acim_sdk import Compiler, CompileOptions, Context, TargetProfile target = TargetProfile.load("targets/rev_b.atarget", "targets/rev_b.achar") compiler = Compiler(target) artifact, report = compiler.compile_onnx( "models/linear.onnx", model_calibration="build/linear.qcal", options=CompileOptions( accuracy_budget=0.005, latency_target_us=100, allow_digital_fallback=True, save_intermediate_ir="build/ir", ), ) artifact.save("build/linear.acx") report.save("build/linear.compile.json") with Context(backend="functional") as context: device = context.open_device(0) session = device.load("build/linear.acx") output = session.run({"input": input_tensor}) with Context(backend="device") as context: device = context.open_device(0) session = device.load("build/linear.acx") event = session.submit({"input": input_tensor}) output = event.result(timeout=1.0) event.trace().save("build/linear.atrace") HAL and backends

entries.heading: Make simulation and silicon execute the same artifact through the same internal interface
entries.text: C++ HAL boundary Internal interface; the C ABI remains the public contract class Device { public: virtual ~Device() = default; virtual StatusOr<Capabilities> QueryCapabilities() = 0; virtual Status BindDeviceState(const DeviceState&) = 0; virtual StatusOr<ExecutableHandle> Load(const Artifact&) = 0; virtual StatusOr<BufferHandle> Allocate(const BufferDesc&) = 0; virtual StatusOr<EventHandle> Submit( QueueId, ExecutableHandle, Span<BufferBinding>, const RunPolicy&) = 0; virtual Status Wait(EventHandle, Duration timeout) = 0; virtual StatusOr<Trace> ReadTrace(EventHandle) = 0; virtual Status Recover(const RecoveryRequest&) = 0; }; class Backend { public: virtual ~Backend() = default; virtual StatusOr<std::vector<DeviceInfo>> Enumerate() = 0; virtual StatusOr<std::unique_ptr<Device>> Open(DeviceId) = 0; }; Backend Purpose Must model Must not claim Exit criterion Functional Bring up artifact, commands, memory, and exact quantized semantics quickly. Shapes, types, saturation, rounding, slices, reconstruction, dependencies, fallback Analog accuracy, timing, energy, area, or silicon behavior Bit-exact against quantized reference for every supported operation Statistical analog Study accuracy sensitivity and hardware-aware training. Programming error, noise, ADC/DAC bounds, drift, IR drop, sign mapping, variation distributions Cycle latency or full-chip energy unless explicitly modeled and correlated Error distributions match held-out device traces within declared confidence Cycle/resource Predict schedule, utilization, queueing, bandwidth, latency, and energy components. Firmware phases, SRAM/NoC, converters, DMA, overlap, contention, fallback, counters Task accuracy beyond inputs supplied by the numerical model Kernel and model timelines correlate with RTL/C++ model and silicon measurements Hardware Execute on the real driver/firmware/device stack. All ABI validation, memory, queues, calibration binding, faults, telemetry, recovery Support not present in the queried firmware/device capabilities Same artifact passes differential, stress, PVT, reset, and long-run tests Adapter strategy: after license and dependency review, use AIHWKit or CrossSim behind the statistical backend, not as the public SDK. Translate the target characterization into their parameters and retain the adapter/version in every report so results remain reproducible when those projects evolve. Executable format

entries.heading: Use a schema with explicit compatibility rules, not an opaque binary blob
entries.text: Illustrative FlatBuffer schema Proposed minimum; field IDs protect parallel schema evolution namespace acim.artifact; table Version { major:ushort (id: 0); minor:ushort (id: 1); patch:uint (id: 2); } table TargetRequirements { device_family:string (id: 0); revision_min:uint (id: 1); revision_max:uint (id: 2); firmware_abi:Version (id: 3); calibration_schema:Version (id: 4); characterization_hash:[ubyte] (id: 5); required_features:[string] (id: 6); } table Executable { schema:Version (id: 0); build_id:string (id: 1); model_hash:[ubyte] (id: 2); target:TargetRequirements (id: 3); graph:[ubyte] (id: 4); constants:[ubyte] (id: 5); weight_program:[ubyte] (id: 6); command_streams:[ubyte] (id: 7); digital_kernels:[ubyte] (id: 8); memory_plan:[ubyte] (id: 9); numerical_contract:[ubyte] (id: 10); recovery_policy:[ubyte] (id: 11); debug_map:[ubyte] (id: 12); compile_report:[ubyte] (id: 13); signature:[ubyte] (id: 14); } root_type Executable; file_identifier "ACIX"; Compatibility rule Required behavior Schema major Mismatch is rejected unless an explicit offline converter exists. Schema minor Readers accept older compatible fields; optional new fields use defaults and feature checks. Firmware ABI Major must match; minor compatibility follows queried feature/opcode support. Target revision Must fall in the compiled range and expose every required physical capability. Characterization Hash must be recognized by the runtime policy; unknown or revoked profiles require recompile. Device state Calibration schema, device family, serial signature, age, and temperature policy are checked at load. Schema CI Run flatc --conform against the previous released schema and round-trip old artifacts. Security Verify hashes/signatures before programming; firmware independently validates every descriptor and bound. Runtime and firmware

entries.heading: Make state transitions and recovery observable
entries.text: Closed No ownership Device handle absent; no mapped memory or pending work. Discovered Capabilities known Revision, ABI, features, memory, and health queried. Bound Calibration accepted Device state signature, age, temperature, and remaps valid. Loaded Executable ready Resources allocated; weights programmed and verified. Running Queues active Requests execute asynchronously with trace correlation. Degraded Recovery required Repeat, remap, recalibrate, refresh, fallback, reset, or fail. Command class Examples Firmware validation Completion evidence Memory DMA copy, fill, bind, release IOMMU handle, bounds, alignment, direction, overlap, lifetime Bytes, cycles, fault address, queue/event IDs Weight lifecycle Erase, program, verify, commit, rollback Array ownership, recipe ID, voltage/current limits, endurance policy, transaction state Program distribution, retries, failed cells, remap, image hash Compute Input encode, MVM phase, ADC read, reconstruct, digital kernel Array/range/mode support, current bound, dependencies, buffers, calibration class Phases, saturation, ADC range, cycles, output checksum Health Read sensors, self-test, calibrate, refresh Privilege, idle state, thermal and power envelope, accepted procedure version Calibration ID, temperature, weak resources, health vector, expiry Control Barrier, event, cancel, timeout, reset Queue ownership, dependency validity, safe reset point, outstanding DMA/programming Final state, canceled/completed work, data validity, reset reason Framework integration

entries.heading: Add framework plugins only after the standalone contract works
entries.text: Stage Integration What to implement Why this order MVP Standalone ONNX CLI and Python compiler Checker, shape inference, MatMul/Gemm import, static shapes, compile, inspect, run Smallest dependency surface; deterministic artifacts; easy golden testing Stage 2 ONNX Runtime plugin EP GetCapability , Compile , allocator/stream if needed, compatibility info, session options Provides heterogeneous CPU fallback and a production application API without owning the whole framework Stage 3 PyTorch export through ONNX Document supported export profile, dynamic-shape limits, QDQ handling, and reproducible model preprocessing Reuses the proven ONNX path instead of creating a second importer Stage 4 StableHLO/PJRT plugin PJRT C API client/device/buffer/executable/event behavior and StableHLO compiler entry Useful for JAX/PyTorch-XLA, but larger ABI, async, sharding, and packaging surface Since ONNX Runtime 1.23, its official guidance is to implement a new provider as a plugin EP . The separate plugin development contract asks GetCapability() which graph regions are supported and Compile() to produce executable compute functions, while another provider can handle fallback. That is a good second integration after the standalone compiler is stable. Execution Provider responsibilities Keep the plugin thin GetCapability(graph, target): validate shapes and dtypes ask libacim_compiler for legal candidate regions subtract regions whose boundary cost or error budget fails return reason-coded supported subgraphs Compile(subgraphs): compile each accepted subgraph to .acx bytes retain compatibility metadata and cache key create compute callback that calls the public acim runtime API Compute(inputs, outputs): bind ORT buffers or copy through declared memory rules submit asynchronously where the EP contract permits translate acim status/faults to ORT status never implement quantization, mapping, or driver logic in the EP First buildable vertical slice

entries.heading: Prove one exact MatMul from ONNX to artifact to simulator
entries.text: Start with [1,128] x [128,64] , INT8 inputs and weights, INT32 accumulation, static shapes, no analog noise, one functional backend, and no framework plugin. This deliberately tests software contracts before physical fidelity. 1 Create ONNX model Known constants and reference output 2 Import to MLIR Validated shape and MVM semantics 3 Lower plan Quant contract and logical slices 4 Map virtual array One target descriptor, no faults 5 Serialize .acx Version, program, commands, debug map 6 Run functional HAL Public C API, buffers, queue, event 7 Compare and trace Bit-exact output and inspectable evidence Developer loop Commands the repository should support before adding Conv or hardware cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build \ -DACIM_ENABLE_ONNX=ON \ -DACIM_ENABLE_FUNCTIONAL_BACKEND=ON cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure python examples/matmul/create_model.py --output build/matmul.onnx acim-compile build/matmul.onnx \ --target testdata/virtual.atarget \ --characterization testdata/ideal.achar \ --emit-ir build/ir \ --report build/matmul.compile.json \ -o build/matmul.acx acim-inspect build/matmul.acx --all acim-run build/matmul.acx \ --backend functional \ --inputs testdata/matmul_input.npz \ --golden testdata/matmul_golden.npz \ --trace build/matmul.atrace acim-profile build/matmul.atrace --summary Definition of done: a clean checkout builds without device hardware; the same .acx is inspected and executed through the public C API; output is bit-exact; malformed artifacts and incompatible targets fail with stable status codes; IR, compile report, command list, and trace IDs identify the original ONNX node. Second vertical slice: extend this exact artifact and HAL with capability, live-health, calibration, binding, and topology epochs. Compile row- and column-parallel linear variants, bind around injected row/column/tile faults, execute collectives on a fake AcimMesh , and recover from one link failure. The scale-out implementation plan defines the schemas, sequence, and acceptance metrics. Physical-board vertical slice: the PCIe board bring-up guide implements the hardware HAL boundary with host/device requirements, UMD and KMD APIs, BAR and queue schemas, DMA/MSI-X ordering, firmware boot, analog program/verify, and a staged YOLO path. Profiling vertical slice: the host Tracy and device cycle-trace guide defines optional CMake integration, scoped host zones, a firmware-safe trace ABI, UMD/KMD drain ownership, clock correlation, ACiM counters, profiling modes, and measurement gates. Implementation roadmap

entries.heading: Separate fast deterministic gates from statistical and hardware qualification

entries.heading: What the existing documents cover, and what this page adds
entries.text: The compiler, artifact, Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL), System-on-Chip (SoC), and scale-out contracts already exist. Their missing implementation boundary was how Linux safely discovers a board, transfers buffers, starts firmware work, receives completion, and recovers a device without exposing arbitrary host memory. Already covered: model build ONNX import, MLIR dialects and passes, partitioning, calibration inputs, scheduling, artifact packaging, and framework plugins. SDK and compiler guide Already covered: platform roles Runtime, driver, firmware, command processors, memory, control plane, data plane, observability, and Application Binary Interface (ABI) principles. NPU/SoC software architecture Already covered: logical device Fault hierarchy, topology epochs, placement, collectives, recovery, hybrid Large Language Model (LLM) partition, and scale-out descriptors. Scale-out and LLM design Added: physical board contract PCIe IDs and capabilities, Base Address Register (BAR) layout, doorbells, Direct Memory Access (DMA) masks, Message Signaled Interrupts Extended (MSI-X), reset, firmware mailbox, health, trace, and Advanced Error Reporting (AER) behavior. Open PCIe implementation Added: protected execution path User-Mode Driver (UMD) and Kernel-Mode Driver (KMD) APIs, buffer ownership, Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) mapping, submission and completion rings, memory ordering, interrupts, and cleanup. Open queue contracts Added: first real workload A proposed YOLO compile, program, execute, postprocess, profile, and accuracy-correlation path with analog and digital placement gates. Open YOLO dataflow Added: whole-chain verification Choose PCIe-card or embedded-SoC deployment; build the correct host, driver, firmware, and model artifacts; use QEMU only for modeled hardware; correlate host/device logs; and stop at explicit gates before advancing. Open the full-chain procedure Terminology map

entries.heading: Define the contract, layer, and measurement behind each term
entries.text: This glossary explains how each term is used in this ACiM design, not only what its letters expand to. A term may name a source interface, binary contract, compiler representation, transport mechanism, hardware block, numerical assumption, or licensing record; treating those categories as interchangeable creates architecture and implementation errors. Categories Interfaces and contracts Models and compiler Host and device I/O Digital hardware Boot, simulation, and debug Analog and numerics Licensing and provenance

entries.heading: Software interfaces, ownership, and versioned contracts
entries.text: API Application Programming Interface The source-level functions, classes, and data types one component exposes. Recompiling can adapt an API change; an already-built binary cannot. ABI Application Binary Interface The binary contract for calling conventions, symbol names, data layout, alignment, opcodes, and version compatibility. This design has separate artifact, runtime-UMD, UMD-KMD, and firmware command ABIs. C ABI C language binary interface A stable function-call boundary using C-compatible symbols and layouts. It is often used for SDK plugins because C++ name mangling and standard-library ABIs vary by toolchain. UAPI Userspace API and ABI The Linux kernel/userspace contract: device files, ioctl numbers, structures, flags, handles, mmap behavior, events, and errors. Once shipped, compatibility must be managed deliberately. SDK Software Development Kit The developer-facing product: headers, libraries, compiler, runtime, tools, examples, diagnostics, documentation, packages, and compatibility policy. An SDK is more than a compiler. HAL Hardware Abstraction Layer A narrow interface hiding transport details so the same runtime can target a simulator, VFIO prototype, Linux driver, FPGA, or silicon backend. Runtime Execution orchestration library Loads compiled artifacts, creates sessions, allocates and binds buffers, selects queues, submits work, waits on events, recovers faults, and exposes profiling. UMD User-Mode Driver An unprivileged userspace library that discovers devices, owns process-local objects, prepares descriptors, and translates HAL/runtime requests into the kernel UAPI. KMD Kernel-Mode Driver Privileged kernel code that owns PCIe resources, DMA isolation, interrupts, reset, power, firmware loading, process cleanup, and device lifetime. Driver Software controlling a device boundary An imprecise word unless qualified. In this guide it can mean UMD, KMD, or both; firmware is a separate device-resident layer. Firmware Device-resident control software Code running on an embedded controller that boots the accelerator, validates command descriptors, sequences engines, manages health, and reports faults. Device ABI Host-to-firmware binary contract The exact command, descriptor, queue, register, status, and error formats accepted by a firmware/device generation. It is not the model IR. ISA Instruction Set Architecture The programmer-visible instructions, registers, address model, and execution rules of a processor or accelerator engine. An ABI may select and constrain an ISA but is not the ISA itself. Microcode Low-level engine control program A compact target-specific sequence that drives internal datapaths. It normally sits below compiler IR and above fixed hardware state machines. Artifact Deployable compiler output A versioned package containing code or commands, constants, buffer metadata, target requirements, debug maps, calibration references, and provenance. It is the hinge between offline build and runtime. Schema Machine-readable data definition Defines fields, types, required values, defaults, and evolution rules for an artifact, command, trace, or capability description. SemVer Semantic Versioning A major.minor.patch convention. It helps communicate compatibility but does not create compatibility unless each ABI and schema has explicit rules and tests. SoC System-on-Chip A chip integrating processors, memory controllers, interconnect, accelerators, security, and peripherals. A PCIe accelerator card may contain one or more SoCs or chiplets. CI Continuous Integration Automated build, static analysis, unit, compatibility, simulator, and regression gates run when code or generated contracts change. CD Continuous Delivery or Deployment Automated packaging and promotion after CI. Driver signing, firmware compatibility, rollback, and hardware qualification make accelerator CD different from a web-only release. DKMS Dynamic Kernel Module Support Linux packaging that rebuilds an out-of-tree kernel module for installed kernels. It eases installation but does not guarantee source compatibility with future kernels. MVP Minimum Viable Product The smallest end-to-end workflow that proves user value. For this stack, a one-operator vertical slice is an engineering milestone, not necessarily a market MVP. SLO Service-Level Objective An internal measurable target such as p99 latency, availability, or recovery time. Several SLOs may support one customer commitment. SLA Service-Level Agreement An external agreement defining promised service and remedies. A silicon accuracy target or benchmark alone is not an SLA.

entries.heading: Model formats, compiler representations, and transformations
entries.text: ONNX Open Neural Network Exchange A serialized model graph format with typed operators, tensors, attributes, and versioned operator sets. It is an input interchange format, not a hardware schedule. Opset Operator-set version The ONNX version governing operator semantics. A model's IR version and opset imports are separate compatibility fields and both must be checked. Graph Operations connected by data dependencies The compiler view of model computation. Dynamic control flow, state, aliases, side effects, and symbolic dimensions make it richer than a simple directed acyclic graph. Tensor Typed multidimensional value Defined by element type, rank, shape, layout, quantization, and memory placement. Equal shapes do not imply equal physical layouts. IR Intermediate Representation The compiler's structured program form between source model and executable. Different IR levels preserve different semantics and expose different optimization choices. HLO High-Level Operations A tensor-operation IR family associated with XLA. HLO names a level of representation; it is not one universal file format or device ABI. StableHLO Versioned high-level ML operation set A portability layer built on MLIR for carrying framework semantics to compilers with compatibility guarantees. It does not define ACiM placement, calibration, runtime calls, or firmware commands. MLIR Multi-Level Intermediate Representation Compiler infrastructure for defining dialects and progressively lowering programs. MLIR is the framework; a particular dialect and pass pipeline form the target compiler. Dialect MLIR vocabulary and rules A namespace of operations, types, attributes, parsers, printers, and verification rules for one abstraction level or domain. Op Compiler operation An IR instruction with operands, results, attributes, regions, and semantics. It may represent a whole convolution, a DMA copy, or one target command depending on the dialect. SSA Static Single Assignment An IR property in which each value is defined once. Dataflow and use-def chains become explicit, enabling analysis and safe rewrites. DSL Domain-Specific Language A language designed for one domain, such as tensor kernels or schedules. A DSL may lower into MLIR; it is not synonymous with an MLIR dialect, which is an IR extension mechanism. Pass Compiler analysis or transformation A staged unit that inspects or rewrites IR. Production pipelines declare ordering, preconditions, invariants, diagnostics, and tests rather than collecting unrelated rewrites. Canonicalize Normalize equivalent IR forms Rewrites expressions into predictable simpler forms. It reduces pattern count but must preserve semantics and is not target lowering by itself. Legalize Replace unsupported constructs Transforms operations, types, shapes, or layouts until every remaining construct is valid for the next dialect or target capability contract. Lowering Move to a more concrete abstraction Converts high-level model meaning into target operations, schedules, buffers, commands, or machine code while recording any precision and fallback decisions. Fusion Combine operations into one execution region Can remove intermediate traffic and launch overhead, but may increase live memory, analog range, converter work, or unsupported-op pressure. Partition Assign graph regions to execution backends Separates ACiM-supported work from DSP, CPU, or other fallback work. Boundary conversion and transfer costs belong in the decision. Frontend Source-facing compiler stage Imports ONNX, StableHLO, or framework programs, validates semantics, normalizes shapes and types, and emits a compiler IR. Backend Target-facing compiler stage Maps legal IR to one device's arrays, memories, converters, command format, code, and artifact ABI. This is the least reusable part across Tenstorrent and ACiM. Codegen Code or command generation Emits machine instructions, microcode, command streams, constants, relocations, and metadata after scheduling and memory planning. AOT Ahead-of-Time compilation Compiles before deployment, enabling qualification and caching. It requires a clear target descriptor and artifact compatibility contract. JIT Just-in-Time compilation Compiles at or near execution time for actual shapes or hardware. It improves specialization but adds latency, security, reproducibility, and cache concerns. ODS Operation Definition Specification MLIR's declarative way to define operations, types, and attributes using TableGen records, from which C++ declarations, verifiers, builders, and documentation can be generated. TableGen LLVM declarative record language and generator Describes structured compiler data and emits repetitive C++ or documentation. It is a build-time generator, not the runtime artifact schema. LLVM IR LLVM low-level intermediate representation A typed SSA representation suited to CPU-like code generation. Tensor and ACiM array semantics usually need higher-level dialects before lowering toward LLVM IR. TOSA Tensor Operator Set Architecture An Arm-defined tensor operator specification and MLIR dialect intended as a common layer between frameworks and hardware-oriented lowering. TVM Apache TVM An end-to-end machine-learning compiler stack with graph and tensor scheduling abstractions. Its architecture can be studied without assuming its cost model fits analog arrays. PJRT OpenXLA uniform device API A C API and plugin boundary through which frameworks access opaque, device-specific implementations. It is neither a model IR nor a kernel driver UAPI. ORT ONNX Runtime A model runtime that can partition supported graph regions to a hardware Execution Provider while retaining other regions on fallback providers. EP Execution Provider An ONNX Runtime plugin that advertises capability, compiles claimed subgraphs, creates runtime state, and invokes the accelerator. Target Target descriptor A machine-readable description of device generation, capacities, supported formats, topology, firmware/ABI versions, errata,

entries.heading: Host/device transport, addressing, queues, and interrupts
entries.text: PCIe Peripheral Component Interconnect Express The host/device interconnect carrying configuration, MMIO, DMA transactions, and message-signaled interrupts. BAR Base Address Register PCIe-discovered address region exposing device control registers or a device-memory aperture to the host. MMIO Memory-Mapped Input/Output CPU loads and stores directed to device registers rather than ordinary RAM. PIO Programmed Input/Output The CPU directly reads or writes device registers/data instead of asking a DMA engine to transfer a buffer. DMA Direct Memory Access Device-initiated transfer to or from host memory without the CPU copying each byte. IOMMU Input-Output Memory Management Unit Translates and restricts device DMA addresses so a context cannot access arbitrary host memory. IOVA Input-Output Virtual Address The address a device places in a DMA transaction after the kernel establishes an IOMMU/DMA mapping. BO Buffer Object Driver-managed allocation or imported buffer represented to userspace by an opaque handle. Descriptor Fixed-format work or transfer record Contains buffer addresses, sizes, operation identifiers, dependencies, flags, and a cookie. Its byte layout is part of the device ABI. SQ Submission Queue Ring where the host publishes validated commands for firmware/device consumption. CQ Completion Queue Ring where the device reports terminal status, fault information, counters, and the matching cookie. Doorbell MMIO notification register A host write telling the device that a queue producer index has advanced. IRQ Interrupt Request Kernel-visible notification that completion, fault, firmware, or health work needs service. MSI-X Message Signaled Interrupts Extended PCIe interrupt mechanism supporting multiple independently configured vectors. FLR Function Level Reset PCIe reset of one function without resetting the entire machine or unrelated functions. AER Advanced Error Reporting PCIe facility reporting correctable, non-fatal, and fatal link/transaction errors. FD File Descriptor Per-process Linux handle used for devices, dma-buf objects, events, and other kernel resources. dma-buf Shared DMA buffer framework Linux mechanism for exporting and importing the same buffer across device drivers. RO/RW/WO Register access modes Read-only, read/write, and write-only. RW1C means writing one clears the selected status bit. DRM Direct Rendering Manager Linux kernel subsystem reused by drivers/accel ; here DRM does not mean digital-rights management. TLB Translation Lookaside Buffer Hardware cache of address translations; a vendor-specific TLB programming model is not portable by default. SMMU System Memory Management Unit Arm's I/O memory-management architecture used to translate and isolate device accesses. NUMA Non-Uniform Memory Access Host architecture where memory latency/bandwidth depends on which CPU and memory node are used. VFIO Virtual Function I/O Linux framework for IOMMU-protected direct device access from a trusted userspace driver. Useful for prototypes, but production ownership and sharing still need design. UIO Userspace I/O A small Linux framework exposing simple MMIO and interrupts. It does not provide VFIO-style IOMMU isolation or a full accelerator memory model. ioctl Linux device-control system call Transfers a numbered request and fixed UAPI structure between userspace and the KMD. Pointer size, padding, bounds, and backward compatibility require explicit design. Fence Asynchronous completion dependency A waitable object indicating that prior work has completed. It orders resource reuse; it is different from a CPU or DMA memory barrier. SG Scatter-gather list A sequence of physical or DMA segments representing one logical buffer so an engine can transfer non-contiguous memory without a CPU copy.

entries.heading: Digital compute, on-chip interconnect, memory, and implementation
entries.text: NPU Neural Processing Unit An accelerator specialized for neural-network operations. It may be digital, analog, or hybrid; the name alone does not identify its arithmetic or memory architecture. HWA Hardware Accelerator A specialized engine offloading work from a general CPU. NPU, DSP, video codec, DMA engine, and ACiM array are all possible HWAs. NoC Network-on-Chip The internal packet or circuit-switched fabric connecting cores, tiles, SRAM banks, DMA engines, converters, and controllers. It is inside the device, unlike the PCIe host link. Tile Repeated compute and memory unit A physical or logical building block containing some combination of array, digital core, local SRAM, router, converters, and control. Its contents are architecture-specific. Core Programmable execution engine A processor that fetches instructions and manipulates state. An analog array performs MVM physics but is not itself a RISC-V-like core. RISC-V Open instruction-set architecture Often used for embedded control, scheduling, scalar work, and firmware. Too much control work can saturate cores and the NoC even when arrays are underused. CP Command Processor A device block or firmware core that fetches descriptors, checks dependencies, configures engines, and publishes completions. Control plane Lifecycle and policy path Owns discovery, allocation, security, power, reset, health, version negotiation, and observability rather than tensor payload movement. Data plane Tensor and command execution path Carries inputs, outputs, weights, partial sums, commands, and completion state through the hot path. DSP Digital Signal Processor A programmable digital engine efficient for vector, activation, reduction, preprocessing, and unsupported operators surrounding the analog MVM path. SIMD Single Instruction, Multiple Data One instruction applies the same operation to several lanes. It describes data parallelism, not the complete processor schedule. VLIW Very Long Instruction Word An ISA style encoding several operations for parallel issue, with much scheduling responsibility placed on the compiler. SRAM Static Random-Access Memory Fast volatile on-chip memory used for activations, commands, scratch data, and partial sums. It is distinct from non-volatile analog weight storage. DRAM Dynamic Random-Access Memory High-capacity volatile memory, usually off-chip, holding models and tensors that do not fit locally. Moving data to and from DRAM is often expensive. L1 Level-one local memory or cache The nearest programmable storage to a core or tile. In accelerator documentation, confirm whether L1 is software-managed SRAM, a cache, or both. Cache Hardware-managed copy of memory Exploits locality and is usually transparent to software. Scratchpad SRAM is explicitly allocated and moved by compiler/runtime, so it is not automatically a cache. Double buffer Overlap transfer and compute with two buffers While one buffer feeds compute, the other is filled or drained. It hides latency only when bandwidth, dependencies, and engine concurrency permit overlap. ASIC Application-Specific Integrated Circuit Fixed-function or specialized silicon manufactured for a target application, unlike a reprogrammable FPGA. RTL Register-Transfer Level A clocked digital hardware description of registers and transfers used to implement and verify controllers, buses, DMA, NoC, and digital compute. SystemC C++ system-modeling library Used for functional, transaction-level, or cycle-oriented models before RTL and silicon. Model timing accuracy must be stated rather than inferred from the language. FPGA Field-Programmable Gate Array Reconfigurable hardware used to prototype PCIe, firmware, commands, and digital engines before ASIC availability; it does not reproduce analog array physics by itself. ROM Read-Only Memory Immutable or protected first-stage device code/data establishing reset-safe boot, identity, and firmware loading. PPA Power, Performance, and Area Three coupled hardware implementation objectives. Improving array arithmetic alone may worsen converters, control, memory, or die area. DFT Design for Test Structures and methods that make manufactured silicon observable and testable, including scan, memory test, analog test modes, and calibration access. BIST Built-In Self-Test On-device logic or firmware that runs known tests for memories, links, arrays, converters, or controllers and reports health. Bandwidth Data transferred per unit time A capacity such as GB/s. Peak link bandwidth, sustained payload bandwidth, NoC bisection bandwidth, and per-array bandwidth are different measurements. Latency Time for one operation or request State the scope and percentile: kernel, layer, model, compile, first-token, per-token, median, or p99. Throughput Completed work per unit time Examples are inferences/s, tokens/s, or frames/s. High batching can improve throughput while worsening single-request latency. TOPS Tera Operations Per Second A peak or measured arithmetic rate. The operation-count convention, precision, sparsity, utilization, and included digital/converter work must be disclosed. TOPS/W Operations per second per watt An efficiency ratio whose value depends on operation counting and power boundary. Array-only peak TOPS/W is not end-to-end application efficiency. H2D Host-to-Device transfer Inputs, commands, constants, or firmware moving from host memory to the accelerator. D2H Device-to-Host transfer Outputs, traces, or status moving from the accelerator to host memory. SKU Stock Keeping Unit A sellable board or device configuration with a defined chip count, memory, power envelope, firmware support, and qualification status.

entries.heading: Boot, system images, simulation, and low-level debug
entries.text: QEMU Machine emulator and virtualizer System emulation runs a guest CPU, memory, and only the devices implemented by the selected QEMU machine. A generic Arm or RISC-V virt board does not automatically contain an ACiM endpoint. BSP Board Support Package The bootloader, kernel configuration, device tree, drivers, firmware, root-filesystem integration, and build metadata needed to boot a specific board. Bootloader Software that starts the host operating system Initializes enough platform hardware to select and load the host Linux kernel, device tree, and optional initramfs. It is separate from ACiM controller firmware. Rootfs Root filesystem The Linux userspace image containing libraries, configuration, UMD, runtime, tools, services, and applications. An initramfs is a rootfs held in memory during early boot. Cross-compile Build on one architecture for another For example, build Arm64 Linux userspace on an x86 workstation or RISC-V controller firmware with a freestanding target toolchain and linker script. JTAG Board-level debug and programming interface Lets a debugger halt a supported target, inspect registers and memory, and load or flash images through a tool such as OpenOCD. It is a bring-up path, not the normal application transport. remoteproc Linux remote-processor framework Platform mechanism for loading firmware, powering, starting, stopping, and reporting crashes for an on-SoC remote core. It is relevant when the ACiM controller is a heterogeneous SoC processor rather than a PCIe card controller. Co-simulation Several models executing one protocol A host or QEMU machine model forwards MMIO, DMA, queues, and interrupts to a functional, cycle, RTL, or analog model so the complete software chain runs before silicon. ELF Executable and Linkable Format A structured binary containing loadable segments, symbols, relocations, and an entry point. Linux executables, kernel modules, and controller firmware may all use ELF but target different machines and loaders. DTB Device Tree Blob Binary hardware description passed to Linux on many embedded systems. It declares platform devices, MMIO ranges, interrupts, clocks, resets, IOMMUs, reserved memory, and relationships such as remote processors.

entries.heading: Analog CIM, numerical formats, model execution, and accuracy
entries.text: ACiM Analog Compute-in-Memory Performs arithmetic through analog behavior inside or adjacent to memory arrays to reduce weight movement. AiCM, AIMC, analog CIM, and analog in-memory computing are overlapping spellings. MVM Matrix-Vector Multiplication Computes y = Wx for one vector. In ACiM, weights map to cell conductances, inputs drive rows, column currents sum products, and converters plus digital reconstruction finish the operation. VMM Vector-Matrix Multiplication Often used in analog literature for the same array operation viewed with a row-vector convention. Confirm tensor orientation instead of assuming VMM and MVM imply different hardware. GEMM General Matrix Multiplication Computes C = alpha AB + beta C for matrices. A compiler normally decomposes GEMM into tiled MVMs, batches, partial sums, and digital accumulation. MAC Multiply-Accumulate Multiplies two values and adds the product into an accumulator. Marketing may count one MAC as one or two operations, so TOPS comparisons need a declared convention. Crossbar Intersecting row and column array Memory cells at intersections encode weights; driven rows and sensed columns exploit Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws for parallel multiply and accumulation. WL / BL Wordline and bitline Row and column conductors used to select, drive, program, and sense memory cells. Parasitic resistance and capacitance make position and array size matter. Conductance Electrical weight representation The inverse of resistance, measured in siemens. Devices encode a weight through one or more conductance states, often using differential cells for signed values. DAC Digital-to-Analog Converter Converts encoded digital inputs into voltage, current, pulse width, or bit-serial drive for an array. Some designs replace a conventional multibit DAC with simpler drivers and more cycles. ADC Analog-to-Digital Converter Digitizes analog column results. Resolution, sampling rate, sharing, range, and calibration can dominate ACiM area, energy, latency, and accuracy. ENOB Effective Number of Bits The useful converter resolution after measured noise and distortion. It is commonly lower than the nominal ADC bit count and varies with speed, range, and PVT. SNR Signal-to-Noise Ratio The ratio of desired signal power to noise power, usually in decibels. SNR helps characterize a path but does not directly equal model accuracy. Partial sum Incomplete dot-product result Produced when a tensor is split across rows, columns, bit slices, arrays, or chiplets. It must be accumulated with declared precision and placement. NVM Non-Volatile Memory Retains state without power. Flash, RRAM, and PCM are different NVM technologies with different programming, variation, endurance, density, and sensing behavior. NOR / NAND Flash memory organizations NOR favors random access and simpler compute mapping; NAND favors density but uses string/page organization and more complex access. A roadmap claim does not make their ACiM backends interchangeable. RRAM Resistive Random-Access Memory Also called ReRAM; stores data through programmable resistance. Analog levels face device variability, nonlinear programming, drift, defects, and endurance limits. PCM Phase-Change Memory Stores state through material phases with different resistance. Multi-level programming, drift, write asymmetry, and temperature sensitivity shape its compute use. Write-verify Closed-loop cell programming Applies a programming pulse, reads the cell, compares against a target, and repeats. It improves weight placement but costs time, energy, and endurance. Calibration Measured correction of hardware behavior Estimates converter offsets, gains, array transfer functions, drift, defects, or per-tile scales and stores parameters used by compiler, firmware, or runtime. Drift Time-dependent state change Stored conductance or circuit response moves after programming. Monitoring, compensation, refresh, retraining, or fallback must be included in lifecycle cost. PVT Process, Voltage, and Temperature Manufacturing and operating conditions that change timing, analog transfer behavior, converter quality, retention, and calibration validity. SPICE Transistor-level circuit simulation Models electrical behavior and corners at high fidelity but limited scale. It complements, rather than replaces, architectural and task-level simulation. Quantization Map values to a finite set of levels Defines precision, scale, zero point, rounding, clipping, and sometimes per-channel parameters. Analog error is additional to digital quantization error. INT8 / INT4 8-bit and 4-bit integer formats Describe logical tensor values, not automatically ADC ENOB or cell bits. A physical implementation may use several cells, slices, reads, or accumulations per logical value. ANA8 Vendor analog-precision label Not an industry-standard numeric type. Treat it as a product claim until input encoding, weight representation, accumulation, ENOB, calibration, and validation are specified. FP32 / BF16 Floating-point formats FP32 has 32 bits; bfloat16 keeps an FP32-like exponent with fewer fraction bits. A floating-point baseline must be named when reporting quantized or analog accuracy loss. PTQ Post-Training Quantization Converts a trained model using calibration data without full retraining. It is fast but may struggle with sensitive layers, outliers, or analog nonidealities. QAT Quantization-Aware Training Models quantization effects during training or fine-tuning so weights adapt. Hardware-aware training may additionally inject measured analog behavior. QDQ Quantize/Dequantize operators Graph nodes that make scale, zero point, rounding, and precision transitions explicit. They describe numerical intent, not necessarily physical converter operations. Scale / ZP Quantization scale and zero point Map real values to integer codes. Scale controls step size; zero point represents real zero in an asymmetric integer range. Clip / saturate Limit values to a representable range Clipping is

entries.heading: Open-source licensing, software inventory, and provenance
entries.text: SPDX Software Package Data Exchange An open standard for machine-readable software, component, license, security, and provenance information. SPDX records facts; it does not grant rights or replace license text and legal review. SBOM Software Bill of Materials An inventory of components and relationships in a product or build. SPDX is one format for an SBOM, but an SPDX file may also describe other lifecycle information. SPDX ID SPDX license identifier A standardized short name such as Apache-2.0 . A source header like SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 labels the applicable license. Expression SPDX license expression A machine-readable combination using operators such as AND , OR , and WITH . The operator changes obligations and choice, so it is not decorative metadata. Permissive License family with limited downstream conditions Common examples include Apache-2.0, MIT, and BSD licenses. Exact notice, attribution, patent, and redistribution terms still differ. Copyleft License conditions tied to redistribution or modification Some licenses require corresponding source or same-license terms in defined circumstances. Scope varies, so architecture labels are not a legal conclusion. Apache-2.0 Apache License 2.0 A permissive license with copyright, notice, and express patent-license provisions. Preserve required notices and inspect separately licensed dependencies and assets. MIT / BSD Permissive license families Generally short licenses centered on retaining copyright and permission notices, but variants differ and must be identified precisely. GPL / LGPL GNU copyleft license families GPL and Lesser GPL have different conditions and version choices. Kernel modules, userspace libraries, linking, modification, and distribution require component-specific review. NOTICE Distribution notice file May collect attribution required by Apache-licensed or third-party material. It does not replace the LICENSE file and should not be discarded during packaging. Provenance Origin and transformation history Records repository, commit, author or supplier, license, patches, generator, model/dataset source, and build inputs so a shipped artifact can be reproduced and audited. Transitive dep. Dependency of a dependency Code or data pulled indirectly into a build. Top-level repository licensing does not automatically describe the full dependency closure. Upstream Original or authoritative project line Contributing reusable changes upstream reduces long-term divergence, but product schedules and target confidentiality may require a maintained downstream boundary. Fork / vendor Maintained copy versus imported snapshot A fork has independent history; vendoring copies a dependency into the product tree. Both need ownership, update, security, license, and compatibility plans. DCO / CLA Contribution attestation or agreement A Developer Certificate of Origin is a contributor attestation; a Contributor License Agreement is a separate legal agreement. Project policy determines which is used. Model license Terms for weights, data, and outputs Model weights, training datasets, tokenizer assets, demo media, and code can have different licenses and usage restrictions; track each artifact independently. Hash / signature Integrity digest versus authenticity proof A cryptographic hash detects changed bytes; a digital signature binds a digest to a trusted key. Neither alone establishes license compliance. Repro build Reproducible build A controlled process that produces byte-identical or verifiably equivalent outputs from declared sources, tools, dependencies, environment, and configuration. Do not confuse

entries.heading: Similar words describe different contracts
entries.text: API vs ABI vs UAPI An API is what source code calls. An ABI is the binary representation and behavior. A UAPI is specifically the kernel/userspace API and ABI surface. Runtime vs UMD vs KMD vs firmware The runtime schedules model execution; the UMD translates userspace objects; the KMD enforces host protection; firmware controls device engines. ONNX vs StableHLO vs MLIR ONNX is a model interchange format. StableHLO is a versioned high-level tensor operation set carried in MLIR. MLIR is the infrastructure used to define many IR dialects and lowering stages. DSL vs MLIR dialect A DSL is a user- or developer-facing language specialized for a domain. A dialect is a structured extension of MLIR; a DSL can compile into one or several dialects. ABI vs ISA vs microcode An ABI defines how binaries and components interact. An ISA defines processor-visible instructions and state. Microcode is a low-level program or control encoding for a particular engine. BAR/MMIO vs DMA BAR-backed MMIO carries small control/register accesses. DMA moves bulk buffers between host memory and the device. PCIe vs DMA vs NoC PCIe is the host link. DMA is an engine/protocol for moving buffers over an addressable path. The NoC is the internal device fabric connecting tiles and memories. SQ/CQ vs doorbell/MSI-X SQ and CQ hold durable command/completion records. A doorbell and MSI-X only notify the other side that records are ready. IOVA vs CPU pointer vs physical address A CPU pointer belongs to a process, a physical address names RAM, and an IOVA is the device-visible address produced by the DMA/IOMMU mapping. MVM vs GEMM vs MAC A MAC is one arithmetic primitive. MVM multiplies a matrix by one vector. GEMM multiplies matrices and is tiled into many MVM-like operations plus partial-sum accumulation. Nominal ADC bits vs ENOB Nominal bits describe output code width. ENOB describes useful measured resolution after noise and distortion; it usually changes with sample rate, range, and PVT. Bandwidth vs latency vs throughput Bandwidth is transfer capacity, latency is time for one request, and throughput is completed work per time. Improving one does not guarantee improvement in the others. Quantization error vs transport error ADC, low precision, and calibration affect numerical accuracy. PCIe AER, DMA, ECC, and queue faults affect reliable delivery and execution. SPDX vs SBOM vs LICENSE/NOTICE SPDX is a machine-readable standard; an SBOM is a component inventory; LICENSE and NOTICE carry legal text and attribution. None substitutes automatically for the others. Driver decision

entries.heading: Does an Analog CIM board need a user-mode driver (UMD) and kernel-mode driver (KMD)?
entries.text: Terms here UMD = User-Mode Driver KMD = Kernel-Mode Driver HAL = Hardware Abstraction Layer UAPI = kernel/userspace contract Architecture conclusion Production PCIe: yes A bus-mastering accelerator should not trust a process with raw physical addresses or unrestricted register access. Keep policy, graph execution, artifact parsing, and batching in a UMD/runtime. Keep isolation, DMA mappings, interrupt ownership, reset, power, device lifetime, firmware loading, and the stable Linux UAPI in a KMD. Firmware must validate the device-side command contract again. A simulator or tightly controlled lab prototype can use a smaller path while the hardware protocol is still moving. Software-only No KMD Use the same HAL against functional, statistical, and cycle backends. Mock BARs, queues, interrupts, reset, and faults. Best for: compiler and runtime CI Trusted FPGA lab VFIO with an IOMMU Userspace owns BARs, DMA mappings, and interrupts through VFIO. Verify the complete IOMMU group, FLR or reset, and locked-memory limits. Best for: protocol exploration Narrow prototype UIO only for simple MMIO UIO maps device memory and forwards interrupts, but has no IOMMU protection. Do not make it the product path for unrestricted bus-master DMA. Best for: mailbox or Programmed I/O (PIO) loopback Product path Dedicated KMD + UMD/HAL Context-bound buffers, validated queues, MSI-X, reset, AER, firmware, telemetry, permissions, and backward-compatible UAPI. Best for: multi-process deployment Subsystem choice: evaluate Linux drivers/accel before inventing a private device framework. The accelerator subsystem exposes /dev/accel/accel* and reuses DRM infrastructure. A small out-of-tree character driver is acceptable for early board enablement, but its UAPI should still be designed as if it must survive old userspace and new kernels. End-to-end architecture

entries.heading: The board is one backend beneath a stable compiler, artifact, and runtime
entries.text: The simulator and hardware must consume the same executable semantics. Only the HAL transport changes. This keeps model correctness separate from PCIe, firmware, and analog variation bugs. Terms here API = callable source interface ABI = binary layout and behavior HAL = transport-neutral hardware interface Firmware = device-resident control software Model and application PyTorch / ONNX Graph, tensors, shapes, QDQ, preprocessing Compiler Support, partition, lower, schedule, package YOLO application Capture, policy, decode, NMS, results Host userspace Framework plugin ONNX Runtime (ORT) Execution Provider (EP) capability and fallback boundary Runtime Artifact load, session, buffers, queues, events User-Mode Driver (UMD) / HAL Hardware Abstraction Layer: discover, query, allocate, submit, wait, trace Stable Linux user-space API (UAPI): ioctl + mmap + poll/eventfd + dma-buf Host kernel Kernel-Mode Driver (KMD) contexts Ownership, lifetime, permissions, Application Binary Interface (ABI) Memory manager Pin/import, IOMMU map, Input-Output Virtual Address (IOVA), fence PCI driver BAR, DMA, MSI-X, reset, AER, firmware PCIe contract: configuration + BAR MMIO + DMA + MSI-X Device control Endpoint + boot ROM Identity, reset, mailbox, firmware load Firmware scheduler Validate, queue, dispatch, complete, recover Trace and health Cycles, bytes, stalls, saturation, faults Device data plane DMA + SRAM Direct Memory Access and Static RAM stage inputs, outputs, commands, and partial sums Analog MVM Matrix-Vector Multiplication: program, encode, integrate, ADC, reconstruct Digital engines Elementwise, resize, activation, reduction, fallback Artifact ABI Application Binary Interface from compiler to runtime and firmware. target + program + constants + commands + debug map Linux UAPI User-space API from User-Mode Driver (UMD) to Kernel-Mode Driver (KMD). caps + contexts + buffers + queues + waits + faults Firmware ABI Application Binary Interface from KMD queues to device validation and execution. SQ/CQ + mailbox + opcodes + status + trace Whole-chain verification

entries.heading: Test one contract at a time before asking the complete board to run a model
entries.text: QEMU is useful, but it is not an analog Compute-in-Memory (CIM) simulator by default. Use it to boot a supported host or controller CPU and its software.
